Alongside the creation of the National Artificial Intelligence Council, Marcos' executive order also adopts the country's governance framework for AI policy formation and development

items: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed an executive order establishing a national AI governance framework and creating the National Artificial Intelligence Council (NAIC) to oversee its implementation.
The AI Governance Framework includes elements such as ethics, standards, risk-based policies, and resources to ensure responsible AI development and use in the Philippines.
The NAIC will coordinate the implementation of the framework, monitor progress, and review it every two years, with a focus on enhancing institutional capabilities and regulatory measures.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has signed an executive order adopting a national artificial intelligence governance framework alongside creating the National Artificial Intelligence Council to oversee and guide implementation of AI tech in the country.

EO 131 was signed on Thursday, November 12, and adopts the AI Governance Framework for the Philippines as the country’s “national strategic guide for policy formulation, regulatory coordination, institutional development, capacity-building, and other governance measures necessary to support and strengthen” the Philippine AI ecosystem.

The NAIC, meanwhile, was set up to serve as the inter-agency body responsible for the coordination, facilitation, and monitoring of Al Governance Framework implementations, alongside other related initiatives.
NAIC will be chaired by an executive secretary, while the Department of Economy, Planning, and Development (DEPDev) secretary will act as vice chair.

Alongside the chairperson of the Commission on Higher Education and the director general of the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority, members of NAIC include the secretaries of the following institutions:

items: Department of Science and Technology
Department of Information and Communications Technology
Department of Trade and Industry
Department of Finance
Department of Education
Department of Labor and Employment
Department of Budget and Management

blocks.text: Further, a representative from the private sector will be appointed by the President for the three-year term with one reappointment.
The AI Governance Framework of the Philippines comprises four interconnected elements: ethics and principles, standards and assurance, a risk-based policy toolkit, and enabling resources.

As per the framework, AI development, deployment, and use must be human-centric, transparent, explainable, secure, safe, pursue fairness and equity, have accountability and integrity measures, and allow for sustainable development.

The framework calls for appropriate technical standards, testing and evaluation, a conformity assessment, interoperability, and other assurance mechanisms to be set up to “support the responsible, safe, secure, and trustworthy development and use of Al.”

Meanwhile, under the risk-based policy toolkit section, the framework noted that Al governance measures should be “proportionate to the nature, context, and level of risk, and may include general and sector-specific guidelines, Al impact assessments, regulatory sandboxes, review of existing laws and regulations, and coordinated complaint and grievance mechanisms.” It added that regulators that currently work in this sector should continue exercising their respective mandates under applicable laws.

Lastly, the framework noted that the government shall “strengthen institutions, data research and development, capabilities, infrastructure, and demand generation to support responsible Al development, deployment, and use.”

A number of technical working groups will be set up to facilitate implementation of the framework, with concerned government agencies to be required to submit and regularly update the required information quarterly.

The NAIC, through DEPDev, will lead overall monitoring and reporting efforts on the implementation of the Al Governance Framework and will be required to report on the status and progress of AI Governance Framework implementation within 30 days from the end of each quarter, alongside any other reports requested by the President.

The NAIC shall review the Al Governance Framework at least once every two years — earlier if needed based on any significant technological, regulatory, or market developments — and will recommend amendments or other measures as necessary to the President.
This executive order takes effect immediately upon its publication in the Official Gazette or a newspaper of general circulation.

articles.title: DEFA 2026: Three ways it benefits Filipinos
articles.summary: At the ASEAN Business & Investment Summit held today at the Solaire Resort Grand Ballroom, H.E. DTI Secretary Cristina Roque announced that the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA) had…

blocks.text: At the ASEAN Business & Investment Summit held today at the Solaire Resort Grand Ballroom, H.E. DTI Secretary Cristina Roque announced that the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA) had just been signed and will be presented to the President tomorrow.
What is DEFA?

This agreement has lasting implications for the digital economy across the ASEAN, from ecommerce, cybersecurity, AI implementation, and more. DEFA has one goal, which is to accelerate regional digital integration and double the ASEAN digital economy’s value from USD 1 trillion to USD 2 trillion by 2030 This agreement has been in the pipeline since 2023 and has been signed today in Manila, with the Philippines as the host country for the 49th ASEAN.
Regional ecommerce reach for local MSMEs

The new agreement will allow small and medium enterprises to easily tap the regional market across ASEAN with less friction, without navigating the different local rules of trade. It essentially breaks down the walls of ecommerce platforms so that online shops can also sell easily across different countries through the usual channels like Shopee, Lazada, and TikTok Shop. It streamlines processes as well as regional payments.

“Platforms no longer have to build separate legal, data privacy, and consumer protection workflows for every individual country. Shared regional rules on electronic contracts, intellectual property, and source code protection lower administrative and compliance overhead.”
Cybersecurity enhancement

With an enhanced trade agreement, this also brings about stronger cybersecurity measures and upgrades through transnational cooperation against scams and other cybersecurity threats. From a platforms standpoint, it promotes shared best practices to establish real standards so every country is on the same page when it comes to securing online platforms.
Cross-border digital payment ease

Imagine having lower fees when transacting online in Thailand or Vietnam? Imagine an OFW within ASEAN easily remitting money with less overhead costs? DEFA essentially makes digital payments more accessible across the entire ASEAN, treating each member country as a real neighbor with better benefits.

articles.title: Ombudsman Remulla questions funding for projects without plans in House-approved 2027 budget
articles.summary: Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Saturday criticized the House-approved version of the proposed 2027 national budget, questioning the allocation of funds for projects that have no concrete plans.

blocks.text: Published November 14, 2026 5:31pm
Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Saturday criticized the House-approved version of the proposed 2027 national budget, questioning the allocation of funds for projects that have no concrete plans.
The People’s Budget Coalition (PBC) has raised concerns over alleged budget insertions worth more than P1 trillion in the House-approved General Appropriations Bill (GAB).
“Nagbago yung attitude ng Congress sa budget, noong araw… Hindi ganoon. You stay humble,” Remulla, a former Cavite congressman, said on his radio program on dzRH.
(The attitude of Congress toward the budget has changed. In the past, it was not like that. You stay humble.)
“Makuha yung pondo, bahala na kung papaano gagawin… walang preparation. Walang design. Walang specific plan. Walang specific comprehensive plan,” he added.
(They secure the funding, then leave it to others to figure out how to carry out the project… There is no preparation, no design, no specific plan, no comprehensive plan.)

Remulla said some local politicians who are not allied with their respective governors may seek separate funding allocations to avoid going through the Provincial Development Council (PDC) and the Regional Development Council (RDC).
“Dapat diyan, yung pulitika diyan, ma-neutralize,” Remulla said.
(The political considerations there should be neutralized.)

GMA News has sought comment from the offices of House Speaker Faustino "Bojie" Dy III and House Committee on Appropriations Chairperson Mikaela Suansing, representative of Nueva Ecija's first district.
Dy had previously expressed willingness to disclose supporting documents to the PBC to promote greater transparency following the group's concerns over the proposed budget.
“Walang dapat itago kung walang ginagawang mali. At walang dapat katakutan kung ang layunin ay maglingkod nang tapat,” Dy said in an earlier statement.
(There is nothing to hide if nothing wrong is being done. And there is nothing to fear if the intention is to serve honestly.)
Political turncoatism
On another topic, Remulla criticized politicians who switch political affiliations depending on who is sitting president.

“Ako talaga, ang tingin ko sa Pilipinas, we have to shift to a completely representative democracy. We create cult figures, and we create people that we look up to, na ina-idolize natin blindly. In the end, tao lang ‘yan eh. It is the institution that needs to be stronger. Kailangan lakasan na natin yung institution,” Remulla said.

(I believe the Philippines needs to shift to a completely representative democracy. We create cult figures and people whom we look up to and blindly idolize. In the end, they are just people. It is the institution that needs to be stronger. We need to strengthen our institutions.)
“Dapat lumakas yung parties. Tsaka bawal yung balimbing dapat. Kung yan ang party mo, diyan ka na dapat,” he said.
(The political parties should become stronger. Political turncoatism should also not be allowed. If that is your party, you should stay with it.)
Remulla himself has been affiliated with different political parties in the past, including the Nacionalista Party and Lakas-CMD.
He described the practice of frequently switching political parties as wrong, saying that political affiliations should be based on principles.

“With due respect lang, may Partido Federal ngayon, mga member diyan, mga dating Liberal Party, dating Lakas… lumipat-lipat na sila ng partido tuwing kung sino man ang presidenta, kakampihan nila. Mali,” Remulla said.

(With all due respect, there are members of Partido Federal who used to belong to the Liberal Party and Lakas. They have switched political parties depending on who the president is and whom they choose to support. That is wrong.)
Remulla also criticized the minimum qualifications for presidential candidates, saying that they should at least be high school graduates. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: ASEAN’s ‘talk shop’ reputation meets Filipinos’ price worries in Manila
articles.summary: Southeast Asian leaders meet in Manila on Sunday, November 15, to cap the Philippines' ASEAN year that's been knocked off course by the US-Israeli war with Iran, a conflict that drove up fuel prices…

blocks.text: November 14, 2026 | 5:28pm

MANILA, Philippines — Southeast Asian leaders meet in Manila on Sunday, November 15, to cap the Philippines' ASEAN year that's been knocked off course by the US-Israeli war with Iran, a conflict that drove up fuel prices globally and made the resulting price squeeze a top issue for the bloc.

Opening the last foreign ministers’ meeting of Manila’s chairship on Saturday, November 14, Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro said the year had brought “unprecedented headwinds,” led by the crisis in the Middle East, and that the Philippines had kept “pivoting our course” in response.

Philippine households continue to be hit hard by the sprawling conflict in the Middle East, which has driven up fuel prices. Inflation accelerated to 7.8% in October, the highest since February 2023, according to the Philippine Statistics Authority.

High prices of goods were also the issue Filipinos most often wanted the country to push as ASEAN host, named by 19% surveyed in a Social Weather Stations poll taken in late March and shared again this week, just above the West Philippine Sea.
ASEAN members imported about half their oil from the Middle East before the war, which began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February and effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz.

An ASEAN pact meant to let members share fuel during supply cuts is still not in force though it remains high on the agenda this week. Only four or five of the bloc's 11 members have ratified it as of late October and any sharing under it would be voluntary and on commercial terms.

Asked how the government would measure the success of the Philippines' year as ASEAN chair, Dominic Xavier Imperial, the government's spokesperson for its ASEAN chairship, acknowledged the region was "still feeling the impacts of the Middle East crisis" and that "additional measures" on energy would be forthcoming.
Tangible benefits

Lazaro told her fellow foreign ministers on Saturday that ASEAN’s work “cannot be measured solely by the meetings we convene or the documents that we adopt,” but by whether it can “deliver tangible benefits to our peoples.”

ASEAN leaders’ main economic deliverable is a region-wide digital economy agreement, due to be signed at the summit, that sets common rules for e-commerce, data and digital payments. Lazaro said it would give small businesses “a smoother path… to sell beyond their home markets.”
The year’s setbacks went beyond the war, the DFA chief added, citing “natural calamities that besieged our nations” and “uncertainties that tested the norms of multilateralism.”
“We must also be clear-eyed about the work ahead,” Lazaro said.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in March said he asked fellow leaders whether they saw the need to postpone the bloc’s scheduled May summit due to the energy crisis brought by the Middle East conflict. Eventually, the government scaled down and shortened the summit into a "bare-bones" program lasting a day and a half.
Manila had made “the difficult decision to recalibrate” its hosting, cutting non-essential activities and moving some meetings online, Marcos told the Cebu summit in May.
ASEAN’s limits

ASEAN, often dismissed as a “talk shop,” holds more than a thousand meetings a year across different levels, but many of the statements and work plans produced are never fully carried out, Anoulak Kittikhoun, a former chief executive of the Mekong River Commission, and Joanne Lin, a former ASEAN Secretariat official, wrote in a column for the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy.

"Its current system—comprising more than a thousand meetings annually, overlapping working groups and siloed sectoral processes—often generates activity without delivering meaningful outcomes," they wrote.
Additionally, decisions made by the bloc need the consent of all 11 members, and the bloc does not interfere in members’ internal affairs.

As a result, many ASEAN agreements are non-binding and enforcement is weak or absent, researchers Mark Anthony Barral and Francis Mark Quimba wrote for the state think tank Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS).

"The differing threat perceptions and the varying levels of economic developments also lead to divisions among member states, hindering consensus-building and effective policy implementation," the researchers wrote.
On top of this, the "principle of non-interference ... limit ASEAN’s ability to provide a prompt response on emerging issues, such as the tension in Myanmar," they wrote.

articles.title: DICT: Additional cybersecurity measures in place at ASEAN 2026 media center
articles.summary: The Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) on Saturday said it was implementing additional security protocols at the 49th ASEAN Summit International Media Center (IMC) in…

blocks.text: Published November 14, 2026 5:23pm

The Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) on Saturday said it was implementing additional security protocols at the 49th ASEAN Summit International Media Center (IMC) in Pasay City following reports of data breaches involving government agencies.
"Since we're putting additional security protocols, [I] would say it lessens the latency for the internet speed," DICT Secretary Robert Joseph de Claro told reporters.
"Considering the importance of the ASEAN for our country, we needed to take additional security measures to ensure that the data and everything is secured coming from the center," he added.
De Claro made the statement after relatively slow Wi-Fi speeds were observed at the IMC.
At least 10 government agencies submitted personal data breach notifications to the National Privacy Commission (NPC) on November 10.
The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) said it had identified those responsible for the data breach.
No specific threat
Meanwhile, Presidential Communications Office Secretary Lino Cayetano said authorities had not monitored any "specific threat" so far.
"There's no one specific threat, but it's really heightened alert and focus on making sure that we do a proper assessment and evaluation [s]o there are no breaches," Cayetano said.
He added that additional security protocols would be installed within the day.
"There's no identified threat today. But we are preparing that it might be AI-driven. So, with that, we need to put additional protocols," Cayetano said.
De Claro also criticized protesters whom he accused of "attacking the government," calling them "anti-people."

"The government is supposed to provide services to the people. And if you try to attack the institutions that are supposed to provide the service, whether it's emergency or just regular service, then you're anti-people," De Claro said.
"We are in the democracy but there are also ways and means and a channel for you to lodge your complaints," he added. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Hungary: Millions in hidden cash found in Orban graft probe
articles.summary: Investigators discovered bundles of banknotes buried in forests and concealed in buildings. The money was seized during an investigation into a former minister accused of accepting millions in bribes.

image.caption: Former Hungarian Development Minister Miklos Sesztak is suspected of accepting millions in bribes during Viktor Orban's rule [FILE: July 30, 2017]Image: Robert Szaniszlo/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Hungarian authorities have recovered nearly $20 million (€17.7 million) in hidden cash during a corruption investigation into a former minister under ex-Prime Minister Viktor Orban.

The country's newly established National Asset Recovery and Protection Office said Friday that investigators discovered the money during searches linked to former National Development Minister Miklos Sesztak.
The discovery is part of a sweeping anti-corruption campaign launched by Prime Minister Peter Magyar, who defeated Orban in April's parliamentary election.
Where did Hungarian investigators find the hidden cash?
The money was discovered during two days of searches in the capital, Budapest, and three Hungarian counties.

Investigators found large quantities of cash buried in forests, concealed in agricultural buildings, warehouses and residential properties, as well as stored in an expensive safe at a secluded location.
The recovered money included 5.07 billion Hungarian forints (€13.3 million, $15.3 million), €2.66 million (€2.9 million) and $1.26 million (€1.08 million).
According to Finance Minister Andras Karman, 12 employees of the Hungarian State Treasury spent eight hours counting the banknotes using five counting machines.
The agency also released a video showing investigators kneeling beside large piles of bundled cash and digging into the ground in what appeared to be a forest at night.
Authorities said the seized money had been deposited into an account belonging to the Hungarian state treasury.
What corruption allegations does former minister Sesztak face?
Sesztak served as Orban's national development minister between 2014 and 2018.

He is suspected of accepting more than $37 million (€33 million) in bribes and kickbacks connected to the purchase of overpriced used buses by state-owned transport companies and state construction projects.
The former minister was taken into police custody in late September. He has denied wrongdoing.
His lawyer, Gabor Papp, so far did not respond to a request for comment on the latest discovery.
How has Hungary's Prime Minister Magyar reacted?
Magyar described the recovered cash as a turning point in his government's efforts to tackle alleged corruption under Orban.
The discovery "officially marks the end of the Fidesz-KDNP mafia," he wrote on Facebook, referring to Orban's former governing coalition.
"As of today, Viktor Orbán is a proven mafia boss. A fallen mafia boss. And Fidesz is a criminal organization," Magyar added.

blocks.caption: Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar has launched a sweeping anti-corruption campaign targeting alleged abuses under his predecessor Viktor Orban [FILE: November 10, 2026]Image: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

blocks.text: Magyar's center-right, pro-European Tisza party won a landslide victory in April, ending Orban's 16-year rule.
The new prime minister has pledged to repair Hungary's relations with the European Union, which had been strained by years of disputes under Orban.
His government established the anti-corruption agency with investigative and prosecutorial powers to pursue suspected corruption and misuse of public funds.
Who else is being investigated in Hungary's corruption crackdown?
Magyar has dubbed the campaign "Operation Purgatory."
Several other senior figures from Orban's time in office have been detained as part of separate investigations.
Among them is former central bank governor and economy minister Gyorgy Matolcsy, once considered one of Orban's closest allies.

Matolcsy is being investigated over the alleged misuse of a central bank foundation that received 288 billion forints ($818 million, €787 million) in public assets. He and other former officials under investigation have denied wrongdoing.
Police also detained Orban's younger brother earlier this week as part of an investigation into suspected human trafficking and influence peddling.

blocks.caption: Viktor Orban's younger brother was detained as part of an investigation into suspected human trafficking and influence peddling [FILE: November 9, 2026]Image: Viktor Veres/HVG/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Orban has condemned the investigations as political "tyranny" aimed at removing him from Hungary's political landscape. He has described his brother's detention as an act of political revenge.
According to a survey by pollster Median published by news website HVG this week, 70% of respondents considered the anti-corruption campaign "very important."
A separate Median survey showed support for Orban's Fidesz party had fallen to 16% of voters by November, roughly half its level before the April election.

articles.title: US loses measles-elimination status after 26 years, WSJ reports
articles.summary: The Pan American Health Organization has reportedly stripped the US of its measles-elimination status after 26 years, as the country battles its worst outbreaks in more than three decades.

image.caption: Canada, Spain and the UK also recently lost their measles-free status after WHO reviewsImage: Paul Weaver/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Pan American Health Organization has revoked the United States' measles-elimination status, ending a 26-year run, after finding the country failed to stop the virus spreading continuously for more than a year, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday, citing people familiar with the matter.
A source close to the process told CNN that an independent commission of experts reporting to PAHO's director concluded the US no longer qualified.
What do we know?

PAHO reviewed Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) evidence on whether one strain had circulated uninterrupted for 12 months or longer, a sign of local spread rather than imported cases. A source familiar with the CDC's findings told Reuters the agency found 12 months of continuous transmission.

The US had held elimination status since 2000. This year, however, the CDC has recorded 5,182 confirmed cases as of Thursday – across 45 states, New York City and Washington, D.C. This is more than double 2025's total of 2,289.

About 7,500 people have been infected and 13 have died since 2025. Nearly all of this year's cases involve people who were unvaccinated or whose status is unknown, and roughly one in nine patients were hospitalized, CNN reported, citing the CDC.

This period has been marked with increased vaccine hesitancy under US Health Secretary ​Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who for years shown skepticism about the safety of measles vaccines, without scientific proof.
Is the US experiencing a vaccine crisis?
Is measles preventable?
Experts point to the fact that measles is preventable through vaccination.

"It is a fully preventable disease. It is unconscionable that we have this amount of measles," said Noel Brewer, a University of North Carolina public health professor who chairs an independent advisory panel on measles. He presented the CDC's report to PAHO on Tuesday, Reuters reported.
Johns Hopkins epidemiologist William Moss told Reuters the loss damages America's reputation as a public health leader and means large outbreaks will continue.
CDC Director Erica Schwartz, before the decision, said that the agency would keep working with states to encourage vaccination.
To regain the status, a country must end transmission and stay outbreak-free for at least 12 months.

articles.title: Microsoft says all services working again
articles.summary: US tech giant Microsoft says it has fixed problems that led to a global outage of its services. The glitch severely disrupted online communications in businesses and governments for more than 24…

image.caption: The Outlook e-mailing app was one of the services affected by the outageImage: Md Mamun Miah/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: The US technology conglomerate Microsoft said on Saturday that a more than 24-hour global outage affecting its Microsoft 365 applications used by businesses and governments across the world has now ended.
"We ​have completed our efforts to address ​the underlying issue of the ⁠incident ​and ​restored service to ​the remaining impacted ‌customers and regions," ​the ⁠company posted on X.
Microsoft applications such as Teams, Outlook and Copilot were all hit by the outage, leading to communications problems in scores of countries.
The company has said it was "not aware" of any outside interference that could have been behind the outage, blaming the problem on server issues.
The disruption was one of the longest in Microsoft's history and the second this year.
Worldwide Microsoft outage causes widespread disruption
What effects did the Microsoft outage have?
The outage, which began around 1725 UTC on Thursday according to web testing and network diagnostics company ​Ookla, affected government agencies and businesses across much of the world.
It made it impossible to carry out activities such as sending emails and holding online meetings.

Germany was no exception, with a spokesperson for its Federal Ministry for Digital Transformation and Government Modernization saying that while the outage did not have a major impact on federal government functions, it did significantly affect ​German businesses.
Britain's state health service (NHS) was also severely affected, with personnel forced to have recourse to paper records rather than those stored online.
Altogether, there were more than 7.4 million reports of problems worldwide logged by Downdetector, which monitors online outages.
The disruption highlights the widespread and perilous reliance of governments and businesses on a very small number of Big Tech companies.
Tthe problems at Microsoft are so far believed to be unconnected with the major communications outage that has affected US aviation.

articles.title: Can the Carney government end homelessness? (Not on its own)

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks about funding for homelessness and health care as Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew looks on. Manitoba is the first province announced to be working with the federal government on its initiative to end homelessness. (John Woods/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Mark Carney is not the first prime minister to embrace an ambitious commitment about homelessness. He is not even the first prime minister to do so in the last 10 years.

In 2017, Justin Trudeau's government released its national housing strategy. As part of a broader plan for housing, the Trudeau government set a goal of reducing "chronic" homelessness by half over the subsequent decade — at the time, an estimated 25,000 people were said to be chronically homeless.
Three years later, in a speech from the throne, the Trudeau government went further, stating that it was now focused on "entirely eliminating chronic homelessness in Canada."

However worthy the goal, and whatever efforts the Trudeau government put toward achieving that goal, it was not met. A progress report released by the federal government last December acknowledged that there had been a 34 per cent increase in chronic homelessness among shelter users between 2016 and 2024.
Carney has committed himself to a more ambitious target — putting Canada on a path to end all homelessness within 10 years.

items: Can Canada end homelessness in the next 10 years?
'Absolutely' possible: Vancouver, Victoria mayors back Ottawa's bid
Montreal mayor endorses PM's plan to end homelessness

blocks.text: "There's no simple answer. This is a hard problem," Carney said in Winnipeg last week. "And hard problems demand the humility to learn from previous well-intentioned efforts that have fallen short. And it demands the resolve to build on what's succeeded."

Homelessness is hardly a new problem, but it was in the wake of the pandemic that homelessness came to the fore as a visible and salient concern in communities across Canada — exemplified by the issue of encampments in public places.

A national homelessness enumeration in 2025 found that more than 65,000 people were homeless on a given night in Canada, a 59 per cent increase over five years. The share of unhoused people living in unsheltered locations, including encampments, had also increased from 23 per cent to 27 per cent.

The underlying factors that might have contributed to the current situation are numerous and thorny: a longstanding lack of government funding for new social housing, an insufficient supply of rental housing, the disruption of the pandemic, the post-pandemic spike in inflation and the increasing cost of living, the opioid epidemic.

"It was on a rapid but slow burn from 1995 and then it hit 2018, 2019 and the housing crisis, pandemic, affordability crisis, toxic drug supply — all came together to create the problem we're seeing today," said Tim Richter, president and CEO of the Canadian Alliance to End Homelessness.
In the face of a problem that was driven by overlapping crises and challenges, the Trudeau government's actions obviously weren't enough to solve the problem.

Nick Falvo, a researcher and consultant who focuses on homelessness, said the national housing strategy lacked an emphasis on supportive housing — "deeply subsidized housing with a lot of social work support."
Richter says the Trudeau-era plan failed to create enough deeply affordable housing of the sort that people on income-support programs could afford.
Carney's homelessness agenda
The Carney plan maintains two pieces of the Trudeau strategy.

As laid out in this month's budget, the Carney government plans to renew funding for the Canada Housing Benefit, a rent supplement for low-income Canadians. Both the Canadian Alliance to End Homelessness and Falvo have argued that an expanded and better-targeted CHB could do even more to reduce homelessness. The Carney government is also maintaining a program — Reaching Home — that provides direct funding to communities to support efforts to reduce homelessness.

On top of that the government is adding three capital funds: $10 billion for supportive and transitional housing, $5 billion for "integrated supports" projects and $2 billion for new health-care infrastructure. The government is also directing new funding to Build Canada Homes in hopes of boosting the construction of non-market housing.
Carney's mission to end homelessness kicks off with joint effort in Manitoba

More broadly, the Carney government is talking about a "renewed partnership" with the provinces, one in which the federal government would provide funding for capital (i.e. building things), while the provinces would fund operations and services.

"The Carney government's announcement is different in a couple of ways. One is they've set themselves a much bigger target," Richter said. "But they've also led with a major capital infusion.… And this conversation with the provinces. So their first steps are different than the Trudeau steps, which I think is important from a first-step point of view."
The challenge that Falvo sees is operational funding — the ongoing expenses that provincial governments will have to be willing to cover.
"I would say [the Carney government's plan] was a very impressive down payment. It showed great leadership," Falvo said. "I'll be very interested to see what happens with the provinces."

The federal government has at least already found one province that was eager for a renewed partnership. In Manitoba, the Carney government committed $800 million toward the construction of 2,000 supportive and transitional homes and $200 million toward a new centre for mental health and addictions. The province will provide funding for the operation of both and cover half of the cost of constructing the centre.
'Canadians want to do something'

In Winnipeg, Carney acknowledged that governments have spent "decades" trying to address homelessness. But, he said, "too often those efforts have been inadequately resourced, poorly co-ordinated and not sustained."

Richter co-authored a proposal earlier this year for a new national accord on housing, which would align all levels of government on solving the larger crisis of housing availability and affordability. On homelessness, Richter says the conversation between federal and provincial governments should focus not just on dollars, but on approaches, priorities and desired outcomes.

Absolutely eliminating the phenomenon of homelessness is unrealistic, Richter says. But he and the CAEH talk about achieving "functional zero," whereby a community is able to house more people than will become homeless in a given month — a situation in which homelessness is rare, brief and not recurring.

If it was somewhat surprising to see the Carney government — a government that has seemed resolutely focused on large macroeconomic issues — use its second budget to make such a headline-grabbing commitment to reduce homelessness, it's perhaps not a surprise that governments are feeling some pressure to do something.
"My theory is that his government started to realize that voters were growing quite unhappy with visible manifestations of poverty, homelessness and social disorder," Falvo said.
How do the feds plan to end homelessness in Canada?

A survey commissioned by the CAEH earlier this year found that 66 per cent of Canadians encountered homelessness at least once per week, 39 per cent considered it a "very" or "extremely" serious problem and 60 per cent believe the problem has gotten worse in their community in the last few years.
(Earlier this year, Carney also told the Globe and Mail that he was reading Encampment by Maggie Helwig, which won this year's Shaughnessy Cohen Prize for political writing.)
But if the problem has become very visible, governments could also think not only about the long term, but also about what they can do to show visible progress in the near term, Richter suggests.

"If you look at the polling, it says like Canadians want to do something. They want to do the right thing," he said. "They feel compassion. They understand a lot of it is housing. It's also mental health and addiction. But they want to see a difference."

If the years since the last ambitious goal to reduce homelessness have unfortunately seen the problem get worse, that has perhaps at least created an even greater impetus for governments to finally solve the problem.
