articles.title: Hundreds of children in England prescribed weight-loss jabs, figures show
articles.summary:
Exclusive: investigation finds prescriptions for children under 12, as experts stress need for specialist supervision and long-term monitoring

Hundreds of children in England are receiving…

blocks.text: Hundreds of children in England are receiving prescriptions for GLP-1 medications, including some younger than 12, the Guardian can reveal.

GLP-1 medications were initially developed to help people with type 2 diabetes control their blood sugar levels, but have since become a popular slimming aid, with products such as Wegovy and Mounjaro becoming household names.
While social media is awash with adults who have lost weight with GLP-1s, data shows a number of children are also being prescribed them.
A Guardian investigation has revealed that in the financial year 2025-26 there were 419 prescriptions issued to children under the age of 18, 10 of which were for children under the age of 12.
And in the four months from April to July this year, 341 prescriptions for GLP-1s were issued to children, 15 of whom were under the age of 12.
The figures, obtained from the NHS Business Services Authority through freedom of information requests, relate to prescriptions in England and dispensed in a community setting anywhere in the UK.
However, they do not cover those prescribed and dispensed via private prescriptions, in prisons, and in hospitals, meaning the figures are likely to be a considerable underestimate.

One private clinic for children has previously revealed it has more than 200 patients receiving the jabs. It is also unclear whether the GLP-1 figures reflect medications that are being given primarily for weight loss.

Martin Whyte, a professor of metabolic medicine at the University of Surrey, said the number of prescriptions was still small relative to the scale of childhood obesity, but those taking the drugs needed long-term change to their lifestyles.
He said: “The important thing is that children who start them do so within specialist services, with support for diet, growth and wellbeing, and a plan for the long term.

“That includes regular monitoring of growth and puberty, nutritional intake, mental health and eating behaviours, and side effects. This matters partly because we know weight tends to return when the drugs are stopped, and partly because we still have limited data on use over many years in growing young people.”

The rising use of GLP-1s comes as levels of childhood obesity are increasing. Figures from the National Child Measurement Programme show that 10.7% of reception-year children (ages 4 and 5) are obese, while that rises to 22.8% for children in year 6 (ages 10 and 11).
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), 400 million children and adolescents aged between five and 19 were overweight in 2024, including 170 million living with obesity.
As part of efforts for early intervention, the NHS began piloting Complications from Excess Weight (CEW) clinics from 2021, aimed at children aged two to 16 with severe obesity.
In May, NHS England revealed almost 6,500 children have since been referred to such clinics, including more than 400 younger than four.

Hundreds of young people have received weight-loss medications through such services – although only some CEW clinics can access funding to offer GLP-1s, and these are typically dispensed through hospital pharmacies.

Dr Dunia Ismail, a consultant paediatrician who runs a CEW clinic, said experts were now looking at widening the use of GLP-1s in such settings. “We have been sticking to 12 [years], although now we are looking at expanding that to eight-plus once licence-approved,” she said.
Last month, new global guidelines from the WHO stated obesity medications, including GLP-1s, should not be given to children under the age of 10.

However, recent data from a trial involving 165 children aged 6 to under 12 – run by the pharmaceutical company Novo Nordisk, which produces Wegovy and Victoza – has suggested GLP-1s can help young children with obesity.

Julian Hamilton-Shield, a professor in diabetes and metabolic endocrinology and a clinician at the Bristol Complications CEW clinic, said typically children who receive semaglutide at CEW clinics had been unable to lose weight through standard dietary and nutritional advice and psychological support.

“Probably, in the vast majority of cases, they have a secondary comorbidity such as type 2 diabetes, obstructive sleep apnoea, liver disease, intracranial hypertension – you name it, they’ve got it,” he said. “So it’s been used as an adjunct after standard therapies haven’t really helped. However, it is used quite frequently and it is a very effective drug.”
Hamilton-Shield stressed GLP-1 medications were given to children who have very high excess weight. “You’d call it morbid obesity if you were classifying it as adults,” he said.
The use of GLP-1s in children has reignited a debate about the drivers of childhood obesity, but experts say it is important to avoid blaming patients or their families.

“We’re a health service that delivers health to the people who require it. We’re not one that makes moral judgments about people,” said Hamilton-Shield. “Nobody’s saying that every child who’s a bit heavy should have a GLP-1.”

Hamilton-Shield added: “These children and young people are from very complex backgrounds, have enormous lack of self-esteem. They’re not attending school. They’ve got all these complications. They’ve got all the stigma. And when you actually give them a drug that helps them to lose maybe 25, 30kg, [it is] the first time they feel they have any agency in their lives at all, and that will have a transformative effect in its own right.”

Ismail also stressed the importance of GLP-1s for children. “We know now that obesity is not a choice, it’s a condition,” she said. “We’re giving them GLP-1s because there is nothing else you can do at this stage. Otherwise, they will die young, they will have heart disease, they will have diabetes … It’s just terrible what could happen to them if we don’t.”

articles.title: Tout offers £1m of U2 tickets on StubHub, raising questions about ‘bot’ clampdown
articles.summary:
Artists and industry figures call for culture secretary to ‘shut down the touts’ by outlawing resale for profit

One tout is advertising £1m of tickets for U2’s long-awaited 2027 tour through…

blocks.text: One tout is advertising £1m of tickets for U2’s long-awaited 2027 tour through StubHub, raising questions about the website’s condemnation of professional ticket traders who use “bot” software to scoop up tickets and exploit genuine fans.
Seats for the four-night London leg of the Irish band’s The Greatest Show on Earth tour sold out last week, shortly after going on sale.
Fans chasing tickets appear to have been beaten to the punch by prolific touts using sites such as StubHub to charge eye-watering mark-ups.
StubHub listings for U2’s gigs at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London show more than 2,000 tickets listed by a single tout despite strict limits on how many can be purchased by each buyer.
Vladyslav Skrypka, who claims to be based in Harlow, Essex, advertised more than 1,800 tickets for one of the nights alone, with some on sale for more than four times face value.
If all of his tickets were to sell for the sums listed, Skrypka would stand to make more than £1m.

The findings come amid clamour from artists and music industry figures for the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, to move forward with plans that she outlined a year ago to “shut down the touts’ racket” by outlawing resale for profit.
A ticket tout ban bill is due to be published during the current parliamentary session, which might not end until well into 2027.
In the meantime, thousands of tickets are still falling into the hands of touts, with some listings bearing the apparent hallmarks of “bot” use, which has been illegal since 2018.

In an interview with the BBC last week, StubHub International’s chief executive, Bob Kupbens, said: “We don’t support bots and we’d love for both the government and primary to do a better job of policing that to make sure those kinds of things don’t happen.”

Adam Webb of the music industry-backed campaign group FanFair Alliance said that the sheer volume of U2 tickets on StubHub indicated either bot use or a practice known as “speculative selling”, where touts agree a sale first, then hope to procure tickets later.
Like the use of bots, “spec” selling is illegal.
Webb said: “StubHub claims all their orders come 100% guaranteed but have they seen evidence of Vladyslav’s receipts?
“Are they not concerned that these tickets may have been acquired by the kind of technology that Mr Kupbens so publicly deplores?”

StubHub International, owned by the US investment group Digital Fuel Capital, did not address specific questions from the Guardian about the listings or possible bot use involved in obtaining the tickets.
The company said it “does not allow speculative selling, and sellers must confirm they own, or have a right to, the tickets they list”.

A spokesperson said: “We are firmly against the use of bots. They are used at the point of primary sale, before tickets reach any resale marketplace, which is why we have called for stronger enforcement at source.”

Ticketmaster disputed the suggestion that it and other primary agents were responsible for bots, saying it blocked 20bn bots a month and spent millions on doing so. It said resale sites, such as Viagogo and StubHub, created the incentive for bot use.

A snapshot of StubHub’s listings, taken this week, showed 7,819 U2 tickets advertised for resale. More than 2,000 were held by Skrypka, with thousands more in the hands of other professional ticket “traders”, an industry term for touts, defined by selling more than 100 tickets a year.
Only 562 were from private sellers, such as fans who can no longer attend or use all of the tickets they bought.

A spokesperson for the Department for Culture, Media and Sport said: “We are fully committed to stamping out ticket touting for good. For too long, fans have been ripped off and we’re determined to right that wrong.
“We are bringing forward legislation in this parliament and will ensure that our measures are truly effective, enforceable and future-proof.”
The Guardian has approached U2 for comment. Messages to social media pages believed to belong to Skrypka went unanswered.

articles.title: Through buri weaving and filmmaking, Sampaloc, Quezon tells a new story
articles.summary: While the women of Sampaloc, Quezon keep the historic buri-weaving tradition alive, the town has also started building on its reputation as a film location to inspire local youth to explore careers…

items: Sampaloc, a town between Mauban and Lucban, is gaining attention as a filming destination, attracting artists like filmmaker Lav Diaz and providing economic benefits through film productions.
The Sine Sampaloc festival aims to develop local filmmaking talent and skills, although it has yet to feature films made by local filmmakers, focusing instead on creative activities for youth.
Alongside its growing film industry, Sampaloc's cultural heritage is preserved through traditional buri weaving, which remains an important part of the local economy and community identity.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Sandwiched between Mauban, the coastal gateway to Cagbalete Island, and Lucban, home of the Pahiyas Festival, the town of Sampaloc is easy to overlook. It remains under the radar while attracting artists such as filmmaker Lav Diaz, who has made the town his second home.

Sampaloc’s appeal is reflected in both its landscape and its people. During the three-month shoot in town for Lav Diaz’s Magellan, locals would spot Mexican lead star Gael Garcia Bernal low-key strolling around town, eating pancit at a neighborhood eatery, and blending in with the community.

The production of Magellan also brought economic benefits to the town. Empty-nesters opened unused bedrooms as homestays to accommodate cast and crew members, while dozens of locals found work as extras and additional film crew.

blocks.caption: Lav Diaz on Cannes-bound ‘Magellan,’ Gael Garcia Bernal, and how he ‘almost died’

blocks.text: Sampaloc has also served as a location for other productions, including the Netflix film Reroute, starring John Arcilla, Sid Lucero, and Cindy Miranda.

In the film, a car breakdown leaves Lucero and Miranda’s characters stranded, eventually leading them to the home of Arcilla’s character. Sampaloc’s landscape helps establish the film’s unsettling atmosphere, demonstrating the range of settings the town can offer filmmakers.

blocks.caption: The house of John Arcilla’s character in Netflix’s ‘Reroute.’ Photo by Marky Ramone Go

blocks.text: Alongside larger productions such as Magellan and smaller independent films shot in Sampaloc, the town hopes to build on its growing appeal as a filming destination.

Instead of just promoting its landscapes to filmmakers, it wants to encourage local youth to explore the different facets of filmmaking, from screenwriting, editing, and production design to acting, directing, and the technical work behind the camera.
Now in its second year, Sine Sampaloc has yet to produce a film made by local filmmakers. The municipality is still working to develop local interest and the skills needed to support film production.
For its second edition, the festival screened 10 selected short films that had won in previous editions of Cinemalaya and the Gawad CCP Para sa Alternatibong Pelikula.

None of the films was shot in Sampaloc or involved local filmmakers or actors. Instead, local participation took other creative forms: students choreographed interpretative dances inspired by each film, while aspiring production designers created tricycle floats representing the movies.

blocks.caption: The vast rice fields can serve as a beautiful backdrop to any film set outside the big city. Photo courtesy of Marboy Sayno

blocks.text: When asked about the inspiration behind Sine Sampaloc, Mayor Nikko Devanadera offered a practical answer. The goal, he explained, is to attract film productions to the town and encourage them to spend locally, while developing a pool of homegrown talent that can support the industry.
“One is to invite film productions and make them spend here. It’s really economic because the youth development aspect is actually skills development, skills pipeline for the productions,” he said.

For Devanadera, the festival’s creative activities serve a practical purpose: preparing young people for opportunities in film production while equipping them with skills they can use in other fields.

The municipality also hopes to expand these opportunities through workshops and equipment for creative work, including video editing and post-production. These skills could open doors beyond film, including in graphic design and visual arts.
High school students who attended the workshops also spent an afternoon with filmmaker Zig Dulay, known for directing Green Bones, who introduced them to the basics of screenwriting.
But filmmaking is not the only creative pursuit Sampaloc hopes to develop.
Somewhere in town, a group of women continues a traditional livelihood that once helped send generations of children to school.
Buri weaving may not attract film production companies, but it remains an important part of Sampaloc’s cultural and economic history.

“During my teens in the ’70s, almost all the kids here in Sampaloc were sent to school through the buri weaving of our parents,” said Hermilina “Aling Tessy” Diaz, 65, who has been weaving buri for almost 50 years.
Today, only a few dozen buri, also called buli, weavers remain in Sampaloc, a far cry from Aling Tessy’s younger years.

“All those kids, of course, grew up to become professionals. Others worked abroad, while others took up different jobs,” she said, explaining how the craft gradually lost its foothold in the local economy.
But buri, Aling Tessy points out, remains part of Sampaloc’s culture.

blocks.caption: A weaver prepares strips of buri palm leaves. Photo by Marky Ramone Go

blocks.text: Buri comes from the leaves of the buri palm, one of the Philippines’ native palms. Its leaves are prized for their strength and versatility and have long been used to make baskets, bags, fans, hats, boxes, and other household items.
In Sampaloc, the remaining weavers have organized themselves as KUMARI Weavers, or “Kababaihang Umaaksyon para sa Maunlad at Responsableng Kababaihang may Integridad.”

The weaving, or paglala, is only one part of the work. Before a single leaf can be woven, the raw buri has to go through a painstaking process: harvesting, stripping, sun-drying, boiling, drying again, flattening, and preparing the strips for weaving. Only then does the actual paglala begin.
Many of the finished bags and baskets sell for only P200 to P400. The obvious question is why they cost so little, considering the time, skill, and labor that go into making each piece.

For buyers, it is worth remembering that bargaining down the price of a handcrafted item can come at the expense of the very artisans whose work deserves support. These women have spent years perfecting their craft. Their work deserves a price that justifies the time and skill involved, not just the cost of materials.

As Sampaloc explores opportunities in filmmaking and other creative industries, its buri weavers remain part of the town’s cultural and economic life. Both represent skills and talent worth investing in.
For KUMARI Weavers, keeping the craft alive means making it a steady source of income and giving younger generations a reason to learn it.
Whether through films or traditional crafts, Sampaloc has a lot of stories and skills to build on. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Nigeria: How the pcoming elections are influeced by the rise of AI disinformation
articles.summary: As Nigeria inches closer to the 2027 polls, the use of artificial intelligence in the electoral process has prompted questions about integrity and institutional readiness. Can Nigerians trust their…

image.caption: Nigeria's 2027 elections take place against the backdrop of AI-driven disinformationImage: Adekunle Ajayi/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Nigeria has just over two months to go to the polls, with incumbent President Bola Tinubu running on a ticket focused on combating raging insecurity and resolving the nation's economic crisis. He faces off against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and senior opposition figure Peter Obi.

The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using artificial intelligence (AI).

Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images, and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died.

The development raises concerns about the body's overall preparedness ahead of the country's upcoming 2027 general elections; instead of making the upcoming vote more transparent by allowing access to its procedures, INEC has come under fire amid broader controversies about the expanding influence of AI in elections across the continent.
Is Nigeria becoming a one-party state?
Fake news: Nothing new in Nigeria
Joash Amupitan, the chairman of the commission, said the body is now investigating the development, focusing on discrepancies potentially created by AI-use.

To this end, he announced the establishment of a dedicated unit to monitor AI-related threats, detect deepfakes and strengthen the integrity of the electoral process, warning that the credibility of the upcoming elections could otherwise be under attack.

However, even prior to the proliferation of AI across Africa and indeed the globe, this would not be the first time that Nigeria finds itself in the unfortunate position of having to deal with the circulation of fabricated images, doctored audio and fake videos online; in the run up to the 2023 elections, deepfakes falsely linking candidates to terror-related activities filled social media platforms.

These are often designed to promote certain candidates, or to discredit opponents in a bid to influence public perception, which now with the use of AI could create disinformation campaigns of new proportions.

blocks.caption: Supporters of a particular candidate in the election can be manipulated easily to believe AI-driven fake newsImage: Sani Maikatanga/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Artificial Intelligence: Various effects on voter behavior
Lois Ugbede, the assistant editor at the factchecking platform DUBAWA, told DW that "based on our monitoring so far, AI-driven disinformation is serious and is becoming commonplace."

"This could influence political discourse and voter behavior ahead of 2027 because we are already seeing parties using inflated crowds to show that they have a large followership or support," she added.

At the same time, rather than influencing the vote in favor of any particular candidate, "the deeper danger is that people may begin to doubt authentic information simply because they know convincing AI generated fakes are possible," says Akintunde Babatunde, Executive Director of the Abuja-based Center for Journalism, Innovation and Development (CJID)."

"We often focus on the risk of people believing an AI-generated falsehood, but there is another problem where genuine evidence can be dismissed as AI generated," he noted, citing instances of a lawmaker who recently made inflammatory remarks during a campaign rally — but then claimed the clips were manipulated.
Have some elections become an empty ritual?
Further pitfalls behind a lack of safeguards against AI

Chibuike Mgbeahuruike, an election consultant at the Centre for Democracy and Development (CDD-West Africa), meanwhile told DW that apart from the spread of synthetic content online, AI intrusion into INEC's portal could also "undermine its institutional credibility, especially with the low level of confidence that we are already witnessing."

He added however that AI itself is not inherently a threat to electoral integrity, but that the real threat rather lies in "the absence of effective accountability for its deployment," as innovations in tech increasingly appear to infiltrate governments and their democratic processes.
"Voters must have confidence … that the technology is also transparent, accountable and independently scrutinized, and ultimately subject to human and institutional oversight," Mgbeahuruike said.

blocks.caption: Journalists can be just as susceptible to disinformation created by AI and other technologiesImage: Emmanuel Osodi/AA/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Director-General of Voice of Nigeria (VON), Mallam Jibrin Baba Ndace, agrees, urging journalists at a recent conference also to not fall into the trap of believing reports, which later could turn out to be false due to AI manipulation.

He stressed the importance of protection measures and due diligence in news media, with the growing inability of public institutions like INEC to provide impartial information due to the use and influence of AI and other election-related tech.
Nigeria's marred relationship with new tech in elections
Beyond AI, Nigeria's electoral processes have undergone various technological shifts over the years in hopes of improving transparency while increasing efficiency.

Electoral authorities first deployed electronic assistance in 2011, when Direct Data Capture Machines were introduced; the devices collect voters' biometrics by scanning fingerprints or capturing facial recognition data with webcams to stop voters from submitting multiple ballots.

Ten years later, a new system called the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) was introduced as the new standard, designed to combine fingerprints with facial recognition; however, during the 2023 general elections, this voting process was marred by system failures of BVAS, as poor cell signal delayed these voter accreditation procedures.

blocks.caption: In Nigeria, voting procedures have increasingly been digitalized since 2011Image: Pius Utomi Ekpei/AFP

blocks.text: However, with INEC tallying more than 103 million Nigerians registered to participate in the coming poll, disinformation, fake news and technological challenges amount to only few of several concerns pertaining to Nigeria's democracy:

Voter apathy has become a particular concern, especially among the country's youth; the 2023 elections recorded the lowest voter turnout since the country's return to democratic rule in 1999, with merely 27 percent of registered voters going to the polls.

articles.title: Microsoft restores service to Outlook and Teams after global outage
articles.summary: Microsoft says server issues were behind the incident that also affected its Copilot AI assistant, and that it was not aware of any malicious activity, ruling out AI as the cause

blocks.text: MICROSOFT. Microsoft Teams app icon in this illustration taken on November 13, 2026.
Dado Ruvic/Reuters
Microsoft says server issues were behind the incident that also affected its Copilot AI assistant, and that it was not aware of any malicious activity, ruling out AI as the cause

items: Microsoft announced the restoration of services across Teams, Outlook, and other products after a global outage lasting over 24 hours, attributed to server issues rather than malicious activity.

The outage significantly impacted businesses and government agencies worldwide, causing disruptions in essential functions like email communication and virtual meetings, with over 7.4 million outage reports logged.

This incident raises concerns about the reliability of major tech companies and their services, as it marks the second major outage for Microsoft in 2023, prompting discussions about the risks of relying heavily on a single provider.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Microsoft said on Saturday, November 14, that services had fully recovered across Teams, Outlook and its other products, ending a global outage that crippled online communications for businesses and governments for over 24 hours.
“We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions,” the company posted on X.
Microsoft had said server issues were behind the incident that also affected its Copilot AI assistant, and that it was not aware of any malicious activity, ruling out AI as the cause.

Outlook and Teams are two of the most widely used workplace applications with hundreds of millions of users. The outage prevented people from performing essential functions such as sending emails, managing calendars and hosting virtual meetings.

It affected government agencies from Australia and Japan to the United States, caused delays at trading firms, hindered some companies from publishing earnings and prompted airlines to warn customers of communication lags, according to public statements.
Organizations that host Microsoft services on their own servers, rather than in the cloud, were somewhat spared.
The outage, reports of which started climbing around 1725 GMT on Thursday according to Ookla, is one of the longest in Microsoft’s history and the second disruption to its services this year.
Microsoft said the outage specifically hit features tied to Exchange Online — its cloud-based email and scheduling hub — leaving unconnected applications operational.
The incident deepens questions about the global reliance on a handful of Big Tech companies that supply both the essential software and the cloud infrastructure that underpins it.

It also highlighted the dependence on Microsoft’s workplace software, with outage reports spiking as employees began their workdays across Asia and Europe, according to Downdetector’s parent company, Ookla.
Downdetector logged more than 7.4 million reports worldwide, peaking at nearly 20,000 a minute, more than 1,500 times normal levels.
“It shows how much of the working day now runs through one provider’s email and collaboration tools,” said Luke Kehoe, lead industry analyst at Ookla.
Microsoft shares closed flat at $523.88 on Friday. The stock has gained roughly 8% so far this year.

Disruptions and financial losses from the outage could result in numerous insurance claims, but the overall hit to insurers is expected to be limited, said Mario De Cicco, vice president of European financial institutions at Morningstar DBRS.

De Cicco estimated global insured losses from the incident at between $300 million and $500 million, well below the $400 million to $1.5 billion financial toll from the 2024 CrowdStrike outage that crashed more than 8 million Windows-based computers and caused widespread disruptions.

Microsoft also faced an outage with its 365 services in January this year and in October last year. Last month, it reported an outage of its Azure cloud platform that impacted its suite of productivity software and a range of industries worldwide.
“The bigger worry is that this is not the first Microsoft 365 outage this year,” said Josh Gilbert, a market analyst at trading platform eToro.
“If reliability starts to look like a recurring problem, it hands every IT department a reason to think twice before putting even more of their business in one provider’s hands.”
Still, some analysts have questioned whether such incidents can push customers on to rivals due to the steep switching costs of replacing tools embedded so deeply in daily operations.
A spokesperson for the UK government said it was working with Microsoft to find a solution for the outage that hit organizations such as the NHS and London’s Metropolitan Police.
Lack of access to emails and other services was impacting the Metropolitan Police’s ability to report some crimes online, though its ability to respond to calls was not affected.
The NHS said its local services were turning to alternate measures such as using IT systems or paper records.
For businesses, the fallout was widespread.
European exchange operator Euronext reported email disruptions, British insurer Aviva activated backups for its earnings calls and Danish shipping giant Maersk warned customers of delayed updates.

American AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic also faced issues with Microsoft connectors that were later resolved, while Indian airlines IndiGo, Akasa Air and Air India said their email support services were impacted.

The outage also disrupted fund management at Taiwanese securities firms, life insurers, and investment trust companies. One of the companies went as far as cancelling a bond repurchase transaction, a source familiar with the situation told Reuters.
Another Taiwanese financial company resorted to using fax to confirm trades, a second source said.
In the US, electric truck maker Workhorse Group rescheduled its results on Thursday to November 16, while Switzerland’s Richemont briefly delayed its first-half results announcement on Friday.
In Australia, where the spy agency and federal police were among organizations caught in the outage, Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke said Microsoft does not suspect a cyberattack.
“The impact that they are dealing with … is very much on email systems,” the minister added. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Espionage accusations: a pressure tactic for Turkish government critics
articles.summary: This week's arrest of an employee of a German foundation in Istanbul has put focus back on the Erdogan administration's pressure tactics. The arrest is far from the first of its kind.

image.caption: Yonca Verdioglu Sik (right) after her release with her husband, journalist and MP Ahmet Sik (left)Image: ANKA

blocks.text: When police officers appeared at her home in Istanbul last Wednesday evening, Yonca Verdioglu Sik was surprised — even more so when they took her in for questioning. Her lawyer says she was accused of political and military espionage.

But, according to transcripts of the interrogation that were published later, Verdioglu Sik was never asked any questions about espionage. Instead the public prosecutor's office appeared to be more interested in the activities of the German organization, the Heinrich Böll Foundation, for whom Verdioglu Sik works. For 18 years, Verdioglu Sik, who was born and raised in Germany, has been the foundation's project coordinator. In her role, she organizes projects that focus on democracy and women's, minority and LGBTQ+ rights.
During the interrogation, transfers of money from the foundation into her bank account were discussed. Verdioglu Sik found out that she was now subject to a travel ban too.
Pressure on politicians

Verdioglu Sik was eventually released. Nonetheless her arrest caused outrage among critics of the Turkish government. Sik is married to investigative journalist and member of parliament, Ahmet Sik. He belongs to the left-wing Workers' Party of Turkey, or TIP, and is known as one of the current government's harshest critics.

Recently Sik has been looking into a stock market scandal, which allegedly benefitted members of the ruling Justice and Development Party, or AKP, headed by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and their associates.
Opposition critics drew a clear conclusion: As a member of parliament, Sik has parliamentary immunity. So instead, the justice system is putting pressure on him through his wife.
"If you take away a state's law, what is left is no longer called a state, but a gang," Sik responded to the arrest in writing.

Verdioglu Sik's arrest is not the first such case in Turkey. Ever since the attempted coup against the Erdogan government in 2016, accusations of espionage have been levelled at a wide variety of groups in Turkey: journalists, opposition figures and human rights activists as well as employees of foreign embassies and staff of foreign institutions like non-governmental organizations and foundations.
Diplomatic disputes

Such accusations were often followed by acquittals or convictions for other offenses, albeit sometimes years later. What the many instances have in common though is what's known as a "chilling effect." Any investigation can mean lengthy pre-trial detention, reputational and professional damage and even social isolation.
In the past such cases have even triggered diplomatic spats.

For example in 2015, Can Dundar and Erdem Gul, both senior journalists at the opposition daily Cumhuriyet, were accused of espionage after reporting that Turkey had tried to ship arms to rebels fighting the Syrian government. Dundar now lives in exile in Berlin.
In 2017, Erdogan said that reporter Deniz Yücel, then working for German newspaper Die Welt, was a "German agent." That led to a serious diplomatic crisis between Berlin and Ankara.

blocks.caption: Journalist Deniz Yücel was labeled a "German agent" by Turkey's presidentImage: Bernd Elmenthaler/IMAGO IMAGES

blocks.text: Espionage charges have also been laid against local employees of the US diplomatic corps and against a lawyer working for the German embassy. US pastor Andrew Brunson and his wife were also arrested because of alleged links to Kurdish anti-government groups. Turkish philanthropist and human rights activist Osman Kavala, who was charged with espionage and attempting to overthrow the constitutional order, remains in prison.
Most recently, espionage charges have been brought against the former Istanbul mayor and Erdogan's political competitor, Ekrem Imamoglu, and a number of journalists.
'Hostage diplomacy'
Hakki Tas, a research fellow and expert on Turkey at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies, or GIGA, notes that the number of such cases have been increasing over the past few years.

On the one hand, Turkey has the right to protect itself from foreign intelligence services — especially given geopolitical competition and conflict in the region, he argues. On the other hand, there's a long tradition of bringing the Turkish opposition to court to face security charges.
"What foreigners or employees of foreign institutions have experienced in recent years is a continuation of this pattern," Tas told DW.
LGBTQ+ communities in Turkey fear intensifying clampdown

Media outlets and NGOs critical of the government have faced investigations, trials and other sorts of state sanctions for years. The ruling AKP party has also brought in its own version of a so-called "foreign agent law."
These sorts of espionage cases serve both a domestic and foreign policy function, Tas observes.

For locals, "contact with a foreign institution, foreign funding or even a perfectly normal salary could become part of an investigation someday," Tas explains. "For opposition figures and civil society organizations, in particular, this can become a security issue."

In terms of foreign policy, the cases also show other countries that there are limits to their activities inside Turkey. These kinds of accusations seem to become more frequent when there's some sort of foreign policy tension — for example, after Western criticism of how opposition groups were dealt with after the alleged coup in 2016, the aforementioned disputes about arms deliveries in connection with Syria, or criticism from abroad about the removal of elected mayors in Turkey.
It can also serve as a kind of "hostage diplomacy," Tas says.

blocks.caption: US pastor Andrew Brunson (center, white shirt) with his wife after his release in 2018Image: Getty Images/AFP/B. Kilic

blocks.text: Punishing process

The case of US cleric Brunson is a good example. After his arrest, the Turkish government proposed a trade with the Americans. They wanted to exchange Turkish preacher Fethullah Gulen, who lived in the US and who the Turkish government blamed for the 2016 coup attempt.

This suspicion of foreign institutions isn't something that the Erdogan government invented, Tas points out. In the early 2000s, several representatives of German organizations were already standing trial in Turkey. At the time, it was alleged that, among other things, the German spy service was using German foundations as a front for conspiracy.
In some of the best-known cases, defendants often don't end up convicted of espionage.
The Kavala case demonstrates this. He was initially acquitted of espionage several times and spent two years in prison, just because of those charges.
But Tas says that's no surprise, referring to a 1979 work about the sociology of law written by US law professor Malcolm Feeley. It's title: "The Process Is the Punishment."
This story was originally published in German.
No future in Turkey?

articles.title: UK-EU breakthrough will allow airport-style checks at Eurotunnel to avoid border ‘chaos’
articles.summary:
Eurotunnel owner Getlink wants to replicate ‘airport experience’ at Folkestone and Calais, without making people get out of cars

Airport-style passport and fingerprinting controls are to be…

blocks.text: Airport-style passport and fingerprinting controls are to be introduced at Eurotunnel in an attempt to prevent “short-term and long-term chaos” in Folkestone and Calais.

In a breakthrough for travellers, the European Commission has agreed to a new system in which an “eagle eye” camera system, already used in Rome and Paris airports to supervise fingerprinting and facial imaging, will be used at the border between the UK and France.
Yann Leriche, the chief executive of Getlink, the Eurotunnel owner, said it had tried to replicate the “airport experience” but wanted to go much further.

Instead of getting out of the car and getting biometrics taken at a terminal building, holidaymakers and business travellers will now be greeted with special drive-through terminals in Folkestone and Calais.

blocks.caption: New airport style drive-in biometrics kiosks at Eurotunnel in Calais. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian

blocks.text: Both sides are now equipped with 120 kiosks under the case of an eagle-eye camera that will be monitored by police, similar to e-gates at airports where police are not physically present at each gate.

In the coming weeks, Leriche will meet UK and French authorities presenting a 40-page proposal to allow Eurotunnel to become a “laboratory” for an “intelligent border” using emerging tech and lessons learned from the US and Singapore.

The entry and exit system (EES) requires all third-country citizens including British passport holders to submit fingerprints and facial images as they enter and exit the Schengen area, but has been delayed for years.
EES was supposed to be active across the EU by 9 September, but nine of the 27 EU member states, including France, have yet to be deploy it fully because of continued technical issues.

blocks.caption: The new drive-in fingerprinting terminals at Eurotunnel. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian

blocks.text: It has always been a logistical nightmare for Eurotunnel and a potential cause of miles-long tailbacks at the approach to the terminal.

Originally, Getlink had planned to use a tablet to hand to the passengers in their cars to allow them to self-fingerprint and capture a facial image. It also looked at a system involving passengers parking up and going into the terminal to get fingerprinting.
But both models would have required the physical presence of police officers for first-time fingerprinting.

Leriche said: “We told the authorities: it is going to be a mess. Many people are going to the wrong place and you can’t have police jumping from one place to the next to solve the issues. It would also means customers would have a bad experience, particularly at peak time.
“This is not something people in airports experience, but nobody approached this before, thinking we could have an airport experience at the border here. But we said: why not?”
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Yann Leriche, the chief executive of Getlink. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian

blocks.text: He said that after “many, many discussions” with the European Commission and the French authorities, finally they were “authorised” to trial “eagle-eye cameras” at each kiosk. “The French authorities are also on board because for them it is more efficient, too, so we are all aligned on the trial,” he said.
The trial will last two years, but Eurotunnel hopes the experiment will become permanent.

Each car will be able to pull up to an individual kiosk, with two stands per vehicle to read passports and take fingerprints and facial images. “It will prevent the chaos in the long term and the short term and if the experiment works, as hopefully it will, then it will become permanent,” said Leriche.
He said the company had been inspired by visits to the US/Mexico border controls, where drivers and passengers remain in their cars.

blocks.caption: The new drive-in border controls at Eurotunnel. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian

blocks.text: The requirement of having a police officer present each time a first-time passenger, or “primo” as they are known, submits their fingerprints was designed as a safeguard against subterfuge. Criminals, for example, could use a fellow passenger for example with a “clean skin” fingerprint.

Leriche said he had no idea when the system will be introduced by France. “It has been delayed and delayed and delayed, but our kiosks are there, they are can function but the connection with the French system is still not working. It is a question was are asking all the time.”
This week it emerged that the EU had filed a lawsuit against IBM and two other companies involved in the implementation of EES.

articles.title: Bristol aims to become UK’s first ‘wetland city’ and reduce flood risk
articles.summary:
Five-year project will create wildlife corridors by building wetlands and increase access to green and blue spaces

Bristol could become home to the UK’s first “wetland city” thanks to a…

blocks.text: Bristol could become home to the UK’s first “wetland city” thanks to a charity’s efforts to create vast wildlife corridors that will reduce flood risk and give people more access to green and blue spaces.

The Wildfowl & Wetlands Trust (WWT) said the five-year initiative would include more than 200 projects to restore and create wetlands across the city. These will range from small household rainwater ponds and street-level rain gardens to restoring river habitats, reconnecting rivers with their floodplains, and creating new wetlands.

It hopes to achieve wetland city accreditation under the Ramsar convention, the international treaty on wetland conservation, which recognises cities that protect and make wise use of their urban wetlands.

blocks.caption: Floating wetlands bring wildlife to Bristol’s harbour

blocks.text: The charity kickstarted the project in September by installing floating wetlands, made of buoyant modules covered in wetland plants, at three sites in Bristol’s city-centre harbour. They help to create a more welcoming habitat for insects, birds and other wildlife.

“Within minutes, dragonflies and other wildlife were appearing. Nature was being drawn to it,” said Peter Lee, the programmes lead at WWT. “It sparked a conversation – people were saying: ‘Why can’t it always be like this?’”

Louise Kennedy, who is managing the project in Bristol, said 40% of species around the world were reliant on wetlands: “At WWT we often say they’re in freefall, given the number we’ve already lost. In a world that is increasingly urbanised, figuring out where pockets of wetland can be restored and protected within our cities massively improves biodiversity.

blocks.caption: Swans, ducks and a goose make themselves at home on one of the floating wetland islands. Photograph: Sam Walker/WWT

blocks.text: “It also improves access to nature for large segments of the population, who wouldn’t necessarily have access to wildlife reserves in rural locations.”

blocks.caption: The urban wetlands in Bristol show how nature can be incorporated into the built environment. Photograph: Jim Johnston/WWT

blocks.text: Lee said that, because wetlands absorb and store water more effectively than impermeable surfaces such as concrete, they are a great way to reuse rainwater and prevent flooding during heavy rainfall. “It’s a rethink of how we manage the water that lands in the city,” he said. “Instead of trying to get water out of the city as quickly as possible through drains and combined sewers, which overflow when it rains, we can actually manage the water where it lands.”
“Rain falling on a roof – that’s some of the purest, best-quality water there is,” he added. “Rather than channelling it straight into a combined sewer, we can use that water as a resource.”

There are 74 accredited wetland cities in 27 countries, 22 of them in China. Lee said bids elsewhere had usually been state-led, often driven by a city’s mayor, but WWT’s project in Bristol is funded by the insurer Aviva, which is contributing £8.9m over the five years.

Lee said he hoped Bristol would become a template for other UK towns and cities, and that it could demonstrate the economic case for wetlands, including commercial returns such as higher mooring fees and more footfall in the city centre.

“By proving the commercial and economic case for investment in wetlands, we won’t always need to rely on a big philanthropic donation – instead that’s seed funding to kickstart a much bigger programme,” he said.

The charity had looked at a number of cities to launch the wetland city project, he added, but Bristol stood out, pointing to the city’s maritime heritage. “Look at the placenames across Bristol – they’re full of water references,” he said. “It’s got 100 miles of waterways within the city, a lot of them hidden and tucked away.”

Tony Dyer, the leader of Bristol city council, said: “Bristol has always been shaped by its relationship with water, and this exciting programme shows how we can work with nature to tackle some of the biggest challenges facing our city.
“By creating and restoring wetlands across Bristol, we can help reduce flood risk, support wildlife, improve people’s health and wellbeing, and help build resilience to a changing climate.”

items: Ateneo de Davao University is facing controversy due to a bullying incident involving a viral video of a student assaulting another in the school's comfort room.

The university has taken immediate action by ensuring the victim's safety, informing parents, and dismissing the student responsible for the bullying, while also escalating the case to the Department of Education.
The school is reviewing its bullying prevention policies and support services, emphasizing the importance of empathy, accountability, and the need for rehabilitation for all affected by bullying.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Ateneo de Davao University has found itself at the center of controversy after a bullying incident struck its junior high school division.

A viral video showed a student physically assaulting another student in the school’s comfort room. The clip showed the perpetrator repeatedly hitting and kicking the victim, while the latter remained defenseless.

On November 11, Ateneo de Davao University said that it immediately moved to ensure the victim was safe, and informed the parents of all those involved. It also brought the case up to its junior high school child protection committee, and escalated it to the Department of Education (DepEd).
“We are deeply sorry for the pain and distress they have endured. They have been receiving guidance and counseling support since then,” the school said.
At the same time, Ateneo de Davao University also reiterated its duty to protect all the students involved from “public judgment, online harassment, and further harm.”

On November 13, Ateneo de Davao University said it dismissed the student responsible for the bullying incident “effective immediately.” It also said that investigations regarding the other aspects of the incident will continue.
The school also promised to support the student who was harmed by the incident.

As investigations continue, the school has also ordered its University Task Force on Bullying Prevention and Safe Learning Environments to review how bullying concerns are addressed. It will also go over its policies and support services.

“Alongside these safeguards, the Task Force will examine how our formation programs and pastoral care can better nurture empathy, respect for human dignity, responsibility for one’s actions, and the courage to intervene when others are harmed. It will recommend ways to strengthen guidance, counseling, spiritual support, and accompaniment for students and families affected by bullying,” the school said.
“This includes helping students who have harmed others recognize the consequences of their actions, accept accountability, and grow in compassion and responsibility.”
Ateneo de Davao University also stressed that violence and bullying will not be tolerated, and that those who harm others will be held accountable with due process.

Under Republic Act 10627, schools are required to enforce anti-bullying policies and ensure that investigations into such incidents are done properly. It also requires schools to put rehabilitation procedures in place for all those affected. – Rappler.com

blocks.text: Here is a roundup of headlines from India on Saturday, November 14:
November 14, 2026
Delhi overtakes Lahore as world's most polluted city
On Friday, Delhi's Air Quality Index (AQI) stood at 334, categorized as "hazardous"making it the most polluted major city globally, according to Swiss air quality monitoring group IQAir.
The Indian capital's AQI was recorded to be higher than Lahore in Pakistan on Friday, which made it the most polluted city globally.

Quoting IQAir's hourly data, Pakistani newspaper Dawn reported that on Friday Delhi's AQI had dropped to 208 at 11.30 a.m. local time (0630 UTC). At the time, Lahore was ranked seventh among the world’s most polluted major cities, with an AQI of 155.
India's official Central Pollution ​Control Board, however, recorded the AQI higher at 403 and ‌rated ⁠it "severe."
The difference between the Indian and Swiss readings is caused by the fact that the two use different AQI scales and methodologies to calculate and categorize air pollution ​levels.
India's worst air pollution crisis isn't in its megacities
Visibility in Delhi is significantly impacted as a thick layer of smog has enveloped the city.
In many parts of northern India and Pakistan, pollution poses a seasonal problem as the ​cold, heavy air of ​winter traps vehicle emissions, construction dust and smoke from agricultural ​burning.

articles.title: Trump, other Quad leaders to meet in Manila on Tuesday, sources say
articles.summary: Leaders of the US, Japan, Australia and India are expected to meet on Tuesday on the sidelines of a key Asian meeting in Manila, two people familiar with the planning said, marking the first summit…

blocks.text: Published November 14, 2026 2:22pm

Leaders of the US, Japan, Australia and India are expected to meet on Tuesday on the sidelines of a key Asian meeting in Manila, two people familiar with the planning said, marking the first summit of the "Quad" nations in two years.

The Quad group of Indo-Pacific powers is widely considered a counterweight to China's growing influence in the region, although its members have said the grouping is not directed against any one country.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio indicated last month that the Quad leaders could meet on the sidelines of the summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, which begins on Sunday in the Philippine capital.
The supply of critical minerals is expected to be on the Quad summit agenda, one of the people said.

"The leaders are likely to take up the issue of free and unimpeded commercial shipping lanes in order to secure energy supplies from across the world," said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity as he is not authorized to speak with the media. "The issue of attacks on commercial ships is very likely to be taken up."

The second person, from the Philippine government and briefed on the preparations, said the Quad leaders were expected to gather shortly after US President Donald Trump arrives in Manila on Tuesday, the last day of the ASEAN summit.
The Manila gathering would be the first Quad leaders' meeting since Trump returned to office last year.
Quad leaders last met in September 2024 in Delaware, reaffirming their commitment to a free and open Indo-Pacific and announcing initiatives to strengthen maritime security cooperation. —Reuters

articles.title: SPECIAL REPORT: The Lopez heirs who ran Rockwell but never controlled it
articles.summary: First of a special report on why Gabby Lopez wants Rockwell Land as ABS-CBN struggles, and why cousin Piki Lopez is letting it go

blocks.text: For years, the children of former Meralco chairman Manuel “Manolo” Lopez have helped run Rockwell Land. But they never owned enough shares to actually control it. That power belonged to First Philippine Holdings Corporation (FPH), the giant conglomerate led by their cousin, Federico “Piki” Lopez.

Now, rewind to April 2026. Four of Manolo’s children joined eight other Lopez cousins to publicly challenge Piki’s leadership of Lopez Inc., the family’s main holding company. They were fighting the cousin who chaired the company that controlled Rockwell, the very business they had continued running after the family gave up Meralco in 2009. (READ: The company the Lopezes gave up Meralco for: EDC, from oil crisis child to takeover target)

Seven months later, everything is about to change. On November 12, FPH announced that its board approved selling its controlling stake in Rockwell Land to Crème Investment Corporation, a firm tied to Piki’s cousin, Eugenio “Gabby” Lopez III and his siblings. The price tag: ₱15.92 billion.

Once the deal closes, Rockwell leaves Piki’s FPH group and moves under Gabby’s private firm. Gabby’s side of the family has backed Manolo’s children ever since the third-generation cousins’ feud broke out.
Here is the catch, though: Manolo’s children aren’t the ones buying Rockwell. Gabby is. Their direct ownership in Rockwell remains tiny. What does change is who holds the reins of the Rockwell.

Rockwell’s ties to Manolo’s family go back decades, to the days when the Lopezes still ran power distributor Meralco. Manolo spent much of his career there and was its chairman when the family gave up control in 2009.

Rockwell, which was built on Meralco’s old power plant lot in Makati, stayed inside the wider Lopez conglomerate. Yet out of roughly 20 third-generation Lopez cousins, it is Manolo’s children who remain the true face of Rockwell.

Manolo chaired Rockwell until he passed away in January 2023. Longtime executive Nestor “Tong” Padilla took over and now serves as chairman and CEO. Meanwhile, Manolo’s sons still hold major roles at the company. Miguel Ernesto Lopez sits on Rockwell’s board and serves as its treasurer and senior vice president for office development. Manuel “Beaver” Lopez Jr. is vice president of Rockwell Land and president of Rockwell Leisure Club.

blocks.caption: RLC BOARD. Rockwell Land Corp.’s board of directors, including (seated from left) Miguel Ernesto Lopez, Nestor Padilla, and Federico “Piki” Lopez; Miguel Ernesto Lopez (standing, extreme right) and Benjamin Ernesto Lopez (standing, third from left). Courtesy of Rockwell Land Corp.

blocks.text: In a recent group photo of Rockwell board of directors, taken before the third generation Lopez cousins’ feud became public in March, Piki and his brother Benjamin “Jay” Lopez appear right next to their cousins. Piki is Rockwell’s vice chairman, and Jay is a director. Those titles show how involved the family still is. But holding a job or a board seat is very different from owning the controlling shares.

These ownership numbers show how the Lopez family split up its businesses across its different branches. Originally, the four second-generation branches held equal shares in Lopez Inc., the private holding company at the very top. Each branch also held smaller slices of individual companies down the line.

Rockwell followed this arrangement. FPH owned nearly 87% of Rockwell’s common shares. Meanwhile, Mantes Corporation, the firm tied to Manolo’s branch, held just 0.53%. Piki and siblings’ Croslo Holdings owned 0.01%, while public stockholders held the remaining 13%. When you include voting preferred shares, FPH controlled 90.74% of the total votes.
Manolo’s branch also had an indirect slice of Rockwell through Lopez Inc., which controls Lopez Holdings, the parent company of FPH.

When the family was getting along under one roof, it was easy to ignore the gap between managing a company and owning it. Manolo’s heirs could run Rockwell and enjoy its success without having the votes to pick the board or decide if the company gets sold. Those big decisions belonged to FPH—and to Piki, who chaired FPH and served as Rockwell’s vice chairman.
That gap between running the company and owning it became a huge deal when the family feud exploded earlier this year.

On April 27, four of Manolo’s children—Beaver, Maria Margarita Lopez Lichauco, Miguel, and Martin—joined eight other cousins to sign a public statement called “A Matter of Trust and Governance.” They announced they had lost trust in Piki and wanted him removed as president of Lopez, Inc.

That April, the majority cousins released two sharp statements questioning Piki’s leadership and First Gen’s multibillion-peso deals with Enrique Razon Jr.’s Prime Infrastructure. “Who is Piki working for?” they asked in one statement. In another, they accused him of acting “like a king without accountability.” (READ: Who writes the Lopez story? How lawyers, headlines, and ABS-CBN shape a family war)
For Manolo’s children, the fight was extra awkward. They were openly challenging Piki while still working at Rockwell—a company controlled by Piki-led FPH.
By September, Piki had consolidated his leadership of Lopez Holdings and FPH.
Then came the November 12 Rockwell announcement.

blocks.caption: Screenshot from Rockwell’s November 13, 2026 disclosure.

blocks.text: Under the new deal, FPH will sell its controlling block of Rockwell common and preferred shares to Crème for about P15.92 billion. The sale still needs regulatory approval from the Philippine Competition Commission and must go through a mandatory buyout offer for remaining public shares.
Once it goes through, Crème replaces FPH as Rockwell’s controlling owner.

Keep one thing in mind: the buyer is Crème (from Geny and Gabby’s side of the family), not Mantes (from Manolo’s side). Whether Manolo’s children keep their management roles and influence will still depend on Rockwell’s board and its new boss.

Still, this is a massive shift for Manolo’s heirs. Rockwell will no longer answer to FPH, the company chaired by the cousin they publicly fought. Instead, it moves under the private firm of Gabby, the cousin who they fought with.

Selling Rockwell doesn’t mean the cousins have completely untangled their finances. Through Mantes, Manolo’s branch still owns about 29.17% of Lopez Inc. Presta Holdings—tied to Presentacion Lopez-Psinakis’s branch—owns another 15.98%. Both branches backed Gabby during the family dispute, and together they still own roughly 45% of Lopez, Inc. Piki’s Croslo holds another 29.17%, while Ramon Ang’s group holds the 25.68% stake it bought from Crème.

blocks.caption: Ramon Ang buys his way into Lopez Inc., which owns what he already builds

blocks.text: Since Lopez Inc. controls Lopez Holdings—which in turn controls FPH—Manolo’s and Presentacion’s branches are still indirectly invested in First Gen and its power businesses, including Energy Development Corporation. Mantes also owns a small, direct slice of FPH.

This puts Manolo’s branch on both sides of the Rockwell deal. They are a minority owner of the property company being sold, and an investor in FPH, which gets the ₱15.92-billion payout. Because that money goes to FPH rather than straight into the cousins’ pockets, their financial upside depends on how the sale boosts FPH’s value and how FPH spends the cash.
Rockwell may be leaving Piki’s corporate umbrella, but Manolo’s heirs still have money riding on the energy empire he runs.

For Manolo’s family, Rockwell was the one business that stayed close to their hearts after the Lopezes gave up Meralco. They kept key leadership jobs at the property firm, even while FPH held the actual ownership power. (READ: The Lopezes, presidents, and the cost of dissent)

This sale flips that dynamic. Rockwell moves from Piki’s FPH to Gabby’s Crème. Manolo’s heirs will stay on as minority owners, with their future roles at the company yet to be decided. Their direct stake in Rockwell stays small, while their indirect money in Piki’s power businesses stays huge.

The cousins are splitting up the companies they run much faster than the investments they still own together. For Manolo’s heirs, the Rockwell deal changes who holds power over the company they helped build. What it doesn’t settle—at least not yet—is who will end up owning what across the rest of the Lopez empire. – Rappler.com

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.

articles.title: Gen Z protests: Do Baby Boomers really have it better than young people?
articles.summary: Should young people in Germany be more worried about their future than Baby Boomers were in the 1980s and 1990s? Or should both generations take to the streets and protest together? DW checked the…

image.caption: 'It's giving anxiety about the future,' reads the sign at a Gen Z protest in Hamburg Image: Marcus Brandt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Young people across Germany and Europe are taking to the streets, voicing fears of a bleak future.
But is that really the case? Does Gen Z face greater challenges than Baby Boomers did in the 1990s? What do the two generations have in common, and where do their experiences differ?

"Of course, it's fair to ask, 'Were things just as tough for you back then?'" youth researcher Simon Schnetzer tells DW. "But young people see that things are difficult for them now, and say that's why they need support today."

Schnetzer, who wrote the annual Youth in Germany study, highlights one key question raised by the recent demonstrations across Europe as: "Have we given young people the conditions they need to live and work here with confidence, and to keep this system funded?"

His straightforward answer is no. A survey of the statistics shows that both Gen Z and the Baby Boomers are affected by major societal changes, but in different ways. DW surveyed data on pensions, education, housing and climate change to find out more.
Pensions and poverty among the elderly

The facts point to a clear trend: Fewer and fewer young people are having to support an ever-growing number of retirees. According to the Germany's public pension insurance system, there were 3.73 contributors for every retiree in 1957. By 2025, that figure had fallen to just 2.1.
By 2045, this number is projected to drop to just 1.73 contributors per retiree. In absolute terms, this means 35.35 million contributors will be financing pensions for 16.82 million retirees.

To cushion this trend and keep contribution rates stable, the pension system already receives around €118 billion [$131 billion] in annual government subsidies. This amounts to roughly 25% of the federal budget. That means an increasing share of the population will be called upon to help fund pensions.

There are also signs that many people's pensions are already falling short of covering their living expenses. The number of retirees relying on federal basic income support has risen from 257,000 in 2003 to 738,000 in 2024.
What Germans young and old think about the pension system
Rent and housing costs

Rising rents hit low-income households particularly hard. According to a report by the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW), the share of income spent on rent by low-income households rose from around 24% in 1990 to nearly 36% in 2021.
This means that in 2021, the lowest-income households spent an average of 14 percentage points more of their income on rent than high-income households.

According to Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), in 2025, an average of 11% of the population spent more than 40% of their disposable income on housing costs. Among people at risk of poverty, the figure was as high as 35%.

However, according to calculations by real estate platform Jacasa, Boomers could actually help ease pressure on the housing market in the coming years. They currently own around 4.8 million owner-occupied houses and apartments.

Over the coming decades, these properties are expected to change hands as former occupants sell them, move into assisted living, or hand them down through inheritance. In some regions, this could lead to an oversupply of properties and, consequently, lower prices, according to Jacasa's projections.
Investment in education

According to the federal government's Education Finance Report, public spending on education for people under 30 has doubled since 2011, rising from around €4,000 to approximately €8,000 per person annually.

Despite this increase, Germany ranks only in the middle of the pack internationally. According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), public education spending accounted for 4.6% of Germany's gross domestic product (GDP) in 2022, compared with an OECD average of 4.7%.

However, the additional funding cannot solve the problem of teacher shortages. According to estimates by the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, Germany will be short of around 27,000 teachers by 2035. The main reasons are the wave of Baby Boomer retirements and declining birth rates, which have contributed to a shortage of young teachers.
Climate change

Back in 1972, the Club of Rome warned of the consequences of global warming in its landmark publication The Limits to Growth. According to the United Nations, the planet is on track for 2.6°C of warming by the end of the century compared with pre-industrial levels.

If the world maintains its current climate policies, children who are six years old today could experience heat waves two to seven times as often as Boomers did over their lifetimes. That was the finding of a 2025 study by Vrije University in Brussels.

The deadly impact of extreme weather is already evident in rising death tolls during recent heatwaves. According to Germany's Robert Koch Institute (RKI), an estimated 16,000 people died from heat-related causes across Germany by mid-September 2026. The vast majority — more than 14,000 — were over the age of 65.

"Gen Z and Baby Boomers are in the same boat. We need to bring them together, because otherwise younger people have no prospects for prosperity, and neither do older generations," youth researcher Schnetzer concludes.

He suggests that both generations take to the streets and protest together, adding that would just be the beginning. "What needs to follow is a constructive process to define goals and measures that everyone can support," he said. "Even if it means making sacrifices."
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: 'Premature' to talk about Sara Duterte's replacement, Deputy Speaker Garin says
articles.summary: House Deputy Speaker Janette Garin on Saturday said discussions on the possible replacement for Sara Duterte as the country's vice president are too early to be held amid her ongoing impeachment…

blocks.text: Published November 14, 2026 2:06pm

House Deputy Speaker Janette Garin on Saturday said discussions on the possible replacement for Sara Duterte as the country's vice president are too early to be held amid her ongoing impeachment trial.
"For me, it's very premature to talk about who the next Vice President will be," Garin said at a news forum in Quzon City.
"It's not yet the time to talk about that kasi dapat tignan muna 'yung impeachment. Hindi naman natin sinasabi na talagang mai-impeach na si vice president," she said.
(It's not yet the time to talk about that because the focus should be on the impeachment trial. We cannot say for sure that she will be convicted.)
"Itong lahat ay depende sa senator-judges at depende sa kampo niya kung masasagot ang mga katanungan," she added.
(This all depends on the senator-judges, and her camp if they will be able to answer the questions raised.)
Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro earlier said President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. has not discussed or considered a replacement for the vice president.
Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano earlier urged fellow senators to decline any potential offers for the vice presidency should Duterte be convicted.
Senator Francis "Chiz" Escudero previously declared he would refuse the post due to a conflict of interest as a senator-judge.
Under the 1987 Constitution, if the vice presidency becomes vacant, the President nominates a new Vice President who must then be confirmed by a majority vote of both Houses of Congress.
"Just in case mayroon nang annointed then we cross the bridge when it comes," Garin said.

Duterte's spokesperson Atty. Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr. earlier said the focus should be on questions involving the fairness of the Senate impeachment court, the constitutionality of the conviction threshold, and alleged due process violations. He likewise said it was premature to discuss about replacements for the vice president. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: UK tells blind Nigerian pensioner to go home to India
articles.summary:
Woman who has lived in UK for 26 years refused indefinite leave to remain under Home Office’s new settlement rules

A blind Nigerian pensioner who has lived in the UK for 26 years has been…

blocks.text: A blind Nigerian pensioner who has lived in the UK for 26 years has been told by the Home Office she can safely “go home” to India.
Comfort*, 67, arrived in the UK in 2000, and shortly after suddenly went blind due to acute glaucoma.

After living here for 20 years, she was granted leave to remain under long residence rules. Those allowed to stay on this route have to renew their visa every 30 months for 10 years and after that can apply for indefinite leave to remain. Under the new settlement rules announced by Shabana Mahmood this week, it is likely Comfort will now have to keep renewing her visa for the next 20 years before she will finally, when she reaches her 80s, be eligible for indefinite leave to remain.

Due to her age and disability, lawyers at Refugee and Migrant Justice applied to the Home Office for her to be granted indefinite leave to remain now rather than having to wait two more decades before becoming eligible. There is a provision to fast-track indefinite leave to remain applications in exceptional circumstances.

However, the Home Office rejected this application, telling her in the first part of the letter that she could return to Nigeria because there are services there for blind people. But the refusal letter concluded: “Your circumstances are not so severe or lacking in potential treatment in India that it would warrant indefinite leave to remain in this case.”

Numerous migrants’ rights’ organisations have raised concerns about the increase in the period of time some will now have to wait for settlement here, after the home secretary’s announcement. For some, the amount of time they have to wait has increased sixfold.

According to freedom of information data obtained by Refugee and Migrant Justice, many people of pensionable age have applied for settlement but, due to their age, are likely to die before satisfying the new, more stringent Home Office wait times. One person on the Home Office data disclosure is a woman from Pakistan aged 103, who will not be eligible for settlement until she is 123 years old.
“In 2022, I got my permission to stay here based on long residence in the UK,” said Comfort. “I’m very disheartened that I may now need to wait nearly 20 years to get indefinite leave to remain.

“I have been living in this country for 26 years. I have found my home here and settled well. I have my friends, my church and do voluntary work. I’m a good citizen, not a law-breaker and am begging the Home Office to have mercy on me and grant me indefinite leave to remain now, rather than making me wait 20 more years.
“I don’t know why the Home Office said I could go back to India. It’s a country I have never visited and have no connection with.”

Nick Beales, head of campaigning at Migrant and Refugee Justice, who is supporting Comfort, said: “This woman is blind, in her late 60s and has lived in the UK for a quarter of a century. She meets the rules to remain here and there is no public interest in making her continue to renew her visa.

“Rather than viewing these vulnerable people as human beings, the government is fixated on appearing tough. Shabana Mahmood’s plans to double settlement routes will clearly make these problems even worse, especially as her decision-makers cannot even differentiate between India and Nigeria.

“Government data shows that people over 80 are applying to enter these settlement routes. While it’s unlikely many of these people would survive a 10-year period, Mahmood has not explained what she hopes to achieve by making these octogenarians and older wait two decades before having settlement. The government should admit that their earned settlement model is cruel and counter-productive and scrap these plans once and for all.”
Home Office sources said that corrective action was being taken to re-issue an updated letter to the woman.

A Home Office spokesperson said: “We do not routinely comment on individual cases. All applications for permission to stay in the UK are carefully considered on their individual merits, in line with the immigration rules and based on the information and evidence provided by the applicant.”
* Name has been changed.
