articles.title: Has China’s ‘beauty stratagem’ found a new victim in Nvidia’s Jensen Huang?
articles.summary: As long as important decisions depend on individuals, personal relationships may remain a weakness that rivals can exploit

blocks.text: Extramarital activities have led to the resignation of one of America’s most influential tech bosses, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The saga has also raised the specter of an age-old spying tactic: the “honey trap.”

Huang stepped down following media reports of an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence agencies. She previously worked for Megaspeed, a cloud computing company under US scrutiny for allegedly helping China obtain restricted AI chips.
Jensen Huang acknowledged an affair. And amid reports of a second with a company executive who reports to him, he tendered his resignation to the Nvidia board on Nov. 12, 2026.

The sensitivity of Huang’s work – AI is increasingly seen as central to national security – has turned a company matter into an international issue. China’s Foreign Ministry has denied the espionage allegations and accused the US of “fabricating so-called spy narratives and ⁠⁠⁠⁠using them as a pretext for imposing ⁠⁠⁠⁠a technological blockade.” Nvidia says it has no reason to believe company secrets have been leaked.
Yet part of what makes the accusations so believable is history is dotted with examples of men being distracted, compromised or spied on by attractive men and women deployed for that purpose.
Indeed, in China it recalls an ancient political tactic known as “meiren ji” or the “beauty stratagem.”

As a scholar specializing in US-China relations, I believe that regardless of the particulars of the Huang case, the political logic behind the beauty stratagem – using personal relationships to obtain information, influence decisions and weaken opponents – remains relevant today. As such, it would be no surprise if the tactic was being used amid the growing US-China competition over AI and advanced semiconductors.

“Meiren ji” is one of “Thirty-Six Stratagems,” a Chinese military text of uncertain origin but generally believed to have derived from oral and written histories from the Warring States period — 475–221 BCE. Its 31st stratagem states that personal relationships can be used to influence political opponents and recommends exploiting an adversary’s personal desires and emotional vulnerabilities to weaken their judgment and undermine their leadership.
The “Thirty-Six Stratagems” is both a playbook for warfare and a reflection on past experience.
Indeed, one of China’s most famous beauty stratagem stories dates back more than 2,000 years to the Spring and Autumn period of Chinese history.

In the fifth century BCE, King Goujian of Yue, in modern-day southern China, was defeated by King Fuchai of Wu, its northern neighbor, and forced to submit. But Goujian secretly rebuilt his strength and prepared for revenge.
According to the ancient historical text “Wu Yue Chun Qiu,” Yue sent two beautiful women – Xi Shi and Zheng Dan – to Fuchai, hoping he would become distracted by pleasure and neglect state affairs.
The plan reportedly worked. Fuchai, seemingly enchanted by the beautiful women, gradually ignored Yue’s threat. Meanwhile, Goujian prepared for war and in 473 BCE Yue conquered Wu.
Xi Shi’s actual role in Wu’s downfall remains unclear. Wu’s defeat involved poor political decisions and Yue’s military recovery.
Still, the story illustrated an important idea in Chinese political strategy: exploiting an opponent’s personal weaknesses can sometimes be more effective than confronting him directly.
A similar tactic appears in the 14th-century novel “Romance of the Three Kingdoms,” considered one of the classics of Chinese literature.

It tells the story of Dong Zhuo, a powerful warlord who controlled the imperial court during the late Eastern Han Dynasty. To remove him, Wang Yun, a senior court official loyal to the Han Dynasty promised a beautiful young woman, named Diaochan, in marriage to Dong Zhuo’s military commander. He then offered the same woman to Dong Zhuo.

The scheme fueled jealousy and distrust between the two men, eventually enabling Wang Yun to persuade Dong Zhuo’s underling to kill him. Wang Yun then briefly took charge of the imperial court on behalf of the Han emperor.

In modern intelligence operations, using romantic or sexual relationships to approach targets, obtain sensitive information or exert influence is commonly called a “honey trap.” It is, moreover, certainly not unique to China. Western and Soviet intelligence agencies used intimate relationships for espionage frequently during the Cold War.

Modern China also has documented cases. One example involves French diplomat Bernard Boursicot and the Chinese opera performer Shi Pei Pu. The pair met in Beijing in 1964 and maintained a long-term intimate relationship. Throughout, Boursicot was providing French diplomatic documents to China. The spying was eventually exposed and both involved were prosecuted for espionage in France in the 1980s.

A more recent example involves former U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell and Christine Fang, a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. Swalwell acknowledged in 2015 that he had been physically intimate with Fang on several occasions. At the time, Fang helped raise funds for Swalwell’s campaign and helped place an intern in his congressional office.

Jensen Huang’s position would make him a prime target for such a “honey trap” operation. His company has become central to the technological competition between the U.S and China. As AI becomes increasingly important to economic development, military capabilities and national security, moreover, Washington has repeatedly tightened restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China, hoping to slow its access to computing power.
Beijing is investing heavily in domestic semiconductor development. Yet Chinese companies still need advanced chips to train AI models and build data centers.
From Beijing’s perspective, advanced AI chips matter not only for Chinese technology companies but for future military and technological competition.
This puts Nvidia in a particularly important position and helps explain the national security concerns surrounding Huang.

However, strategic motives do not prove an intelligence operation occurred. Jensen Huang’s importance does not, in itself, establish that he was targeted by a honey trap or that Alice Huang acted for Chinese intelligence. Those are allegations that still require full investigation.

Yet it is surely true that in modern politics – just as in ancient China’s rivalries – rivals seek information about opponents, try to influence important decisions and exploit weaknesses to gain strategic advantages.
What has changed is who controls important strategic resources.

In ancient China, influencing a ruler through personal relationships could affect a country’s political and military decisions. Today, approaching a major technology executive could offer access to sensitive technologies.
More than 2,000 years ago, a powerful state could lose its advantage through a ruler’s personal weaknesses. Today, political and technological power are distributed differently.
But as long as important decisions depend on individuals, personal relationships may remain a weakness that rivals can exploit. – Rappler.com
Linggong Kong, Ph.D. Candidate in Political Science, Auburn University

articles.title: Airport chaos continues after US ground stop lifted – as it happened
articles.summary:
This blog is now closed. See our full reports:

  • US aviation agency lifts nationwide ground…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 3h agoClosing summary
4h agoUS airport chaos continues – in pictures
5h agoAirlines start resuming flights after ban lifted
6h agoWhat we know so far about the US flight fiasco that's grounded thousands of planes nationwide

blocks.text: Closing summary

We’re wrapping up this live coverage of the US ground stop and travel chaos that followed – it’s just passed 12.50am in Washington DC. Below’s a rundown on what happened, and you can read a full report here. Thanks for being with us.

items: The Federal Aviation Administration declared a nationwide ground stop on Friday afternoon, throwing airports into sudden chaos, after a communications failure at air traffic control centres.

More than 6,600 flights were cancelled and 8,600 delayed, with another 1,500 already cancelled for Sunday, according to FlightRadar24. Aviation analysts said the four-hour nationwide grounding could disrupt airline ⁠schedules for days. It was the longest flight shutdown since the attacks of September 11 2001.

The FAA lifted the ground stop later on Friday, with transportation secretary Sean Duffy saying US airspace reopened at 8.15pm ET (0115 GMT). But departures would ⁠resume gradually and it would take ​time for airlines to restore normal operations, he warned. “It’s going to be slow.”

blocks.caption: Passengers queue at a terminal at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta international airport in Georgia after the FAA’s ground stop.  Photograph: Elijah Nouvelage/Reuters

items: All US-bound departures from European airports are suspended until 5am UTC on Saturday, according to a notice published by the European traffic control agency, Eurocontrol.

US airlines including American, United and Southwest began resuming flights on Friday night. “Thank you for your understanding as we work as quickly as possible to fully restore normal operations,” Delta said.

Duffy said the federal government had “identified the problem” that brought down the US air traffic control system on Friday and it was “operational right now”. The system was “incredibly old”, he said. “Our routers actually got overloaded with data, and … they started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers. And because of that, we shut the system down.”
There was no indication from preliminary investigations that the communications stoppage was tied to a “nefarious attack”, homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin said.
Duffy blamed Congress for failing to fund a new air traffic control system that he said could prevent such outages, and called for $50bn to modernize it.

blocks.text: US airport chaos continues – in pictures
Here are some of the latest images coming in from US airports as the disruption from the FAA’s nationwide ground stop continues while some airlines slowly start resuming flights.

blocks.caption: Aeroline’s workers check in passengers while some aircraft remain grounded on Friday at Miami international airport, Florida.  Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPA
An Alaska Airlines employee listens to stranded passengers at Ronald Reagan Washington National airport in Virginia during the ground stop, which has now been lifted. Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPA
Passengers in Miami international airport’s waiting area.  Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPA
Planes are parked on the tarmac at LaGuardia airport in New York amid the flight ban.  Photograph: Ryan Murphy/AP
Airplane luggage from cancelled flights piles up at Reagan national airport outside Washington DC. Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPA
A person looks at a flight information board at LaGuardia airport in New York. Photograph: Ryan Murphy/AP
Passengers search for information using their phones at Chicago O’Hare international airport. Photograph: Kamil Krzaczyński/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Just to recap, travel plans were thrown into chaos across the US on Friday afternoon as passengers on planes and in airport terminals were suddenly thrust into limbo due to the nationwide ground stop.
Even now that the stoppage has been lifted, airlines will not be able to return to normal operations immediately because so many of their planes and crews are out of position.

At New York’s John F Kennedy airport, passengers found their travel plans abruptly cancelled – some even after they’d boarded, reports Edward Helmore in New York. Steve Honberger, heading home to Portland, Oregon, with his wife and daughter, said he’d been on a plane about to take off when the shutdown was announced.
double quotation markThey didn’t seem to know what’s happening, and they wanted to hold off as long as possible.
The plane sat at the gate for an hour and 40 minutes.

blocks.caption: Travellers with children rest on the floor at JFK airport during the ground stop.  Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPA

blocks.text: Delta has also said it is restarting flights, posting on social media:

double quotation markThe FAA-mandated ground stop has been lifted and we are safely resuming flights. Thank you for your understanding as we work as quickly as possible to fully restore normal operations.
Southwest Airlines said it was resuming a limited number of flights on Friday evening after consulting with the FAA.
The airline would “continue to adjust our plans as needed”, it said.
Airlines start resuming flights after ban lifted
US airlines have slowly begun resuming flights on Friday night after the FAA-mandated ground stop was lifted.
United Airlines said it was resuming operations, “including some Friday night flights”.
“Safety is our highest priority as we take care of our customers and employees,” the airline said in a post to X.

blocks.caption: Travellers wait at a United terminal at Los Angeles international airport on Friday amid the flight disruptions.  Photograph: Ethan Swope/AP

blocks.text: American Airlines says it will operate as many flights as possible on Friday night and aim for a strong recovery from the disruption.
The airline posted on social media:

double quotation markThe FAA’s nationwide ground stop has been lifted. We’re focused on operating as many remaining flights as possible this evening while positioning the airline for the strongest possible recovery in the days ahead.
It advised cutomers to check the status of their flights on the airline’s app or website.

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
All US-bound departures from European airports are suspended until 5am UTC on Saturday, according to a notice published by the European traffic control agency, Eurocontrol.
Forty-two European countries are members of Eurocontrol, including the 27 EU countries, the UK, Turkey and Israel.
The notice, issued by Network Manager Operations Centre Brussels at 10pm UTC, has been made on request of the US Federal Aviation Administration.

Looking in the opposite direction, however, several planes bound for Europe – including Dublin, Copenhagen, London, Milan, Paris and Rome – were allowed to depart from airports in Boston, New York and Washington in the past two hours.

blocks.caption: The Vaclav Havel airport in Prague, Czech Republic. Photograph: Michal Čížek/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Ben Doherty, a Guardian Australia reporter, is currently on a plane at Sydney airport, waiting to fly to the US. He writes:

US-bound flights out of Sydney in Australia have been held on the tarmac, some for up to three hours. Flights are being gradually cleared for departure after being held in Australia by the FAA out of concern planes would not be able to land once they reached the US.
Our flight has had to take on extra fuel after running the air-conditioning (needed for a plane full of people) for several hours while waiting for clearance.
It’s 13 hours from Sydney to LAX. We’ve been on board for three hours so far, haven’t yet moved, but about to taxi shortly.
It’s not been too bad. We’ve been kept informed by the captain, but the messages have reflected the uncertainty over this incident.

We were delayed, and then boarding was brought forward, reinstated at the original time. We were granted clearance to leave, but then this was rescinded. Even from a distance of 12,000 kilometres, the impacts of this are being felt.

blocks.caption: Planes at Sydney international airport in a file shot.  Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAP

blocks.text: What we know so far about the US flight fiasco that's grounded thousands of planes nationwide

If you’re just joining us, we’re continuing our live coverage of the major systems failure that led US aviation officials to ground flights nationwide for more than four hours on Friday. That continues to cause chaos for thousands of air travelers across the US and the world.
Here is what we know about the rare nationwide “ground stop” issued by the FAA that was in place from just before 4pm Eastern Time in the US until 8.15 pm.

items: Outages in communication, radio frequencies and radar began in Chicago, according to the Air Current, an aviation news site.
There is, as of now, no clear explanation of what, exactly, caused the “telecommunications outage” that forced the sudden halt to all departures at US airports.
According to the tracing site FlightAware, 8,553 flights were delayed on Friday, and there were 6,816 cancelled flights.

While Donald Trump was uncharacteristically silent throughout the crisis, his secretaries of transportation and homeland security, Sean Duffy and Markwayne Mullin, appeared to suggest that the cause of the outage was that older technology became overwhelmed with data after new technology was introduced by the FAA.
Mullin, a former Oklahoma senator now leading the US Department of Homeland Security, said “we’ve seen zero evidence that this was a cyber-attack.”
This is just the second nationwide ​ground stop of all departures since the 9/11 attacks. The previous one came in January 2023, when the FAA paused all ⁠domestic departures for less than two hours.
As disruptions ripple through the global aviation system, we will continue to track the impact of the outage, and look for answers as to what, exactly, went wrong.

articles.title: Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says
articles.summary: Trump will discuss the "reduction of nuclear weapons" during the unprecedented talks, a spokeswoman says.

blocks.text: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.

The historic meeting between the leaders of the US, Russia and China will take place as Trump attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," she said.
It is understood Iran may also be discussed during the meeting of the world's biggest nuclear powers, but not Ukraine. Moscow and Beijing are yet to comment.
No agreement was expected to follow the talks, an unnamed, senior American official said, according to news agencies AP and Reuters.

Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day summit between the 21 member states. He will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president returned to office in 2025.

"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People's Republic of China, and the president of the Russian Federation," Wales said.

She said Trump's trip, which will also include attending an Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo Pacific".

A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February, leaving the world's biggest nuclear arsenals without major guardrails and effectively marking an end to the arms control co-operation which helped to resolve the Cold War.
The UN has urged both sides to agree a new framework without delay. Trump however said he could replace the deal with a better agreement which included China, which has been building up its arsenal.
Former senior US officials and analysts told the BBC at the time that seeking Beijing and Moscow's co-operation could turn up major hurdles and take years.
Xi separately hosted both Putin and Trump in Beijing just days apart earlier this year, while the US president welcomed his Chinese counterpart to Washington in September.
Beijing has become a crucial trading partner for Moscow since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which has isolated Russia and left it subject to Western sanctions.

But a controversial US deal to import Russian diesel and the suspension of sanctions targeting the biggest buyers of Moscow's oil and gas - including China - heightened European concern about the Trump administration's softening towards the Kremlin last month.

Trump and Xi have meanwhile sought to project warmer ties at summits in Beijing and Washington this year - though little significant progress appeared to have been made on key issues such as trade, their race for AI dominance, and Taiwan. The war in Iran has also been a sticking point, with Beijing the largest buyer of Tehran's oil and its biggest trade partner.

Chinese state media reported on Friday that Xi would take part in "bilateral" talks on the sidelines of the Apec summit, citing a foreign ministry spokesman, but has not reported on the trilateral meeting.
Earlier this month, Russian state news agency Tass reported that Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov had said there were "signals confirming readiness" for such talks at the summit.

articles.title: Philippines, Canada conclude free trade deal talks, eye 2027 signing
articles.summary: The Philippines and Canada have concluded negotiations for a free trade agreement (FTA), with both countries eyeing its signing in 2027, Malacañang said Saturday, November 14.

blocks.text: November 14, 2026 | 1:44pm
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney shake hands during their meeting on the sidelines of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits on Nov. 14, 2026.
Presidential Communications Office via Facebook
MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines and Canada have concluded negotiations for a free trade agreement (FTA), with both countries eyeing its signing in 2027, Malacañang said Saturday, November 14.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met on Saturday on the sidelines of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits, where they discussed the trade deal and other areas of cooperation.
The proposed agreement covers trade in goods and services, investments, digital trade and small and medium-sized enterprises.

In a statement posted on Facebook, the Presidential Communications Office (PCO) said the FTA could help Philippine businesses expand their reach in the Canadian market and create more income opportunities for local entrepreneurs and workers.
The agreement could also benefit Filipinos providing services online through provisions covering digital trade.
Marcos and Carney also discussed investment opportunities under the Luzon Economic Corridor, particularly in transportation, infrastructure, agri-food, food logistics and cold-chain technologies.
The two leaders likewise reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening defense, security and maritime cooperation, as well as promoting peace and stability in the Indo-Pacific region.
The conclusion of negotiations follows the two leaders' meeting during Marcos' official visit to Canada in July, when they committed to completing discussions on the FTA within the year.
Both governments are now working toward signing the agreement in 2027, the PCO said.

articles.title: Prosecution sees no need for more evidence in Sara Duterte impeachment trial
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel does not see the need to present more evidence on the alleged unexplained wealth of Vice President Sara Duterte in her ongoing impeachment trial.

blocks.text: AMID DOLLAR ACCOUNTS
Published November 14, 2026 1:23pm
The House prosecution panel does not see the need to present more evidence on the alleged unexplained wealth of Vice President Sara Duterte in her ongoing impeachment trial.

At a news forum in Quezon City, House private prosecutor Benjamin "Jay" Tolosa Jr. said the panel is satisfied with the pieces of evidence it presented already on the supposed unexplained wealth and undeclared assets amounting to P817.87 million held by Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases “Mans” Carpio.
“We’re satisfied with that. We don’t see the need to present additional evidence,” Tolosa said.
This came amid reports that the Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) informed the Senate impeachment court that the Vice President held dollar accounts in the bank.
Duterte’s defense team, however, decided not to present a witness from the BPI.
Nonetheless, Tolosa said the prosecution was ready to cross examine the witness from BPI concerning the alleged dollar accounts of the Vice President.

“All other foreign currency denominated accounts hindi po ‘yan na-subpoena dahil nga hindi ‘yan pinayagan dahil sa applicable bank secrecy laws. So, we’re just mentioning na napansin namin na itong inatras na testigo may naka-mention na sa mga dokumento pertaining to foreign currency, dollar accounts ng Vice President,” he said.

(All other foreign currency denominated accounts were not subpoenaed because it is not allowed under applicable bank secrecy laws. So we're just mentioning that we noticed that this witness which was withdrawn was mentioned in documents pertaining to foreign currency, dollar accounts of the Vice President.)

The lawyer noted that the prosecution team is confident on the pieces of evidence, such as records of foreign currency transactions of Calle88, which is 47.5% owned by Carpio, it has already presented during the trial.
Meanwhile, the defense panel of the Vice President is likely to finish presenting its case before the end of November.
The next proceedings for Duterte’s impeachment trial are scheduled for November 19 to 20, after which the Senate will take a break from the trial to focus on the 2027 national budget.
Thereafter, the next trial day is expected to resume on December 1. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: University hounded out of Hungary by Orbán reaches out to new government
articles.summary:
Prospect of partial return to Budapest by Central European University suggests confidence in Hungary’s future

A university that Viktor Orbán tried to chase out of Hungary is open to…

blocks.text: A university that Viktor Orbán tried to chase out of Hungary is open to expanding its presence in Budapest, in a mark of confidence in the country’s democratic future.

Carsten Q Schneider, the interim president and rector of Central European University (CEU), said it was interested in increasing its programmes in Budapest, as long as this did not damage the student experience.

So far the CEU has not held formal talks with Hungary’s new government, which has promised to restore academic freedom, “but our hand is reaching out, their hand is reaching out – it is just that they have many things to do”, the academic told the Guardian.

The CEU relocated its main activities to Vienna from Budapest in 2019, after pressure from the previous government led by Orbán. But the outlook changed when Péter Magyar won a landslide victory in April pledging to root out corruption and reform the state.

The CEU, founded by Hungarian-American financier and philanthropist George Soros in 1991 to entrench democratic change in the region, was forced to cease awarding degrees in Budapest in response to a law widely seen as targeting the institution.

The EU’s highest court struck down Hungary’s “Lex CEU” in 2020, finding that it violated the EU charter of fundamental rights, but the verdict came too late for the university. The CEU retains 312 staff in Budapest, mostly administrative, but the majority, 476, and all its teaching, are in Vienna.

blocks.caption: CEU’s main building in Budapest, pictured in 2018. Photograph: Bernadett Szabó/Reuters

blocks.text: Schneider said upgrading the status of the CEU, which is privately funded, in Budapest would be “a symbol for academic freedom [and] of resilience” but depended on goodwill and funding independent of the Hungarian government. He said a decision on its future in Hungary would be taken by the CEU’s 13-member board, whose members include Soros and his son, Alexander Soros.
“We don’t want special treatment,” Schneider said. ‘“We are a great asset, so let’s work out something.”

But the CEU, which he said was “thriving tremendously” in Vienna, does not plan a wholesale return to Budapest. Any change would have to ensure the quality of the student experience, for instance, assuring that students would be able to combine courses, say in economics and history, without having to travel the 200km-plus distance between the two cities.
Focused on social sciences, law and humanities, the CEU has more than 1,400 students from 103 countries, mostly doing master’s and PhD programmes.

According to Schneider, for the first time in the CEU’s 25-year history, students from the US now make up the largest cohort of master’s students (10%). The CEU has seen an increase in US applicants since Donald Trump returned to the White House and launched a sweeping campaign against elite universities, including slashing federal funding and seeking to exert control over internal policies.

The CEU rector has had informal talks with US academics on how to maintain academic freedom under pressure from rightwing populists. He described his message as: “Don’t be naive for a second. These people have a plan, so it’s not by accident that they attack universities. They want to have cultural hegemony.” He added, however, that Trump and allied movements, such as Germany’s Alternative für Deutschland, have identified “real problems”, such as in the US how universities have entrenched “a reproduction of elites”

When coming under political pressure, he said universities needed “to look for allies”, among other academic institutions, students, alumni and parents. Institutions also had to stand up for disciplines under attack, such as gender studies, Schneider added.
after newsletter promotion
He recalled the outpouring of support for CEU – when tens of thousands of people protested in Budapest in defence of the university – as “one of the most humbling experiences I have had”.
Schneider, a German political scientist who specialises in the study of democracies and regime transition, said Magyar had successfully used Orbán’s political machine against him.

“Nobody has a better idea than [Magyar] how to defeat the most potent and the most skilled illiberal populist [Orbán]. So he knows something.” He added: “The people and skills that you need to bring a non-democratic regime down are not the same and sometimes the opposite of what it takes to establish a democracy. So the question now is whether he [Magyar] has the skills to basically reinvent liberal democracy for the 21st century.”

Schneider said Hungary could be the world’s first “post-illiberal democracy” – a model for democratic restoration, just as Orbán inspired rightwing populists around the world. But he also raised doubts about this thesis, saying there were questions about how Magyar and his Tisza party might develop in the context of Hungary’s “very difficult economic situation”.

The test would be, he suggested, when Magyar faces losing support and, eventually, defeat at the ballot box. “So what happens when he loses support and then cracks in his movement appear? Will he be the visionary leader who manages … to establish a three, four, five-party system, where people compete? That is to be seen.”

articles.title: WATCH: Protests staged vs. Trump's arrival in PH for ASEAN Summit 2026
articles.summary: Several groups on Saturday staged protest actions ahead the arrival of US President Donald Trump in the country for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit.

blocks.text: Published November 14, 2026 12:36pm
Several groups on Saturday staged protest actions ahead the arrival of US President Donald Trump in the country for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit.

In a tweet by John Consulta of GMA News, a number of protesters were seen holding tarpaulins bearing their grievances against Trump, the US-led Pax Silica initiative, and reliance on fossil fuels, among other issues.
The program of activities of the 49th ASEAN Summit will proceed as scheduled even though Trump is expected to arrive minutes before the international conference concludes.
Foreign Affairs Assistant Secretary Dominic Xavier "Dax" Imperial, spokesperson for ASEAN Affairs, reported on the matter in a press briefing on Friday.
Based on the ASEAN organizer's advisory, Trump is scheduled to arrive in the Philippines on Tuesday, the day of the closing ceremony of the ASEAN Summit.
Meanwhile, Trump and President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. will have a bilateral engagement on Wednesday, November 18.
Trump's attendance has raised concerns among several civil society groups, with many announcing protests to denounce his visit to the Philippines.

On Friday, students staged nationwide campus walkouts to protest Trump's arrival and Pax Silica, the proposed semiconductor and industrial hub that is set to rise in New Clark City in Tarlac. Amid the public outcry, the Marcos administration has clarified that Pax Silica will not host artificial intelligence data centers.
Transport group PISTON, meanwhile, has announced that it would conduct a transport strike on Monday, November 16, to convey their indignation against Trump's arrival in the country. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Senegal Youth Olympics in Dakar end on high note
articles.summary: Enthusiastic crowds attended the games in Senegal, with China taking home the most gold medals. It's the first Olympic Games since Russia's war on Ukraine where Russian athletes can compete under…

image.caption: The Summer Youth Olympics in Dakar was held from October 31 to November 13 Image: Sylvain Cherkaoui/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Senegal Summer Youth Olympics in Dakar ended Friday after two weeks of games on a high note.

It's the first time an African country has hosted an Olympic event, and African nations also brought home a record haul of medals. The Games were met with enthusiasm, with Dakar's streets and beaches filled with sports fans.
Nearly 2,700 young athletes took part in the games, which featured 153 medal events across 25 sports.
IOC president on Senegal games: 'Expectations have been exceeded'

"There is a beautiful African proverb, 'It take a village to raise a child.' And if these Youth Olympic Games have shown us anything it is what can happen when an entire country comes together for its young people," International Olympic Committee President Kirsty Coventry said in a thank-you ceremony on Friday.

Coventry praised the Senegalese people for hosting the games: "You have shown the world what Senegal and Africa are capable of, and when people come together behind a shared dream, how strong that can make us. You have every reason to be so proud."
She said earlier in the week that "expectations have been exceeded" when it came to Senegal hosting the games and that it shows what African nations are capable of in the future.
Which countries took home the most medals?
China took home the most gold medals at 18.

Japan took home 11 gold medals, whereas Russia received eight. It was the first time Russian athletes took part in an Olympic event under their own national flag since the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022.
Egypt won six gold medals, and Ethiopia and Senegal each earned five.

blocks.caption: Female wrestler Elisabeth Diatta, who is 16 years old, took home Senegal's first gold medalImage: Kadir Caliskan/United World Wrestling/picture alliance

blocks.text: It was the first time Senegal had ever won an Olympic gold, with 136 Senegalese athletes participating in the games.
The next Summer Youth Olympics will take place in 2030, with Chile, Paraguay and Thailand having confirmed their bids to host the games.

articles.title: Trump to meet Xi, Putin for three-way huddle on nuclear arms talks
articles.summary: The White House has said President Donald Trump will urge Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin to discuss cutting nuclear arsenals in Shenzhen next week, though a senior US official expects no agreement.

image.caption: The meeting would be the first of its kind if it happens as scheduled Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: United States President Donald Trump will push for nuclear arms reductions when he meets Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China next week, the White House said Friday.
A senior US official said no agreement is expected, Reuters reported.
What do we know?
The meeting is set for Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen and would be the first of its kind.

"He will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," White House spokesperson Olivia Wales told reporters. Trump will also raise the US-Israeli war against Iran but is not expected to bring up Ukraine, the official told Reuters.

"We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement," the official said. "This is a difficult topic for China to address, but we do think it’s time for China to sort of step up, you know, to the adults’ table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things."
Where does China stand?
China has long resisted nuclear talks with Washington, arguing that Russia and the US, which hold larger arsenals, should speak directly.
In October, its Foreign Ministry said it would be "neither fair, reasonable nor realistic to ask China to join the so-called trilateral nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage."
Chinese state media have said Xi will hold "bilateral" talks at the summit but have not mentioned a trilateral meeting. Moscow and Beijing have yet to comment on the White House announcement.

The US-Russia New START treaty expired in February, leaving the world’s biggest arsenals without major limits. Russia has the most stored warheads, followed by the US and China, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
Trump leaves Monday for a four-day Asia trip that includes a stop in the Philippines.

articles.title: What we know about the longest ground stop since 9/11
articles.summary: US officials say the disruption was caused by old equipment overloading and not a cyber-attack or a Microsoft outage.

blocks.text: US ground stop caused by 'incredibly old air traffic control system', Duffy says
The US Federal Aviation Administration has lifted the longest nationwide ground stop of flights since the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks.
The FAA said Friday's stoppage, which lasted more than four hours, was "due to extraordinary circumstances" from a communication issue affecting all air traffic control centres.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of an attack and that everybody was safe.
Here's what we know.
How many flights were affected?
The ground stop led to more than 8,500 delayed and nearly 8,000 cancelled flights on Friday, according to FlightAware.
The FAA's initial announcement at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) said all flights departing within the US would be grounded until further notice.
More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air at the time. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.
Hours later, some flights were allowed to take off from San Francisco International airport.
The Federal Aviation Administration opened skies again at until 20:15 EST.
'We'll get home one day' - US travellers impacted by nationwide ground stop
What about international flights?
All US-bound air traffic from Eurocontrol member states was suspended "on request of the FAA due to technical issues", according to Eurocontrol's website.
There are 42 Eurocontrol member states, including dozens of EU nations, the UK, Ukraine, and Turkey, as well as Israel and Morocco.
Australia's largest international airport, Sydney, grounded all US-bound flights until further notice.
Air Canada cancelled flights between the US and Canada.
When will normal service resume?
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a news conference on Friday night that the outage would cause a ripple effect for a few days.
"It's going to take us some time to unwind what's happened this afternoon," Duffy said.
Tens of thousands of people were stranded in airports around the country, many of them "without any knowledge of where they're going to sleep tonight", Duffy said.
Delta Air Lines and United Airlines said they were resuming operations.
American Airlines said it was "focused on operating as many remaining flights as possible this evening". JetBlue said it would resume flights on Saturday morning.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Luggage from cancelled flights at Ronald Reagan airport

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
Luggage from cancelled flights at Ronald Reagan airport
What caused the ground stop?
Duffy said a legacy air traffic control communications system became overloaded.
"So this is analogue telecom. Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data and they went down," Duffy said.
He said this had affected communications and radar. The system needs a complete overhaul, he said, estimating a $50 billion price tag.
"It's going to continue to fail," he said.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told the news conference said they had seen "zero evidence" it was a cyber-attack.
He also ruled out any link to the global Microsoft outage that began on Thursday.
Mullin said the introduction of some new technology into an old air traffic control system had overwhelmed it.
Both cabinet secretaries insisted the public was never in danger during the stoppage.
When was the last ground stop?
It was only the second such nationwide stoppage since the immediate aftermath of the al-Qaeda plane hijackings of 11 September 2001.
"This looks like the worst since 9/11, but clearly not on that scale," Dr Guy Gratton, an associate professor of aviation at Cranfield University, told BBC Verify.
Dr Gratton pointed to a US grounding in 2023 due to a failure in the Notice to Air Missions (Notam) system.
"That lasted 1 hour and 52 minutes, delayed about 9,500 flights and cancelled about 1,300," he said.
The 2023 outage meant air traffic safety notices could no longer be published, and flights were grounded until that system was restored.
But Friday's incident lasted longer than the 2023 event.

blocks.text: Politics
Canada and the Philippines have concluded talks for a free-trade agreement, which is expected to be formally signed next year.
Negotiations on free-trade deal began just over a year ago
Prime Minister Mark Carney is meeting with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in Manila at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit.
The two leaders are overseeing the signing of a document that formally ends negotiations for the Philippines-Canada Free Trade Agreement, which had started just over a year ago.
Last October, Carney rebooted trade talks with the Philippines, which Ottawa first started formally exploring in 2015.

During consultations, corporations were broadly supportive of the deal to increase trade, but civil society raised concerns about the Philippines' track record on the environment, labour and human rights.
Canada is also pursuing a broader trade agreement with the ASEAN bloc, which includes the Philippines and 10 other countries, including Thailand.

articles.title: PAL monitors US flight situation after nationwide ground stop
articles.summary: Flag carrier Philippine Airlines is monitoring its flights to and from the United States after the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted a nationwide ground stop that disrupted air travel…

blocks.text: November 14, 2026 | 11:11am
Passengers watch departure flights screens at Chicago O'Hare International Airport in Chicago, on November 13, 2026.
AFP / Kamil Krzaczynski

MANILA, Philippines — Flag carrier Philippine Airlines is monitoring its flights to and from the United States after the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted a nationwide ground stop that disrupted air travel for several hours on Friday.
In an advisory on Saturday, PAL said it continues to monitor its US flights as operations normalize.
"Passengers are advised to check their flight status through PAL’s official communication channels for the latest updates," the airlines said.
The FAA imposed the nationwide ground stop following a communications outage that US officials attributed to the country's aging air traffic control system.
The disruption left hundreds of thousands of passengers stranded, with some travelers forced to disembark from planes shortly before departure.
Nearly 6,000 flights were canceled, including some international routes, according to flight tracking service FlightAware.
US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the outage on outdated equipment, including switches, routers and copper telephone lines used by the country's air traffic control system.
Duffy described the incident as a legacy system problem and renewed his call for Congress to fund the modernization of the US air traffic control system.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, meanwhile, said there was no evidence that the outage was caused by a cyberattack or an artificial intelligence-related attack.
The FAA lifted the nationwide ground stop after about four hours. However, flight disruptions were expected to continue as airlines worked to address delays and cancellations caused by the outage.

articles.title: ‘It’s frustrating’: chaos at US airports as stoppage grinds travel plans to a halt
articles.summary:
Travelers and crew feeling ‘pissed’ or ‘lucky’ depending on level of upset amid nationwide ground stop

The US Federal Aviation Administration’s decision to ground all flights on Friday threw…

blocks.text: The US Federal Aviation Administration’s decision to ground all flights on Friday threw airports and travel plans into chaos across the country, as passengers on planes and in airport terminals were suddenly thrust into limbo.
At New York’s John F Kennedy airport, passengers found their travel plans abruptly cancelled – some even after they’d boarded.
Steve Honberger, heading home to Portland, Oregon, with his wife and daughter, said he’d been on a plane about to take off when the shutdown was announced.
“They didn’t seem to know what’s happening, and they wanted to hold off as long as possible,” Honberger said. The plane sat at the gate for an hour and 40 minutes.

blocks.caption: Passengers inside an airplane at JFK airport in New York City on Friday. Photograph: Angelina Katsanis/Reuters

blocks.text: They realized they were just going to be sitting at the gate, so they eventually asked to deplane and rebook.

Many still thought it worth showing up despite the uncertainty of when flights would resume. Rashid Kahn, heading for Miami, said he’d “heard about the ground stop on the news, but the airline said we might take off 10 or 11pm”.
“I am hopeful,” he added. “But maybe it’s something to do with the date. I’m not super serious, but it’s Friday the 13th.”

Tom Rolenaitis, returning a Shiba Inu show dog named Tsuki to Finland, said it was frustrating. “It’s cutting into a three-day trip and I have to get him back to his owner. We have no idea what’s happening.”

A flight attendant headed for Barcelona, who declined to give his name, said he had been told his American Airlines flight would be slightly delayed and all incoming international flights were being allowed to land.
Another crew member from the flight said cheerfully: “Things happen. Hopefully it will all be resolved.”

As the day wore on, passengers on international flights began to be boarding, prompting applause to erupt at the gates. “It’s moving, so that’s good,” said an airline representative. “But only international is going.”

The FAA issued the nationwide ground stop on Friday afternoon, citing a communications problems at regional air traffic control centers, according to an FAA notice. Four hours later, FAA sent out an advisory lifting the stop.

blocks.caption: Planes parked on the tarmac at JFK airport on Friday. Photograph: Angelina Katsanis/Reuters

blocks.text: “You can’t moan about this kind of thing ... it’s such a first-world problem,” said Laura, a woman who lives in New York and was heading for San Francisco when her JetBlue flight was grounded. She still hoped her flight would go. “That what I have to figure out,” she said, sitting on the floor of the terminal.

With the lifting of the ground stop, more chaos followed. “My flight was cancelled, then I go to a kiosk, put my information in and it says I’m leaving at 3am. Then I talk to the desk and they know nothing,” said Larson Welsh, heading to Las Vegas from Paris.

The outage has nonetheless caused upheaval for thousands of passengers. There have been 10,343 flight delays within, into or out of the US so far, according to the website FlightAware, and 1,479 cancellations. More than 1,000 aircraft were bound for US when the ground stop was announced, according to Flightradar24.
Only two national ground stops have previously been issued: on 11 September 2001, after the terrorist attack on the World Trade Center; and in January 2023, after a communications failure.

The ground stop also snarled the sports world, leaving NBA, NHL and college teams stranded as they tried to reach their destinations before a big weekend of games. It also was unclear whether referees, who typically fly to their assignments the day before games, would make it on time.

blocks.caption: Travelers at JFK airport on Friday. Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPA

blocks.text: Back at JFK, travelers expressed frustration and resignation.

“My flight to California was cancelled with no information and no rebooking. My flight was cancelled last night as well due to bad weather. Now I’m missing a family event,” said a man who gave his name only as Andy. “It’s frustrating. And I’m pissed.”
Honberger, meanwhile, tried to stay optimistic, saying: “There are people sitting on tarmac, so we count ourselves lucky and we were able to book ourselves a hotel for the night.”
Tom Johnson and agencies contributed reporting

articles.title: SpaceX launches Starship rocket, fails to recover booster
articles.summary: SpaceX had planned to catch and reuse both stages of its biggest rocket for the first time. But the booster exploded over the Gulf of Mexico, while the spacecraft continued into orbit.

image.caption: Fingers crossed that Saturday's landing of the top part of the rocket won't end like the boosterImage: Ricardo Arduengo/AFP

blocks.text: US company SpaceX has successfully launched the latest flight of its Starship spacecraft into orbit but did not recover the booster rocket as planned.
The company, owned by tech billionaire Elon Musk, is hoping to develop a fully reusable rocket system. It had planned to recover both the booster and the upper stage, which is the spacecraft itself.
Instead of landing back at the launch site, the booster exploded above the Gulf of Mexico. The upper stage is currently in orbitand the plan is to recover it on Saturday when it returns to Earth.
It is to be caught by mechanical arms upon landing back at the launch pad, marking the first time the spacecraft would return to Earth. It could then potentially be reused in the future.
In addition to testing the reusable rocket system, the mission also delivered 26 of SpaceX’s satellitesfor its Starlink network.
How did the launch go?

SpaceX's Starship is the world's largest and most powerful rocket system. At 124 meters (407 feet) tall, it consists of a spacecraft mounted on a booster rocket. Both stages were designed from the outset to be fully reusable.

At the launch, both the spacecraft and booster successfully lifted off from the SpaceX South Texas Starbase site. While the Friday launch was an uncrewed mission, Starship is designed to carry both crew and cargo.

blocks.caption: Both booster and Starship at the launch of the missionImage: Steve Nesius/REUTERS

blocks.text: On its return path, the booster diverted from its flight path to the launch site and steered to a designated area over the Gulf of Mexico where it exploded over the sea surface. The reasons for the failure of the controlled landing were not immediately clear.
"Not sure right now why we weren't able to bring it back," SpaceX's Dan Huot said.
The upper stage continued into orbit and soon after began releasing the 26 satellites it was carrying.
It is scheduled to return to Earth on Saturday.
Developing a fully reusable rocket system is key to SpaceX’s goal to drive down the cost of spaceflight.

In previous launches, the Starship booster was successfully recovered. The upper stages of the 14 previous Starship missions have all ended up in the ocean though, either by design or because of failures.
The new objective of Friday’s launch was to recover both stages of the Starship launch system.
Currently, SpaceX is mostly using smaller Falcon rockets, which are not fully reusable because the second stage cannot be recovered.
Musk said he expected SpaceX to conduct Starship launches once a week by early 2027.
The project has received billions of dollars in NASA funding, with SpaceX also investing at least $15 billion.
The main goal of the program is to put astronauts on the Moon by 2028 although outstanding technical challenges could delay that schedule.
China's new rocket heats up space race, challenging SpaceX

articles.title: What we know about Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang
articles.summary: Alice Huang had a long career in Chinese finance before later emerging as an executive in the global race for artificial-intelligence chips.
articles.byline: WEN-YEE LEE, ANDREW SILVER, LAURIE CHEN, Reuters

blocks.text: Published November 14, 2026 10:23am
Alice Huang had a long career in Chinese finance before later emerging as an executive in the global race for artificial-intelligence chips.

Known also as Huang Le, she was a top executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based tech company that was an Nvidia business partner in the Asia-Pacific region. Her reported affair with Jensen Huang led in part to his resignation as Nvidia CEO on November 12.

Several news organizations, including the New York Times and the Wall Street Journal, have reported that US and other government authorities had suspicions that Alice Huang was spying for Beijing. In the spring of 2026, Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of a classified memo detailing intelligence indicating that China's Ministry of State Security had recruited Huang to target Nvidia's CEO, the New York Times said.
Reuters has not been able to verify any of the allegations made in the New York Times, along with other media reports, about Huang's suspected spying for China.
Beijing has denied Alice Huang is a spy. Reuters attempts to reach Alice Huang have been unsuccessful. Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are not related.
Here are more details about what is known about Alice Huang:
Suspicions of spying, government statements

The New York Times reported on November 10 that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had briefed President Donald Trump aboard Air Force One en ​route to China in May about US intelligence indicating Jensen Huang was involved with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.

The briefing marked at least the second time in seven months that Trump had been told about the intelligence, the Times ​reported, citing people with knowledge of the matter. Reuters was not able to confirm these warnings to Trump.

President Trump said on November 9 that the FBI was looking into the spying allegations. He said Jensen Huang told him he had no idea of the spying allegations, and also said he did not need to act on intelligence when he was briefed.

US Attorney General Todd Blanche said on November 12 that the Department of Justice had not yet reached a conclusion as to whether Alice Huang was a spy for China. CNN reported that day that US intelligence officials are still working to understand their relationship, citing people who say there is disagreement about the strength of the evidence that she was recruited to spy for Beijing.

Singapore's home affairs ministry said on November 12 that it had seized Alice Huang's passport in 2025 while investigating her for other offenses, including buying servers that were exported via Singapore to Malaysia without entering the Singapore market. The ministry said there was insufficient evidence to establish Alice Huang had committed any offenses.

The country's foreign ministry also said it received "limited" help from the US in its probe that began in 2025 into false declarations in the purchase of servers and other related offenses. Alice Huang left the country in February and was barred from re-entering following Singapore's investigation, the ministry said.
Ties to Jensen Huang

The Financial Times reported on November 6 that Alice Huang had a romantic affair with Jensen Huang. On November 8, Jensen Huang released a statement acknowledging an extramarital affair, without naming Alice Huang in the statement.
Reuters has verified photos of Jensen Huang and Alice Huang together at several different events over the last two-plus years, with the earliest dating to December 2023.
Role at Megaspeed

Huang became the controlling shareholder of Singapore-based cloud-computing company Megaspeed International in March 2023, according to Washington-based research group C4ADS, which reviewed corporate records.

In October 2025, the New York Times reported the company was under US investigation over whether it was helping Chinese customers obtain advanced Nvidia chips subject to Washington's export controls. China has denied this allegation, and there has been no public finding that Megaspeed violated ​the rules.
Earlier this week, The Information reported that Jensen Huang's ties to Alice Huang facilitated at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip sales to China.
Megaspeed said on November 12 that it has cooperated with US inspections.
Corporate roles

Alice Huang previously worked in banking and investment management, according to Chinese fund-industry records and an indexed profile on private-fund database ​Simuwang, which also listed an earlier career in television journalism. She also held senior positions at Shanghai Hexi Investment Management, a Chinese investment firm.
She held senior roles ​at a Shanghai investment firm before her role at Megaspeed, according to financial records, corporate filings and company materials reviewed by Reuters. — Reuters

articles.title: US lifts nationwide ground stop for airports hours after halting all departures
articles.summary: The US federal aviation regulator has lifted a nationwide ground stop for all airports. Trump administration officials blame "overloaded" and "outdated" systems for the hourslong halt to departures.

image.caption: Flights were delayed at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, which serves the nation's capital Image: Jonathan Ernst/REUTERS

blocks.text: The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) canceled a ground stop on all national flights hours after stopping departures at US airports on Friday.
"We have old switches, old routers, we use 1980s old copper lines. We use an old system," US Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said. "It was a legacy network problem."

US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication the communications breakdown resulted from a cyberattack or artificial intelligence and that the ⁠public ​was ​never ​in danger.

Over 4,500 flights were canceled Friday and about 700 for Saturday and over 10,000 flights within, into, or out of the United States were delayed, according to the FlightAware aviation tracker. With some 11,000 flights scheduled to depart from US airports after 4 p.m. local time (2200 UTC), more cancellations were expected, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company.
What do we know so far?
"All departing traffic should remain groundstopped until further notice," the FAA had said earlier Friday.

The agency said the ground stop was "due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety." The FAA cited a temporary telecommunication outage and said, "Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis."
The agency said flights were halted "out of abundance of caution."
In a post on X, Duffy said the stop was due to a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.
"FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them," he wrote.

The European Organisation for the Safety of Air Navigation, Eurocontrol, said all flights departing for US airports from its 42 member states were suspended following a request from the FAA to deal with technical issues.
Canada implementing 'traffic management' measures at major airports

Canada's air navigation service provider, NAV Canada, said it is closely monitoring the US ground stop and later said, "It was implementing traffic management measures at Toronto Pearson, Montreal-Trudeau, Calgary and Vancouver to safely manage traffic volumes."
"Travelers should expect delays and check with their airline. Our systems are operating normally," NAV Canada added.
Toronto Pearson Airport said flights between Toronto and the US have been impacted by the ground stop.
The FAA ground stop order came a day after Duffy asked Congress for $30 billion to upgrade and modernize the US Air Traffic Control System.

"This investment is critical to complete the modernization of our national airspace — delivering a resilient telecommunications backbone for air traffic controllers, modern hardware and software, state-of-the-art control towers, and world-class airport infrastructure," Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought wrote in a letter to lawmakers.
It's the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when the FAA dealt with a system outage. Prior to that, the last ground stop was after the September 11, 2001 terror attacks.

Passengers bound for southern Luzon flock to the Cubao Bus Terminal on March 28, 2026
The Philippine STAR / Michael Varcas

MANILA, Philippines — The Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board issued special permits to 372 passenger buses in anticipation of an influx of passengers traveling during the five-day long Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit break.

Northern Luzon routes received the most permits with 245 units, followed by Central Luzon routes at 111 buses. The remaining 16 permits were granted among buses bound for Bicol, Southern Luzon and Western Visayas.
Bus stations along the Epifanio de los Santos Avenue Busway were also inspected ahead of the long weekend, following directives from Malacañang to ensure continuous operation during the break.

The Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange saw fewer travelers heading to the provinces for Undas this year as many chose to wait for the ASEAN Summit on November 16 to 18, which has been declared a special non-working holiday in Metro Manila.

Heightened security protocols during the duration of the summit. Travelers have been advised to plan ahead in light of disruptions including flight cancellations and schedule adjustments, road closures and traffic advisories.

In an interview on Super Radyo dzBB, DSWD spokesperson Assistant Secretary Irene Dumlao said "close to hundred" jeepney drivers serving the Baclaran-Divisoria route were among the beneficiaries of P10,000-cash aid for those affected by ASEAN preparations.
"Nasa 2,500 na ang nabigyan natin ng assistance. Ito 'yung mga eatery workers, vendors, sari-sari store owners, jeepney drivers na naapektuhan," Dumlao said.

"Nu'ng Thursday, nasa Parañaque naman tayo. Nasa mahigit 1,400 na mga vendor, lalo na sa may Baclaran area ang nabigyan din ng assistance. Kahapon, bumalik tayo ng Pasay City... close to a thousand ang nabigyan din natin ng tulong-pinansyal," she added.
The DSWD has apologized to those affected by ASEAN security measures and preparations.

"We have worked with the local government units kaya naging mabilis ang provision ng assistance. Batid naman kasi ng pamahalaan na ang pagkakaantala ng kabuhayan ay talagang nakakapagdulot ng krisis sa pamilya," Dumlao said.

articles.title: All passengers and crew accounted for after New Orleans boat crash in ‘miracle on the Mississippi’
articles.summary: No passengers or crew were killed or critically hurt after a tanker collided with a river cruise ship on the Mississippi River, officials say
articles.byline: Ramon Antonio Vargas and Lucy Campbell in New Orleans

blocks.text: In what the city’s mayor declared a “miracle on the Mississippi”, all passengers were accounted for – with none killed or critically hurt – after a tanker collided with a river cruise ship docked on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday afternoon.

Thirty-two people were taken to local hospitals after the Atlantic Asphalt tanker struck American Cruise Lines’s American Heritage at about 12.30pm – but none of their injuries were considered critical, New Orleans’s mayor, Helena Moreno, said at a news conference.

Zero passengers or crew members were unaccounted for, Moreno said. She attributed that fact to a hectic but effective multi-agency rescue effort after the American Heritage was struck and a number of people ended up in the river, whose waters are cold and its currents are infamously perilous.
That “truly is a miracle on the Mississippi,” Moreno said near the scene of the crash, as a group of fellow officials around her applauded.
The American Heritage had 197 passengers onboard when it was hit, Port of New Orleans press secretary Kimberly Curth said in a statement.
About two hours before that, the American Heritage had docked at the port to begin passenger disembarkation, Curth said.

Thirty of those reported injured were on the American Heritage, and they were said to have mostly had bumps and bruises. Two others were harbor police officers who were on the river boat after the crash participating in rescue efforts.

Officials did not immediately provide details about what caused the crash. Moreno said investigators would explore whether there was some loss of steering on the Atlantic Asphalt before it struck the American Heritage, as an emergency response source had said earlier – but that had not been immediately confirmed.

The website marinetraffic.com showed the Atlantic Asphalt’s path was seemingly uneventful as it went around the challenging Mississippi River bend near New Orleans’ Algiers Point neighborhood. It had just made it past the Crescent City Connection bridge linking New Orleans’ central business district and the community’s Algiers section when it began heading generally to its starboard – or right – side.

Video provided to Guardian reporting partner WWL Louisiana showed the Atlantic Asphalt then T-boned the side of the American Heritage. The cruise ship eventually slowly rolled on to its side where it was struck, according to the video, which the CBS affiliate obtained from Barry Kern, proprietor of Mardi Gras World, a tourist attraction near the scene of the crash.
One witness, Jamie Holford, told local NBC News affiliate WDSU that it took 15 minutes “from impact to where it rolled over”.
“Surreal,” Holford said. “That’s what that was.”

Maritime law expert Martin J Davies of New Orleans’ Tulane University told local Fox affiliate WVUE that the Atlantic Asphalt was fortunate to have not hit the Crescent City Connection, which could have endangered motorists on a two-span, cantilever, steel truss bridge that is estimated to carry about 160,000 cars daily.
“This is obviously a really bad incident,” Davies said. “But it could also have struck the bridge, which it didn’t.”

A video from WDSU showed crew members of a tugboat working to pull people in lifejackets or holding on to flotation rings out of the river. An emergency response that drew in firefighters, US Coast Guard helicopter and boat crews, as well as port and city police – among others – also helped pull out people who ended up in the water in plain view of cameras and eyewitnesses.

One image on social media showed people climbing on the side of the cruise boat – specifically, on stateroom balconies – after it was struck, with chairs and tables strewn about after it evidently took on water.

Blake Paterson, an independent New Orleans journalist, who publishes Perdido Street.News, interviewed 65-year-old American Heritage passenger Tamara Carrasco about what she saw at the time of the crash.

The retired Atlanta elementary school teacher told Paterson that she was dining on the first floor of the riverboat when she saw the tanker careering toward the American Heritage. The tanker dropped its anchor, and she could see its crew running away on its deck, according to what Carrasco told Paterson.

Carrasco began running to the other side of the river boat, but she was knocked to the ground when the tanker hit. She said water began pouring into the dining room, making her think it was “like the Titanic”.

An employee at the Ernest N Morial Convention Center next to the scene of Friday’s crash said she realized something was awry when she could see from her vantage point that the tip of the American Heritage was tilted. She then grasped the nature of situation when she heard desperate shrieks.

“People were screaming for help,” said the employee, who asked to not be named. She recalled how she and colleagues assembled wheelchairs, water and other items in case survivors would soon need them.
The American Heritage’s passengers were brought inside the New Orleans port’s administration building, next to the convention center.

At the news conference where officials then confirmed there were no casualties, Louisiana governor Jeff Landry echoed Moreno in invoking the term “miracle”, especially “when you think about the population that was on that cruise ship – and the ability for us to get them off and out of the water”.
“The Mississippi River is not some quiet pond,” Landry said. “There were challenges out there.”

With everyone accounted for, New Orleans’s US Coast Guard commander, Melanie Burnham, said the focus would shift to re-opening the river to traffic. It had been closed from mile markers 93 to 96 to facilitate rescue efforts.
US House majority leader Steve Scalise, a suburban New Orleans Republican, said on Friday that the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) would investigate the crash.

A statement from American Cruise Lines on Friday said “guests and crew were evacuated” from the American Heritage but did not elaborate. “We are deeply concerned for everyone involved,” the cruise operator’s statement added.

The American Heritage, a 300ft paddle-wheel ship, was built in 2015 and previously sailed as the Queen of the Mississippi. It has more than 80 staterooms and operates cruises on the Mississippi River, including ones which depart from New Orleans.

The Atlantic Asphalt is a oil tanker built in 2017 measuring approximately 160 meters in length and has a deadweight of 17,764 metric tons. It flies the flag of the Marshall Islands and is owned and commercially operated by Nave Shipping SA, a company registered in Liberia. Its maintenance, technical and safety operations are overseen by Singapore-based Thome Ship Management, according to online records.
The vessel, which had a next recorded destination for Singapore, does not appear on the international sanctions lists checked by maritime tracking services, including Magic Port.
However, it was previously fined C$7,800 by Canadian authorities for a violation of the Canada Shipping Act and related vessel pollution regulations.

The penalty, recorded on 11 August 2020, stemmed from an officer failing to properly carry out their duties while supervising a transfer operation aboard the oil tanker, according to the Canadian government.

To many in New Orleans, the crash involving the Atlantic Asphalt called to mind an episode nearby – nearly 30 years earlier – when a cargo ship struck a wharf adjacent to the city’s Riverwalk shopping center and Hilton Riverside hotel.

No deaths resulted from that case, which occurred on 14 December 1996 after the Liberian-registered Bright Field lost propulsion power, an NTSB report later said. But there were more than 60 injuries reported, including four which were considered serious.
Maya Yang contributed reporting

articles.title: Stuart Bonds made ‘racist’ and ‘divisive’ comments. But One Nation is showing no sign of dumping the NSW candidate
articles.summary:
The former coalminer’s claim Australians are being ‘demographically replaced’ sparked wide criticism, but his party has shown no signs of dumping him

  • Get our

blocks.text: In a Facebook video from a Sydney anti-immigration rally on Sunday, as a man dressed like a medieval knight watches on, One Nation leader upper house candidate Stuart Bonds launches into a speech against “mass” migration.
“Make no mistake, we are being demographically replaced inside our own nation,” he says.
“If we don’t support Australian mothers having Australian children, we [are] going to pay for other cultures’ children to be brought up in our lands.”

In an apparent allusion to the “great replacement theory”, a far-right conspiracy theory that white westerners are being actively “replaced” by non-white immigrants, he continued: “That’s the socialist plan, is to destroy and bring down and tear down the fabric of your civilisation.”

The comments sparked a wave of criticism, but the party has shown no signs of taking Bonds off the ticket for the 2027 New South Wales state election. One Nation did, however, dump one candidate this week: the Victorian branch disendorsed a lower-house candidate over an old social media post describing Hitler as the GOAT, an acronym for the greatest of all time.

The rally was not a one-off. On a podcast released on Monday with the rally’s organiser, the Australian Lobby Group, Bonds appeared to double down on the remarks. He did not challenge host Scott Challen’s assertion that Labor governments were building “ethnic voting blocks with Middle Eastern and subcontinent people … to stack the numbers to entrench power for themselves”, instead responding: “Mate, and that’s why we’re going to get rid of all of the multicultural grants, right?”

On Wednesday, in an interview with ABC Upper Hunter, Bonds responded to questions about his comments by citing Australian Bureau of Statistics data that shows the proportion of Australians born overseas has trended upward since the end of the second world war, from 10% in 1945 to 32% in 2025. He did not mention that the proportion of Australians born overseas was at its highest – 32.4% – in 1891, the first year of available data.
Bonds said with the Australian birthrate beneath the 2.1 required to replace the population, “I would just like to know what people assume is going to happen.”
“Where are these people going to come from?” he said.

NSW Labor pounced on the rally comments immediately, with the state’s premier, Chris Minns, calling them “frankly outrageous and racist”. The government passed motions in both houses censuring Bonds, not yet a member.
The Coalition followed four days later. On Wednesday afternoon, the opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, said Bonds’ language was “clearly divisive”.
But she did not rule out a confidence and supply arrangement with One Nation after the March state election.
“We will not form a coalition with One Nation, [but] we’ll work with anyone post-election if we’re in a minority government,” she told reporters.

The Australian Financial Review has reported many of her MPs privately expect the party to go into a Coalition with One Nation. And with the Coalition consistently polling behind One Nation, that makes Bonds not a fringe candidate, but a potentially influential figure.
One Nation could ‘clean the deck’ in regions
The ABC’s former election analyst, Antony Green, said the remarks played straight into Labor’s hands.
“This will certainly be something the Labor party uses in all those multi-ethnic seats in Sydney,” he said – seats like those on the rural fringes of Sydney, which One Nation said it plans to target.

Indeed the deputy premier, Prue Car, who has Indian heritage and whose electorate of Londonderry is one of the seats in question, gave an impassioned critique of Bonds’ comments in question time on Tuesday.
“Who’s he [Bonds] talking about when he talks about this?” she said. “I tell you who he’s talking about – he’s talking about families like mine, and families that I represent.”
after newsletter promotion

Kos Samaras, a former Labor strategist who is now a director of polling group Redbridge, said that while the comments likely won’t play well in Sydney seats – including alienating moderate Liberal voters worried about the party going into Coalition with One Nation – “you might be able to get away with it in certain parts of NSW”.
And Bonds, a former coalminer, has made his base in the Hunter.
Samaras said One Nation could “clean the deck” in the regions, including Labor-held seats in the Hunter, and “pretty much anything else the coalition hasn’t got bolted down to the ground”.

The NSW One Nation leader, Mike Newman, who in September said he “made a mistake” when he told a Sydney rally he wanted to stop abortions, did not respond directly when asked if he agreed with Bonds’ comments or if he would rein in his first-placed upper house candidate.
“What I will say is that what Stuart Bonds is a patriotic Aussie. He’s a coalminer. He has very, very strong views,” he said on Tuesday.

Newman, who previously rejected claims that One Nation was racist, said on Tuesday: “What we want to do is … protect Australian values, and that is the fundamental thing that Stuart Bonds is pushing for. It’s about assimilation.”
The NSW treasurer, Daniel Mookhey, whose parents immigrated to Australia from India in the 1970s, told the ABC that Bonds’ comments were not grounded in reality.
“I think he’s saying that there is a deliberate conspiracy to use migrants to replace the way he puts it, native-born Australians for political reasons,” Mookhey said.
The quota for election to the upper house is 4.5%, making Bonds all but guaranteed to be elected, with One Nation polling in the high 20s and low 30s in recent months.

Green expects the party to pick up four or five seats in the upper house; so far it has only named three candidates: Newman, Bonds and Jeff Bacon, a firearms manufacturer who is second on the upper house ticket.
But unlike Victoria, NSW has optional preferential voting, which means when that state goes to the polls in March, lower house preferences flows aren’t guaranteed.
But Bonds has downplayed whether he may have jeopardised a future preference deal with the Coalition.
“If the Coalition have a problem with facts, the same as the Labor party, then maybe it will,” he told the ABC.
“But I’m not here to impress the Coalition.”
