articles.title: Eisenkot accuses Netanyahu of ‘racist’ campaign against Israel’s Arab minority
articles.summary:
Statement a rare instance of a prominent Jewish political leader taking a strong stand in defence of Arab Israelis

Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot accused caretaker premier…

blocks.text: Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot accused caretaker premier Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday of fuelling a “racist” campaign against the country’s Arab minority, after he sought to delegitimise the community’s lawmakers by linking them to Hamas.
Eisenkot’s statement was a rare instance of a prominent Jewish political leader taking a strong stand in defence of Arab Israelis, who make up more than 20% of the population.

Two Arab-majority parties, Raam and the Joint List, secured a combined 19 seats in last month’s election, winning nearly a sixth of the 120-seat parliament and potentially emerging as kingmakers in efforts by Eisenkot to form a government.
“Arab citizens of Israel are an integral part of the Israeli story,” Eisenkot wrote on X on Friday.
“They have been subjected to a racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimisation, fuelled by the outgoing prime minister and those around him for political purposes,” he added.
“The attempt to marginalise them and vilify them collectively is a profound violation of the principles of civic responsibility.”
Netanyahu and his allies have repeatedly criticised leaders of Arab parties for refusing to describe Hamas as a “terror group” following its unprecedented 7 October 2023 attack on Israel.
All leaders of Arab parties have condemned the attack, in which Arab Israelis – descendants of Palestinians who remained in what became Israel in 1948 – were also among those killed.
Netanyahu has also repeatedly alleged electoral fraud by Arab-majority parties, but electoral authorities have rejected the claims.
In a speech, Netanyahu lamented that the two Arab lists refused to recognise Israel as a Jewish state, although Raam leader Mansour Abbas has done so in the past.
He further claimed that they sought to establish either an “Islamic state” or a “nationalist Palestinian state”.
During the same ceremony, national security minister Itamar Ben Gvir heckled Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen during his oath of allegiance, accusing him of having “pledged allegiance to Hamas”.

“It is entirely legitimate to disagree with representatives of the Arab parties, even to strongly disapprove of some of them. But it is neither legitimate nor acceptable to malign an entire community, and I will not allow it,” Eisenkot said.

President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with forming a new government on Sunday after consultations in which a majority of political parties, including the two Arab lists, recommended him for the role.
But one of Eisenkot’s rightwing allies, Avigdor Lieberman, has said he will back out of the coalition if Arab Israelis are part of it.
If Eisenkot fails to form a government within 28 days, he may request a 14-day extension. Should he still fall short, the mandate would pass to another lawmaker, most likely Netanyahu.

articles.title: Moncton man charged in child luring case has 'spent time in' 5 provinces, RCMP say
articles.summary: New Brunswick RCMP have released the photo of a Moncton man facing several charges in connection with a child luring investigation, as well as a list of communities he has "spent time in" across…

image.caption: Timothy Roy, 45, of Moncton, appeared in Moncton provincial court on Sept. 18 for a bail hearing and was remanded into custody. (RCMP)

blocks.text: New Brunswick

New Brunswick RCMP have released the photo of a Moncton man facing several charges in connection with a child luring investigation, as well as a list of communities he has "spent time in" across Canada to encourage people with information to come forward.
Timothy Roy, 45, faces several charges, as police ask anyone who had 'interactions' with him to come forward
Codiac Regional RCMP have released the photo of a Moncton man facing several charges in connection with a child luring investigation.
Police have also released a list of several communities Timothy Roy, 45, has "spent time in" across Canada since 2000.
"Obviously it's really rare," spokesperson Cpl. Luc Picard told CBC News about the update issued Friday.

But investigators want to encourage anyone who "may have had interactions with [Roy] or who believes they may have been victimized to come forward and contact the RCMP or the local police, depending on where they live," Picard said.

Roy, who worked as a realtor in greater Moncton, is charged with sexual assault, sexual interference of a person under the age of 16, human trafficking of a person under 18, child luring, and obtaining sexual services for consideration from a person under 18.
Picard declined to elaborate on the nature of the allegations or reveal how police determined the list of communities, citing the ongoing investigation and the matter being before the courts.
The locations include:

items: Ontario: Kingston (2000-2003); Belleville, Bancroft, York (2014-2019)
British Columbia: Abbotsford, Vancouver, Saanich, Victoria, Oak Bay (2006-2012)
Labrador (2018-2019)
New Brunswick (2020-2026)
Nova Scotia (2025)

blocks.text: Tip prompted investigation
Picard said police launched an investigation on Aug. 26 after they received information that a 45-year-old man was in contact with underage girls for a sexual purpose.
During the evening of Sept. 10, officers located the suspect's vehicle parked at a hotel on Mountain Road in Moncton, he said.
According to Picard, the man was seen exiting the hotel the next day with a female under 16 and was arrested at the scene.
Roy was charged in Moncton provincial court on Sept. 15 and remains remanded in custody. He is due to appear in court at a later date.

Roy is no longer authorized to trade in real estate in the province, effective Sept. 16, the New Brunswick Real Estate Association confirmed. His licence has been cancelled, spokesperson Angela Boudreau said.
The RCMP investigation has included members of the Codiac Regional's general investigative section, patrol, crime reduction, prolific offender and property crime units.
Anyone with information is asked to contact the RCMP at 506-857-2400 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-TIPS (8477).

articles.title: Alberta government asks judge to dismiss First Nation’s challenge of its sovereignty act
articles.summary: Alberta's government is asking a judge to strike down a First Nation's constitutional challenge of its sovereignty act, arguing the law hasn't had any impact on treaty rights.

image.caption: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith speaks to the media in Calgary on Oct. 21, 2026. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Edmonton
Alberta's government is asking a judge to strike down a First Nation's constitutional challenge of its sovereignty act, arguing the law hasn't had any impact on treaty rights.
Onion Lake Cree Nation argues legislation is unconstitutional
Premier Danielle Smith won leadership of the United Conservative Party with the sovereignty act as her signature proposal in 2022, and it became her flagship first law.
Smith said the Alberta Sovereignty within a United Canada Act was needed to push back against federal encroachment into provincial jurisdiction.
When she invoked it for the first time, Smith conceded she didn't need the law to implement new measures to fight against Ottawa's energy regulations and that the act's use was symbolic.
Onion Lake Cree Nation argues the act is unconstitutional because it goes against the Treaty 6 relationship with the Crown and should be declared unenforceable.
The province argues the act doesn't authorize anything that would go against the Constitution or federal law and that Onion Lake's claim doesn't show the act has impacted any treaty rights.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Lisa Johnson
The Canadian Press
Lisa Johnson is a reporter for The Canadian Press based in Alberta.

articles.title: Hungary seizes $19.5m in cash found buried in forests amid graft inquiry
articles.summary:
Anti-corruption agency carried out searches as part of investigation into Orbán-era minister accused of taking bribes

Hungary’s anti-corruption agency said on Friday it had seized cash worth…

blocks.text: Hungary’s anti-corruption agency said on Friday it had seized cash worth $19.5m (£14.8m) buried in forests and hidden elsewhere while investigating an ex-minister of nationalist former leader Viktor Orbán.

Miklós Seszták, Hungary’s minister of national development between 2014 and 2018, is accused of taking bribes in a scheme involving the state transport company, purchasing secondhand buses at inflated prices.

The prime minister, Péter Magyar, won a landslide election victory in April, ending Orbán’s 16 years in power after promising to investigate alleged corruption and abuse of office during his rival’s rule.
Seszták, two other Orbán-era ministers and the former premier’s brother have been taken into custody in different cases as graft inquiries have gathered pace in recent weeks.

The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH), an anti-graft body with sweeping powers established as part of Magyar’s accountability drive, said it searched multiple locations on Thursday and Friday as part of the criminal proceedings against Seszták.

“During the search, investigators found large amounts of cash: buried in forests, hidden in agricultural and warehouse buildings as well as residential properties, and stored in high-value safes in secluded locations,” the statement said.
“The total amount of cash found during the two-day search was 5,071,632,000 forints, €2,658,350 and US $1,257,100,” it added, bringing the combined value to $19.5m.
NVVH said its staff deposited the cash into the Hungarian State Treasury’s account.
“Upon receipt, 12 Treasury employees spent 8 hours counting the money using 5 counting machines,” finance minister András Kármán said on Facebook.
Magyar hailed the seizure as a potential turning point.
“This officially marks the end of the Fidesz-KDNP mafia!” he said in reference to Orbán’s former governing coalition.
The former leader did not react to the latest development. Orbán had previously denounced the probes targeting his inner circle as “political persecution” aimed at imprisoning him.

articles.title: 'I sincerely apologize': Blue Jays outfielder Santander apologizes days after anti-Muslim social media posts
articles.summary: Santander said in an Instagram post Friday that reflection and conversations with people he trusts made him recognize he should have been more thoughtful about what he shared.

image.caption: Toronto Blue Jays' Anthony Santander apologized Friday for anti-Muslim social media posts he shared on Nov. 4. (Chris O'Meara/AP)

blocks.text: Toronto
Santander said in an Instagram post Friday that reflection and conversations with people he trusts made him recognize he should have been more thoughtful about what he shared.
Conversations with people he trusts made him recognize he should have been more thoughtful, he says
Toronto Blue Jays outfielder Anthony Santander apologized Friday for sharing anti-Muslim social media posts, saying the content caused hurt and fell short of his own convictions.

In a statement on Instagram, Santander said reflection and conversations with people he trusts made him recognize he should have been more thoughtful about what he shared and the responsibility that comes with having a public voice.
He expressed respect for the Muslim community and pledged to avoid sharing content that promotes hate.

Santander shared the posts on Nov. 4 and deleted them the next morning. They included a video of a Christian preacher disparaging Muslims and another suggesting Sharia law would be imposed on the United States after Abdul El-Sayed’s election to the Senate in Michigan.

His apology came a day after Blue Jays president and chief executive officer Mark Shapiro apologized to the Muslim community and fans following a meeting with community leaders, and after general manager Ross Atkins asked Santander to publicly address the controversy.

The 32-year-old Venezuelan signed a five-year, $92.5-million US contract with Toronto in January 2025 but missed the entire 2026 big-league season because of injuries. It remains unclear whether the team will discipline him over the posts.

articles.title: Flights grounded across U.S. due to outage affecting air traffic control, FAA says

image.caption: A traveller walks past a view of an air traffic control tower at Philadelphia International Airport in March. (Matt Rourke/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: A plane at Chicago O'Hare International Airport in 2025.
(Adam Gray/The Associated Press)
The Latest

items: The Federal Aviation Administration has grounded all flights across the United States, citing an air traffic control system issue creating critical safety concerns.
The agency said an outage is affecting "all air route traffic control centres."
The website FlightAware shows nearly 7,000 flights have been delayed or cancelled across the U.S.

November 13All U.S. airports 'ground stopped until further notice,' FAA saysA traveller walks past a view of an air traffic control tower at Philadelphia International Airport in March. (Matt Rourke/The Associated Press)The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration has ordered all commercial flights across the country grounded due to what it is calling "extraordinary circumstances." "All airports are ground stopped until further notice," said an order from the FAA Command Center issued shortly before 4 p.m. ET. That means no planes can take off from any U.S. airport and the agency warned airlines that flights in the air may be ordered to fly in a holding pattern. In a post on social media, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed what he called a communication issue affecting the regional centres that control air traffic between airports. The website FlightAware shows nearly 7,000 flights have been delayed or cancelled at airports across the U.S.

articles.title: Tanker collides with cruise ship on Mississippi in New Orleans
articles.summary: A freighter collided with a cruise ship carrying around 130 people in New Orleans, causing the paddlewheel vessel to capsize. More than 30 people were hospitalized but all passengers have been…

image.caption: At least 180 people were rescued from the ship after it was hit and capsized on FridayImage: Enan Chediak/The Advocate/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: More than 30 people were hospitalized but no deaths were reported after a freighter collided with a cruise ship on the Mississippi River in the US on Friday.

Authorities said at least 180 passengers and crew were rescued. New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno described it as "a miracle on the Mississippi," adding that none of those hospitalized had critical injuries.
Footage showed the paddlewheel cruise boat capsizing following the impact with the much larger cargo vessel and rescue teams rushing to get people in life jackets out of the water.
'It was just chaos'
The accident happened near the port of New Orleans when the freighter Atlantic Asphalt hit the cruise ship while it was docked.
"It was just chaos," local witness Devon Flanagan was quoted by news agency AP.

"You had all types of ships, like other barges and other companies down there trying to help out, which also was a little convoluted because you had people still in the water," he described the scene.
The company operating the passenger ship, American Cruise Lines, said in a statement that "guests and crew were evacuated, and we are deeply concerned for everyone involved."

blocks.caption: The collision happened in the busy port area of New OrleansImage: Enan Chediak/The Advocate/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: According to AP, the cruise ship was built in 2015, is five stories tall and can hold up to 150 passengers. It was finishing an eight-day cruise to several Mississippi River destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi.
When news of the collision broke, it was long initially unclear whether there were any fatalities and how many people were injured or missing.

Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry said he was on his way to New Orleans. "We are aware of the incident on the Mississippi and we are in close contact with local officials and law enforcement," he wrote on X.

US Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin wrote on social media that "we are throwing every asset we have to helping rescue missing passengers" and that his department was coordinating closely with state officials.

articles.title: Microsoft 'deeply sorry' for global outage after almost 24 hours of disruption
articles.summary: Experts say the event is a "stark reminder" of how heavily the world relies on a small group of big tech providers.

blocks.text: Microsoft has said it is "deeply sorry" for the service outage to its products, including Outlook and Teams, which has caused disruption around the world.

Services were broadly recovering by Friday afternoon, nearly 24 hours after issues began. Microsoft said it was making "encouraging progress", but added it does not know when services will fully recover.
The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide.
Microsoft said it was a technical issue introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and not related to cyber or artificial intelligence agents.
Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers.
Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday.

By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America.
In the UK, some parts of the NHS, including GPs and hospitals, were affected, as were some schools and police forces.
UK cyber minister Liz Lloyd said the incident had "limited" impact on critical frontline services such as 999 calls, and there had been no disruption to the transport network.
In Canada, however, the national rail network said passengers may not be able to receive email updates about their trips, and hospitals across the country also had issues with emails.
In the US, staff members from the House of Representatives told Politico it had set back an entire day of legislative work as everything was on Microsoft's Outlook.
Singapore's government acknowledged some of its systems had been impacted, and in India, the outage disrupted work for many on Friday.
In Turkey, advisers and officials attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya were left frustrated by being unable to access Outlook.
The issues also affected smaller businesses and individuals.

Microsoft first acknowledged users in the Americas were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes at 17:54 GMT on Thursday, and shortly after warned the disruption was possibly affecting Microsoft 365 globally.
While it launched an investigation and engineers began working to restore services, by 04:36 on Friday Microsoft was reporting only a "partial recovery" in some parts of the world.
By 13:32, the tech giant said there were "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" across much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia Pacific region.
Microsoft said it restored services gradually due to the scale of the problem and to help ensure services remain stable once they are up and running again.
"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," a Microsoft spokesperson said.
"We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously."
Microsoft said it has no "ETA" for when services will be fully recovered.
A full post-incident report will be released once Microsoft has completed a review.
Experts said while workers may have been happy to not have email access for the day, the incident showed the dependence many organisations have on these cloud-based services.
"The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of big tech providers," said Rob Demain, chief executive of cybersecurity firm e2e-assure.
Matt Saunders, field chief technology officer at tech consultancy Adaptavist, said it would be challenging to mitigate against a similar problem.
"Classic IT disaster planning strategies suggest using a second service for resilience, but in practice, it's almost impossible for a business to function without tools such as Microsoft," he said.
"In the wake of this outage, organisations must have a plan in place for how to work without such tools, for when incidents like this occur."

articles.summary: A tanker struck a cruise boat with 129 passengers on board in New Orleans on Friday, partially submerging the boat.

image.caption: Emergency personnel and crews respond after a tanker crashed into a river cruise boat in New Orleans on Friday. (Enan Chediak/The Advocate/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
A tanker struck a cruise boat with 129 passengers on board in New Orleans on Friday, partially submerging the boat.
People in life-jackets seen in Mississippi River as emergency crews respond
Rescues were underway on the Mississippi River, officials said. Authorities did not immediately release whether there were injuries or deaths.
Video from the scene showed the much larger Atlantic Asphalt tanker hit the paddlewheel river boat while it appeared to be docked.

People were seen in the river in life-jackets or standing near the boat's railing as the other side of the American Heritage paddlewheeler listed further into the water. Other footage showed people being pulled from the water and debris, including deck chairs, floating in the river.
The boat is operated by American Cruise Lines.
Lt. Stephanie C. Norwood with New Orleans Emergency Medical Services said all agencies are responding to rescue efforts.

articles.title: Russia is ‘setting traps’ in Ukraine talks, EU foreign policy chief warns
articles.summary:
Kaja Kallas says Moscow is trying to divert attention from its aggression by raising issue of European security

The EU’s foreign policy chief has warned against “walking into the traps that…

blocks.text: The EU’s foreign policy chief has warned against “walking into the traps that Russia is setting” as she said Moscow was trying to start a debate about European security in order to divert attention from its aggression.

“We have one aggressor and one victim, and the aggressor does not have security concerns,” Kaja Kallas said on arrival at an EU leaders’ summit in Dublin. “Nobody has ever attacked them. They have attacked others. I mean, keep the focus, people.”

In talks on the Ukraine war, Russia has revived its hardline demands for a total overhaul of European security – demands that were rejected in 2021 because they were seen as an infringement of the sovereignty of central and eastern European countries. The latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US was held this week in Abu Dhabi.

Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, said on Thursday night that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to expand the next round of peace negotiations to include the Europeans. However, Russia quickly contradicted that assurance.

European leaders have long said they will support Ukraine in any peace talks, but want to see a ceasefire before negotiations. They also stress the continent has an extensive web of security agreements that Russia has violated.

Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor, said: “Russia wants to talk about questions of a European security architecture. We do not need to discuss that; it already exists.” He added that it was a “given” that his country would be part of any European delegation.
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said it was “self-explanatory that Europe is included in the peace talks to safeguard our interests, but also to support Ukraine”.

The Kremlin said on Friday: “Once we understand [Europe’s] real intentions and their willingness to contribute to the peace process, then we can make a decision on holding talks in an expanded format.” Russia’s lead negotiator in Abu Dhabi, Vladimir Medinsky, said it was “unclear what there is to discuss” with Europe.
The US call to involve Europe in talks has turned the spotlight on who would represent it.

Speaking after a summit of EU leaders in Dublin on Friday, the European Council president António Costa said leaders had agreed on a negotiating team: the EU institutions and E5 countries, namely Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland.
“Europe must speak with one clear and united voice in all discussions that shape the future of Ukraine and the security of our continent,” he said. “This is ultimately a team effort.”

The format had already emerged in recent months, but the need to formalise the grouping gained momentum after Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, this week urged his European allies to decide who will represent Europe in negotiations.

Kushner also mocked the absence of a single person to speak for the entire continent. “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiations,” he said earlier this week.
after newsletter promotion

But there was an increasingly settled view that Europe would not be represented by a single person, but by different interlocutors from the wider continent. Paris and Berlin had argued for a continued role for their own envoys in the E3 format of Britain, France and Germany, alongside EU representatives. Smaller member states put the emphasis more firmly on the EU representatives: Costa and Kallas, the EU’s high representative for foreign affairs and security policy.
Earlier in the day, Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, said the discussion on who should represent Europe was “slightly overstated” as it had differing interests.

Some of the issues in peace talks were “pure EU interests”, he said, citing financing Kyiv and Ukraine’s future membership in the bloc. He also supported other formats, such as the “pretty uncomplicated” E3 and the “very legitimate” E5, which includes Italy and Poland, as well as a role for EU representatives. He said: “I am quite flexible on that. I think what we actually say is more important than the exact configuration of the people in the room.”

Several at the summit, including Kallas, also pointed to the importance of including the UK, a founder member of the coalition of the willing, a broad group of countries committed to future peacekeeping in Ukraine.
Ireland’s taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said the UK and Norway each had a significant role and “that all has to be taken into consideration because it’s a European, continent-wide issue”.

The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it was for the EU to decide who would represent the bloc. He said there was a strong view among European leaders that it was for Europe – in the wider sense – “to decide its own arrangements” on security.

articles.title: SpaceX to attempt double catch of huge Starship rocket
articles.summary: Elon Musk’s company will try to grab both parts of the rocket for the first time.

blocks.text: The 124m-tall rocket is scheduled to blast off from the Starbase launchpad in Texas at 1645 local time (2245 GMT) with a 75-minute-long launch window.
After six and a half minutes, the first planned catch will be attempted when the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - returns to the launch tower.

The top part of the rocket, called the Ship, will continue its journey to space and deploy 26 satellites. These will form part of the Starlink constellation that provides high speed internet from space.
The Ship is then due to complete 14 orbits around the Earth before returning for the second catch attempt about 22 and a half hours after taking off.
Until now, SpaceX has managed to catch the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights.
But the upper stage of the rocket, which only reached orbit for the first time in September, has never been grabbed by the chopsticks. Instead it's splashed down in the ocean.
SpaceX said it would only decide to try to catch the Ship after carefully assessing the vehicle while it's in space.
If any problems are detected there are various points during the flight when the rocket stage can be brought down in the ocean.
After SpaceX went public earlier this year, its shareholders will be carefully monitoring this flight, as will the US Space Agency.
The progress of Starship has direct implications for Nasa's attempt to land humans on the Moon in 2028 - a highly ambitious timeline.
SpaceX has been given a Nasa contract to configure the Ship into a lander that will eventually take astronauts down to the lunar surface.

But it's not the only company working with the US Space Agency. Blue Origin, owned by rival tech billionaire Jeff Bezos, also has a contract to use its New Glenn rocket and lander for the Moon touch down.
Both companies will also play a key role in Artemis III, which is currently planned for summer 2027- another challenging schedule.
This mission will see four astronauts in Nasa's Orion spacecraft attempt to dock with both SpaceX and Blue Origin's landers.
Starship will need to make a lot of progress in the coming months to meet these commitments - the pace of the rocket's development has been far slower than SpaceX had intended.
But Blue Origin also has much work to do. The company suffered a major setback earlier this year when its rocket exploded, totally destroying its launchpad in Florida.
Blue Origin had said they would be back in action by the end of this year, but a return to flight has now been delayed to early in 2027.

Nasa is under pressure to meet its timelines. Its administrator Jared Isaacman has said America is in a race with China to get to the Moon. China plans to land its Taikonauts on the lunar surface by 2030.

articles.title: Ukraine updates: Europe to send united front to potential peace talks
articles.summary: Germany, France, the UK, Italy and Poland — as well as the EU itself — will jointly represent Europe in possible peace talks. Meanwhile, a second car bomb in two days has exploded in Moscow.

image.caption: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz (left), EU chief Ursula von der Leyen (center) and French President Emmanuel Macron (right) were among those at the Dublin meetingImage: Brian Lawless/PA Wire/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: November 13, 2026
Russian Foreign Ministry contradicts Kushner on European participation in talks

Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova on Friday directly contradicted US envoy Jared Kushner's Thursday statement that President Vladimir Putin had voiced willingness to have European representatives join upcoming talks designed to end his war of aggression against Ukraine.

Responding to a request for comment from Germany's DPA news agency, Zakharova said, "As far as Russia's Foreign Ministry is aware, the issue was not discussed during the talks with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow."

No Foreign Ministry representatives were present during a Thursday meeting between Putin and US envoys Kushner and Steve Witkoff according to Russian state media, which said Putin was accompanied by his own foreign policy advisor Yuri Ushakov, Russia's chief negotiator Vladimir Medinsky and envoy Kirill Dmitriev.

articles.title: David Walliams: UK police launch sex offense probe into comedian
articles.summary: Walliams has been accused of engaging in sexual misconduct and inappropriate behavior towards young women and girls. The 55-year-old denies the allegations.

image.caption: Walliams had attended the London premier of the historical drama film 'The Choral' in 2025 (FILE: October 12, 2025)Image: Scott A Garfitt/Invision/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: London police on Friday said they are opening an sexual offenses investigation into British actor, comedian and children's author David Walliams.
The Metropolitan Police said they "received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offenses involving a man now in his 50s."

It comes after British outlets ITV News and The Guardian paper reported that Walliams misused his power and celebrity status to prey on women and girls over a period of more than 20 years. The media outlets produced an hourlong video documentary on the allegations against Walliams, entitled "David Walliams: Power and Silence."

blocks.caption: Walliams recently lost a High Court bid to block the publication of sexual misconduct allegations against himImage: Geoffrey Swaine/Avalon/IMAGO

blocks.text: The documentary reported on a woman who said she was sexually assaulted by Walliams when she was 15. The outlets also highlighted sexual harassment and inappropriate conduct allegations regarding "Britain's Got Talent," where he was a judge, and his book publisher HarperCollins.

"We would encourage anyone who has been the victim of a sexual offense to come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened," said Detective Mike Cagney, who is in charge of the Met Police investigation.
The Met Police investigation is based on allegations against Walliams that are separate from those reported by the two news outlets.
Walliams denies allegations
Neither Walliams nor his lawyer have responded to the Met Police investigation. However, Walliams did respond earlier to the ITV and Guardian report about him.

"I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me," Walliams told the outlets in a letter. "Whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something I never did."

The allegations against Walliams have already have already had repercussions on his career. The BBC took down content featuring Walliams from its platforms, including comedy sketch show "Little Britain."
Walliams' publisher, HarperCollins UK, dropped him last year after The Telegraph newspaper reported on inappropriate behavior towards women at the publishing firm.

blocks.caption: HarperCollins, which published Walliam's children's books, cut ties with him last year Image: Hannah McKay/REUTERS

blocks.text: UK media and entertainment industry faces sexual abuse reckoning
The allegations come as several male comedic and literary figures in the UK have faced either sexual assault charges or accusations in recent years.
Media personality and actor Russell Brand on Monday was sentenced to 10 years and 6 months imprisonment after he was convicted of rape and assault.

blocks.caption: Russell Brand is now behind bars after he was convicted of rapeImage: Thomas Krych/ZUMA Press Wire/IMAGO

blocks.text: In 2024, children's book author Neil Gaiman was accused of sexual assault, leading companies such as Disney and DC Comics to drop adaptations of his works. Gaiman denies the allegations.

"The media industry will need to look at itself and ensure whether it is taking all of the steps needed to protect the safety of woman and girls who work within the industry," British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Thursday.

British Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy is expected to meet with entertainment industry leaders next week, where she will deliver a warning that the UK government could intervene if they do not protect those who blow the whistle on sexual assault and misconduct.

articles.title: Eurovision is finally coming to Asia - meet the stars gearing up to take the stage
articles.summary: On Saturday, the biggest and longest-running international song contest will make a leap into unknown territory.

blocks.text: On Saturday, the biggest and longest-running international song contest will make a leap into unknown territory.

Eurovision, the pan-European competition famed for zany gimmicks, slick, sometimes over-the-top staging, the drama of its complex voting system and, occasionally, for outstanding music, celebrates its 70th birthday this year.
And to mark it, the European Broadcasting Union is trying out audiences in Asia.
It's an idea that's been talked about for two decades but never materialised, despite many false starts.
Until now - Eurovision Asia will hold its first grand final in Bangkok, starting at 20:30 ICT (13:30 GMT).

Transferring one of the most successful television formulas that has worked in Europe for 70 years to Asia has not been straightforward, says Sarun 'Note' Kungbunpot, a Eurovision enthusiast and Thai singer who has won several competitions in this region.
"It's still very new in Asia. I'm not sure many people have heard about it yet," he says, adding that he thinks it will take a bit of time for audiences to adjust.
"When we look at contests in Thailand, the Philippines and Korea, we actually compete based on the singer.
"It's all about popularity – fans are looking for their idols. But Eurovision is all about the song, not the singer. I think this needs to be communicated clearly."

Then there is the long history of Eurovision in Europe. It began in 1956 as a project to encourage greater cultural exchanges in a Europe which was trying to forge a common future after two world wars.

This was the very start of the age of mass television ownership, and Eurovision became such a fixture it is now an indelible piece of Europe's shared cultural heritage. It has no such resonance in Asia, and arrives in this region in the digital age, when traditional TV formats are struggling to cut through.

Only 11 countries are taking part in this first Eurovision Asia contest – host Thailand, along with Malaysia, the Philippines, Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, South Korea, Mongolia, Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan.
Asian giants India, China, Japan and Indonesia are noticeably absent, although there are negotiations ongoing to try to get them into next year's contest, assuming there is one.
There have also been problems with the organisation of this event.

A sudden million-dollar (£760,000) budget cut just three weeks before the final meant many of the technicians familiar with staging Eurovision were not brought to Thailand, and there have been a number of staff resignations too.
Eurovision fans - and there are many passionate followers around the world - have noticed, criticising audio and lighting in rehearsal videos.

In Europe, there have long been reports of co-ordinated voting to back neighbours, for example the four Nordic countries voting for each other. This seems less likely in Eurovision Asia, but political differences, for example between Thailand and Cambodia after their border war last year, could influence how their audiences vote.

Filipinos, with their passion for singing, are expected to be enthusiastic participants and the 11 million who live overseas might make a difference. But as most live and work in countries which are not participating, their votes will only go into the "rest of the world" pool.

For Bhutan, with a population of less than a million, this is a rare chance to shine on a global stage, which puts some pressure on 24-year-old Thukten Nyendra, the singer representing the Himalayan kingdom in Bangkok with his song Lhayi Semo (The Angel). Before coming here he had never left his country or been on a plane before.

"I'm not a star. I'm just Nyendra over there," he told the BBC. "Nobody knows me. But Eurovision has given me a huge platform. Actually winning would mean the world to us... If I really make it through all of this, it would mean the entire freaking world to us."

articles.title: Pope Leo celebrates Mass in his former diocese of Chiclayo, Peru
articles.summary: Over a million people have gathered for Mass with Pope Leo XIV on Friday. The event in northern Peru, where he served as bishop before becoming head of the Catholic Church, is the centerpiece of his…

image.caption: Pope Leo XIV expressed thanks for the 'affection, support and prayers' of his former parishonersImage: AFP

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV was greeted by another enormous crowd on Friday as he arrived at Pampas de Pimentel, a vast desert park outside the northern Peruvian city of Chiclayo, to celebrate an outdoor Mass in a diocese that he served as bishop for eight years before being summoned to Rome in 2023, where he was later elected pontiff.
The Vatican estimates that roughly 1.5 million faithful braved scorching sun and heat of 31 degrees Celsius (87 degrees Fahrenheit) to attend.
The event was the centerpiece of Leo's 12-day South American tour, throughout which an estimated 12 million people have turned out at stops in Uruguay and Argentina and now Peru.

blocks.caption: Some 1.5 million people braved sun and heat to be with Pope Leo in ChiclayoImage: Pilar Olivares/REUTERS

blocks.text: 'Padre Roberto' returns home as 'Papa Leon'
Pope Leo, born Robert Prevost in Chicago, Illinois, had already referred to Peru, where he served as a missionary for some 20 years, as his homeland in remarks delivered on Wednesday.
Beyond US and Vatican citizenship, Leo also holds a Peruvian passport.

Leo, whom locals still refer to as "Padre Roberto" and "amigo," arrived from the capital Lima on Friday morning in a plane adorned with stickers reading "Leo XIV flies home." The leader of the Catholic Church's 1.4 billion members will remain in Chiclayo until Sunday.

An agricultural and commercial hub on the Pacific coast, Chiclayo is Peru's fourth largest city and has a population of 700,000. Beyond locals, many of those attending Mass on Friday told reporters that they had journeyed from far-flung regions and even neighboring countries to receive the pope's blessing.

The crowds that Leo has attracted throughout his trip, undertaken shortly after he underwent surgery for lung cancer in Rome, have grown along the way, with the largest gathering coming in Lima on Wednesday, where an estimated 3.5 million people turned out.

blocks.caption: Pope Leo XIV celebrated Friday's Mass in a temporary structure in the coastal desert  at Pampas de PimentelImage: Andrew Medichini/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Pope overwhelmed with emotion, thanks Chiclayo faithful for their prayers
Though normally reserved, Leo has openly displayed his emotions since returning to Peru — laughing, singing and tearing up while interacting with crowds of faithful both young and old.
After making his way through the massive crowd to celebrate Mass on Friday, Leo began his sermon with words of thanks.
"What a joy it is to return to Chiclayo!" Leo said at the start of his homily, "It is a blessing for me to be with you once again."
"As I look your faces, a prayer of thanksgiving to the Lord arises in my heart for the blessing you have been and continue to be in my life."
"Thank you for your affection, support and prayers, especially for my health during this time of trial which, with God's help, I am overcoming," Leo told the crowd.
Pope Leo starts jam-packed South America tour just weeks after surgery
Pope Leo will deliver remarks at university named for role-model missionary
On Friday afternoon, the pontiff will deliver a speech at Chiclayo's St. Turibius de Mogrovejo Catholic University, where he once served as chancellor.
The institution is named after a sixteenth century Spanish missionary who would become the first archbishop of Lima. He served as a role model for Leo during his own ministry.
Mogrovejo was known to travel long distances on horseback to spread the gospel, as well as for standing up for the rights of indigenous and enslaved peoples.
Leo, too, is remembered for his outreach and for championing human rights and social justice, especially for the poor.

blocks.caption: Before becoming Pope Leo XIV, Bishop Robert Prevost spent nearly two decades caring for the poor and underprivileged in northern PeruImage: Elkin Cabarcas Mora/Janinna Sesa's personal archive/picture alliance

articles.title: The Peruvian city that has embraced Pope Leo as one of its own
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV is in Peru as part of his Latin America tour, just weeks after having surgery for lung cancer.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters / Pilar Olivares
The Pope, who has Peruvian citizenship, lived in Chiclayo for several years
ByJosé Carlos Cueto
BBC News Mundo in Chiclayo, Peru
Pope Leo XIV has celebrated mass near the Peruvian city where he made his name as a compassionate bishop who worked closely with poor and migrant communities.
The ceremony was held on Friday at a park in Pimentel, about 10km (six miles) from Chiclayo in northern Peru as part of his tour of Latin America.
The Vatican estimates more than 1.5 million people gathered to welcome the pontiff.
"Thank you for your affection, support and prayers," the Pope told followers.
"Especially for my health during this time of trial which, with God's help, I am overcoming," he added, referencing the surgery he had for lung cancer which took place just weeks ago.
Some of the crowd arrived 12 hours in advance to wait in vigil before the mass began.
"We spent the night praying, alongside family, excited to welcome the Pope from Chiclayo," said Isa Orderique.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Pope Leo celebrated mass in front of a jubilant crowd

blocks.text: Image source, Tiziana FABI / AFP via Getty Images
Pope Leo celebrated mass in front of a jubilant crowd
Many came from across Peru and even neighbouring countries to attend.
Merli Cruz Guerrero, from an area near the Ecuadorean border, travelled several hours by bus to attend. She also spent the entire night waiting.
Of all the events the Pope has attended so far during his visit to Peru, this felt particularly emotional.
The crowd fell into a hushed silence as the pontiff's motorcade approached.
They waited eagerly for his arrival despite spending long hours out in the open with the temperature pushing past 30C.
For many living here, the fact that the Pope worked extensively in this region before becoming the head of the Catholic Church has put them in the spotlight.
"The Pope has come home and Chiclayo is celebrating," said Lisbeth Díaz, a teacher who worked with Pope Leo when he served as the city's bishop between 2015 and 2023.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Lisbet Díaz says Chiclayo is celebrating the Pope's return

blocks.text: Lisbet Díaz says Chiclayo is celebrating the Pope's return
Peru is the longest stop on the first tour of Latin America by the pontiff, who was elected in May 2025.
The trip has also taken in Argentina and Uruguay, but his time in this country carries particular significance.
The Pope not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities.
Around Chiclayo, it is hard to meet anyone who doesn't claim to be a friend of the Pope or have a special anecdote about him.
Some recall how he would enjoy sampling Peruvian delicacies at El Trébol, a restaurant next to the city's cathedral. Others remember his love of tennis.
But for many it's the more serious moments of his time here, such as helping launch soup kitchens during the Covid-19 pandemic, or wading through deep waters on horseback when floods hit the area.
Several of these images are on display in a small museum dedicated to him at the entrance to the bishop's residence.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Commemorative pictures of the Pope are sold in the main of square of Chiclayo, including a famous image of him visiting a remote village on horseback

blocks.text: Commemorative pictures of the Pope are sold in the main of square of Chiclayo, including a famous image of him visiting a remote village on horseback
But for the city, and for a country that calls him the "Peruvian Pope", his return home means much more than a collection of photographs and anecdotes.

"It is the return of the man who brought Peruvians closer to the Church," said Samuel David Miranda Atoche, a local parish priest from Chiclayo who was ordained by the Pope back when he was still the bishop and known under his birth name of Robert Prevost.
And it is not just local people he connected with, according to Díaz, who came to Chiclayo from Venezuela.

"It was difficult for him to see so many migrants living on the streets," she added, recalling the time when large numbers of Venezuelans came through Chiclayo escaping the political and economic crisis in their home country.
"So, he got in touch with the migration authorities and coordinated with other organisations to speed up the paperwork needed for many of us to obtain legal residency and work permits."

Robert Prevost's time here as bishop also involved difficult decisions, such as having to deal with the controversy and scandal surrounding the dissolution of Sodalitium of Christian Life, a Peruvian Catholic organisation that had faced decades of sexual abuse allegations.

Santiago Roncagliolo, a Peruvian writer and journalist who has studied the Pope's life, believes his handling of that crisis earned him the favour of his predecessor, Pope Francis, and helped set him on the path to the papacy.
Father David also stressed the role the now-pontiff played in bringing people together.
"If there is one thing Bishop Prevost worked for here," he added, referring to the Pope by his previous title, "it was unity".
That unity has been on display in the run up to the mass, with the square in front of Chiclayo Cathedral filled with joyous celebrations for days.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Father David says the Pope brought Peruvians closer to the Church

blocks.text: Father David says the Pope brought Peruvians closer to the Church
Normally, 800,000 people live in the city and its surrounding area, but estimates say the Pope's visit has caused that to double.
Local businesses have been capitalising on the Pope's popularity to boost sales and hotels have sharply increased their nightly room rates.
But that didn't seem to put off the faithful who gathered for the mass.
Shouts of: "The Pope is from Chiclayo!" echoed across the field during the event.
Their affection was clearly reflected by the pontiff.
"As I look at your faces, a prayer of thanksgiving to the Lord arises in my heart," he said from the stage, "for the blessing you have been and continue to be in my life."

articles.title: 3 dead after boat crash in flooded river near Squamish, B.C.
articles.summary: Three people are confirmed dead after a boat crashed on the Squamish River on Thursday.

image.caption: Heavy rain has swollen the Squamish River, which is seen here on Thursday. Officials have confirmed three are dead after a boat overturned in the river. (Alanna Kelly/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Three people are confirmed dead after a boat crashed on the Squamish River on Thursday.
Police have confirmed the boat hit something and threw passengers into the water
Three people are dead and a number of others had to be rescued after a boat crashed into a unknown object on the Squamish River Thursday amid stormy conditions.
The RCMP confirmed the third fatality on Friday after finding the body of a person who had been listed as missing. The identities of the deceased have not been confirmed.
Insp. Robert Dykstra with the Sea-to-Sky RCMP said there were approximately eight people on the boat when the accident happened.

"I don't have any details specifically about exactly the type of boat ... but I understand that it ran into something and that's what caused it to stop and people to be thrown into the water," he said.
"A number of people did get off the boat and they were rescued. They're on the on the other side [of the Squamish River] where we don't have direct access to by road right now, but they're safe."
Squamish Valley Road, which gives access to the remote area by vehicle, is closed at the Pilchuck Bailey Bridge due to flooding.
The Squamish Valley Road was washed out around two or three kilometres north of the Cheekye area. (Submitted by Glen McEachran)
Dykstra said investigators are trying to understand who owns the boat and why it was on the river in Thursday's harsh conditions.
"It could be any number of reasons. It's tragic. It's dangerous water. The flooding was quite substantial. The rainfall over the last 48 hours has been significant," he said.
Squamish RCMP responded to the accident at 1:52 p.m. PT Thursday. Cpl. Ashley MacKay said conditions that day were extremely difficult and unsafe for emergency responders.

"The weather and river conditions have played a significant role in the response efforts," she said. "Weather patterns, water levels, and river conditions can change rapidly, and those factors are being continuously assessed as search and recovery efforts continue."
The Squamish Valley Road is seen closed due to flooding on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026. (Troy Charles/CBC)
Police are asking the public to stay off the water due to dangerous flow rates and debris throughout the river systems.

items: Shelter-in-place advisory issued for Pemberton Valley, parts of Squamish as flooding closes roads
More stormy weather forecast for B.C. with warnings for flooding, heavy rain, fog

blocks.text: ​RCMP Air Services, the Lower Mainland District Integrated Emergency Response Team, the Lower Mainland District Underwater Recovery Team, and West Coast Marine Services were involved in the search.
"We send the condolences out to those who are affected. We're working hard to figure out exactly what happened in this investigation," said RCMP Cpl. Brett Urano.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Alanna Kelly is a CBC News journalist based in Squamish, B.C., covering the Sea-to-Sky region, including Whistler, Pemberton and the Sunshine Coast. You can email story ideas to alanna.kelly@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Stelco recalling 175 laid-off workers at Hamilton steel plant
articles.summary: Hamilton steelmaker Stelco is recalling 175 workers that had been laid off earlier this fall.

image.caption: The Stelco Hamilton Works is pictured on Oct. 9, 2026. The company says it is recalling 175 laid-off workers by Dec. 1. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Politics·Breaking
Hamilton steelmaker Stelco is recalling 175 workers that had been laid off earlier this fall.
Federal government told company to recall workers or face possible legal action

Stelco made the announcement in a news release on Friday, saying that the workers would be back in the factory by Dec. 1. The company also indicated that it would retroactively pay the workers for the time they were laid off.
The American parent company, Cleveland-Cliffs, announced in September that it planned to lay off as many as 500 workers as it idled certain steel production at Stelco.
The federal government said that any move to lay off workers would violate "binding commitments" Cleveland-Cliffs made when it bought Stelco in 2024.
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly wrote to the Ohio-based company in mid-October, demanding that it reverse the layoffs or face possible legal action.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Major is a senior writer for CBC's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa. He previously worked as a digital reporter for CBC Ottawa and a producer for CBC's Power & Politics. He holds a master's degree in journalism and a bachelor's degree in public affairs and policy management, both from Carleton University. He also holds a master's degree in arts from Queen's University. He can be reached at darren.major@cbc.ca.

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Canadian pop-punk princess Avril Lavigne has welcomed her first child — a baby girl — with an unnamed partner.
“Our Mini F--king Princess has arrived,” she wrote on social media

"Our Mini F--king Princess has arrived 🎀👑🍼🩷," Lavigne shared in a post on Instagram, accompanied by a carousel of photos, including her and her mystery partner holding the newborn's hand and a row of three classic checkered slip-on Vans — lined up in a row on a skateboard.
Lavigne, 42, hasn't revealed the baby's name or who her father is; the Sk8er Boi singer is not publicly linked to anyone at the moment.

Lavigne has been married twice in the past to fellow well-known Canadian musicians: Sum 41 frontman Deryck Whibley (2006–2010) and Nickelback's Chad Kroeger (2013–2015). She was also once engaged to American rapper Mod Sun, and has been previously linked to Tyga, Brandon Davis, Wilmer Valderrama and Brody Jenner.

Her latest release came in 2024 in the form of a career-spanning greatest hits album, including 20 songs across her seven studio albums — everything from Complicated to Girlfriend to Head Above Water.
Love Sux, her most recent studio album, was released in 2022 and produced by Mod Sun, Travis Barker and John Feldmann.

While Lavigne has not toured in 2026, she embarked on a 69-show Greatest Hits Tour starting in Vancouver in 2024. The run included 13 stops across Canada, concluding at the All Your Friends Festival in Oro-Medonte, Ont., in June 2025.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Griffin Jaeger is a reporter and producer with CBC's entertainment unit. He also formerly hosted and produced content for The National’s digital platforms. You can reach him at griffin.jaeger@cbc.ca

articles.title: Estonia bans Russian athletes as backlash intensifies
articles.summary: Estonia is the latest country to say it will not allow Russian or Belarusian athletes to compete on its territory as a result of the ongoing war in Ukraine.

blocks.text: Estonia has become the latest country to say it will not allow Russian or Belarusian athletes to compete on its territory as a result of the ongoing war in Ukraine.
It comes after Norway, Finland and Canada made similar announcements.
The moves come amid a mounting backlash over the reinstatement of athletes from Russia and Belarus.

In September, the International Ski Federation (FIS) relaxed its rules, saying competitors from the two countries would be granted access to its events "provided that they sign a declaration of neutrality".
They had previously faced more stringent background checks on any voluntary link or paid duty with the military.
Participation remains limited to individual events, with athletes banned from displaying national symbols such as flags, anthems or uniforms.

However, it has now emerged that Estonia's government has written to the FIS, claiming that allowing entry to competitors from Russia and Belarus would undermine the country's support of Ukraine, and present an opportunity for propaganda. It said a ban issued in 2022 will be maintained.

In a statement issued to BBC Sport, the FIS said it "is committed to offering full support to athletes, national ski associations and local organisers - with most of which we have a long-standing relationship - in the process of navigating what we know to be a very complex situation.

"With that said, the Individual Neutral Athlete policy is clear in stating that notwithstanding eligibility, the host country visa and entry policies remain in place and are determined solely by the host country. FIS bears no responsibility for denial of visas or entry to any person granted eligibility under the FIS Individual Neutral Athlete Policy."
On Thursday, Scandinavian neighbours Norway and Finland both said they would also block visas for Russian athletes because of the war in Ukraine.

Norway is preparing to host the cross-country skiing World Cup next month, while Finland is due to stage the figure skating world championships in March. The International Skating Union (ISU) has said it "believes that athletes should not be punished for the actions of their governments in a world where, sadly, many conflicts are ongoing", and that it was "seeking clarifications" from officials in Finland.

This comes in the wake of last month's decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) to overturn a ban of Russia by the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF), a move condemned by the British, German, Finnish and Czech federations.

Russia have been suspended from competing in IIHF events since the country invaded Ukraine in February 2022, but the Russian Ice Hockey Federation (RIHF) then successfully appealed that decision at Cas. The court said that IIHF arguments citing safety and security were "not supported by sufficient evidence", but the Hockey Federation of Ukraine said the ruling caused "special outrage".

The Canadian government has since informed its hockey authorities that it will not issue visas for Russians to play in next month's World Junior Championship, including those who currently play for teams in Canada, as long as the war continues. A number of countries had said they would refuse to play against Russia, if they were allowed to take part.
Despite the controversy, the return of Russia and Belarus to international sport has been gathering pace this year.

In March, several athletes from the two countries were allowed to compete under their national flags at the Winter Paralympics after partial suspensions by the International Paralympic Committee were lifted.
In July, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) provisionally reinstated Russia to its competitions, stating a ban introduced in 2023 after the invasion of Ukraine was "no longer applicable".

However, sports federations can still enforce their own eligibility criteria. While World Gymnastics, World Aquatics and World Boxing have all removed restrictions on Russian athletes competing, a total ban has been maintained by World Athletics.

Last month, it was announced that Moscow will host the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships - the first time an Olympic federation has chosen to stage a global event in Russia since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title: The dangers of revising Europe's security architecture
articles.summary: Experts warn against revising Europe's security framework because they say it would mean granting Moscow its longstanding wish of renegotiating postwar security on the continent.

image.caption: European leaders and diplomats met in Dublin to reaffirm their support for Ukraine as US-mediated peace talks gained momentum this week.Image: Virginia Mayo/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: European leaders have so far found compromises in response to many of US President Donald Trump's demands.
But they were surprised to hear Trump say that he raised Europe's security framework with Russian officials.
"It's going to be a big agreement and it's going to involve more than Ukraine," Trump said after meeting Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House last week.
He said that deal might include all of Europe. But what he meant by "all of Europe" was not clear.
US envoy Jared Kushner also wrote that Europe and Russia had struggled to establish a sustainable security framework for more than 30 years.
Kushner said he was looking at a "broader" European architecture before he flew to meet with Russian and Ukrainian representatives in Abu Dhabi.

European diplomats immediately pushed back on Washington's approach to secure a peace deal in Ukraine because they feared that a peace settlement could restore Russia's sphere of influence and undermine NATO.

"We ​already have European security ​architecture in place. NATO and the European Union both have their ​respective roles. We ​must make sure Ukraine is integrated ‌into ⁠this architecture," said Kaja Kallas, the European Union's foreign policy chief.
The issue with revising Europe's postwar security framework
Russia made clear during talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this week that they were keen to discuss a broader European security framework before tackling the specifics of the war.

"Phrases about the European security architecture are certainly Russian talking points and not only talking points but, to a degree, part of a media propaganda effort that Russia makes to frame the war as it wishes to frame the war," said Michael Kimmage, a historian of the Cold War.
Russian leaders, including Vladimir Putin, have long alleged that the US and NATO repeatedly violated pledges they made in the early 1990s not to expand the alliance into the former Soviet bloc.
They have seen NATO's enlargement during this period as having put them in a humiliating position in which they could do very little.

At the same time, in the 1990s, the European project saw the birth of the European Union, the single market that ensured the free movement of goods and people across member states, the Schengen agreement for border-free travel, and the euro.
The core idea was to extend peace across the continent.
"Europe can mean so many things, but the European project was not designed for war. It was designed for peace," said Kimmage.
During this period, there were even suggestions of Russia becoming a NATO member.
But that relative period of stability changed after Russia invaded Georgia in 2008, annexed Crimea in 2014 and launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

"Russia wants to redraw all of this by force. And I think that that's fundamentally unacceptable to Europe with all the diversity and variations that you get within the European landscape on what's acceptable and not acceptable. I think the large-scale redrawing of borders by force is just not the European project," said Kimmage.
"So to the extent that the redrawing of borders by force is the lifeblood of Russian foreign policy, and I think that's a pretty easy case to make, Russia and Europe are at an impasse," he said.
What was to happen to Ukraine's security?

The Trump administration very quickly turned to making sure that "existing European security institutions" would be intact, with Jared Kushner having said late Thursday that the next round of negotiations would include "our European partners."
Kushner, along with Steve Witkoff, flew to Moscow to talk to Putin after talks in Abu Dhabi. Then they flew to Dublin, Ireland, to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Kushner had earlier Thursday signaled some "really incredible" postwar plans for Ukraine, saying that it could not be concluded without Europeans at the table.

"We should not allow a diktat from Russia that would result in some kind of neutralization or significant reduction in the military forces of Ukraine going forward, because that would make Ukraine very, very vulnerable to future aggression and pressure coming from Russia," said Hiski Haukkala, the director of the Finnish Institute of International Affairs.
That would mean that Ukraine would also be completely dependent on the security guarantees that the US or Europeans are able and willing to provide.

"We are supporting Ukraine because we are supporting international law and the basic norms of decency and international security when it comes to European security architecture. And this is the vantage point from which we are operating," he said.
The European Union has repeatedly pointed to some of the basic treaties that Russia broke, including:

items: The UN Charter
The Helsinki Act of 1975, which established the ten core principles of European security, including the non-use of force or threat against territorial integrity.
The Charter of Paris for a New Europe that built on Helsinki commitments
The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), which was one of the few multilateral security forums where the West and Russia engaged.
The Budapest Memorandum of 1994 in which Russia, the US and the UK provided security assurances to Ukraine and others in exchange for them giving up their nuclear weapons.

blocks.text: "Russia walked away from these principles and smashed them to pieces in the process. And they are not interested in reinstating the previous security architecture order. They want something different in its stead. And as long as this is not on the table, the Russian form of negotiation is to wage war. War is a form of bargaining," Haukkala said.
"And they are signaling strategic intent to change the makeup of European security, to subdue Ukraine and to change the very essence of European security," he added.

blocks.caption: US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with Volodymyr Zelenskyy after having met Vladimir Putin in Moscow.Image: Peter Morrison/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What is the way forward?
Daniel Fried, a former assistant secretary of state for European Affairs in the George W. Bush administration, said Russia is very good at sticking to its demands.
He said Russians know how to negotiate and "right now, they are not negotiating," referring to talks in Abu Dhabi.
Some experts said there was no possibility of having a new security architecture with the Russians at this point because there was no trust or common vision to align with Russia at the moment.
Others like Balazs Jarabik, an expert on post-Soviet politics, said that Russia was part of the European security architecture whether Europeans liked it or not.

"And the question is whether it's included as our enemy. Obviously, Russia is not going to be a partner, right? We have to find a modus operandi to reduce the risk of a horizontal escalation and potentially a bigger European war, even a bigger one than what we have now."

A host of European leaders on Friday rejected the Russian demands to discuss Europe's security framework as well, with a spokesperson for the German government saying that Berlin was looking to host a meeting of the "Coalition of the Willing" to secure funding for Ukraine's defense and reach a unified position regarding future peace talks.
Can Germany make Europe pay more for Ukraine?

articles.title: Former Hamas bodyguard convicted of Birmingham knife crime also wanted in Germany
articles.summary:
Mohammed Alfatih rearrested over alleged plot to target Israelis in Europe while detained for attack on bailiff

A former Hamas bodyguard convicted of knife crime in the UK is wanted in…

blocks.text: A former Hamas bodyguard convicted of knife crime in the UK is wanted in Germany for allegedly plotting to murder Jewish people.
Details of the plot can now be reported after Mohammed Alfatih, also known as Mohammed Naim, was found guilty on Friday of a knife attack on a bailiff outside his home in Birmingham.
The 40-year-old was found guilty by a majority verdict of unlawful wounding, possession of two knives and criminal damage. He was cleared of the more serious charge of wounding with intent.
He was under surveillance by a counter-terrorism unit when he attacked the bailiff last year.
Alfatih, the son of a senior Hamas official, could not be named during his trial because of reporting restrictions.
He had been photographed working for a former leader of Hamas before being granted asylum in the UK in 2015 and British citizenship in 2020.
While detained for the attack on the bailiff in Birmingham, he was rearrested after authorities in Germany said he had been part of an alleged plot to attack Israeli targets in central Europe.
Alfatih, who was born in Germany, is expected to be extradited to the country after he has served his sentence in the UK, with his connection to Hamas stated in the German extradition request.

German prosecutors charged seven suspected Hamas members in September over an alleged plot to target Jews or Israelis in Germany or Austria around the second anniversary of the 7 October attack on Israel.

They said “Mohammed A” played a prominent role in transporting and storing weapons but was being prosecuted separately after UK authorities arrested him in London and noted he had not yet been returned to Germany.
German authorities said he was connected to Hamas’s leadership and was said to have produced a video in advance to take responsibility for the attack on its behalf.
The attack was disrupted by Germany’s domestic intelligence service after a tipoff from the Mossad, Israel’s secret service.
During a two-week trial at Birmingham crown court, the jury was shown video footage of Alfatih lashing out with a knife at the broken window of a van on 14 October last year.
The bailiff, Kevin Bucknall, was left with cuts to his head and required hospital treatment. The defendant pleaded not guilty on the grounds of self-defence.
The jurors, who convicted Alfatih after being shown film footage of him brandishing two large kitchen knives outside his home in Kings Heath, Birmingham, were not told of his links to Hamas.
They were also not told Alfatih was under surveillance by a counter-terrorism unit after being released on bail on suspicion of a terror offence days before the bailiff was attacked.
A government source said: “This is a staggering example of the loss of border control under the last Conservative government, who granted his asylum claim and gave him citizenship.
“This Labour government has just introduced reforms that ensure those who gain citizenship must first show they are a good citizen and have contributed to this country.”
