articles.title: EU leaders urged to 'act now' to stay AI competitive with US, China
articles.summary: EU leaders in Dublin were called on by an AI executive to move quickly in the tech race with the US and China. EU official Metsola, however, expressed frustration with the idea that the bloc is…

image.caption: EU leaders met in Dublin amid concerns that the bloc could be falling behind in AI development Image: Cathal McNaughton/REUTERS

blocks.text: European Union leaders met in Dublin on Friday at the first ever summit on artificial intelligence (AI). The meeting came at a critical moment, as the bloc seeks a unified policy on the rapidly evolving technology.
The meeting took place in Dublin's Convention Center, which was also the meeting place of the European Political Community summit this week.
Mistral's CEO Mensch urges EU to 'act now'
French AI company Mistral's CEO Arthur Mensch, as well as Nobel-prize winner and researcher Geoffrey Hinton, widely known as the "godfather of AI," spoke to EU leaders at the summit.
"Europe has all the technology and the talent to lead the AI race," Mensch said during the event. "What it needs is speed, financing and a strong coordination between member states."
Mensch urged the leaders to "act now" to stay competitive with the US and China in regards to AI development.

"AI is the most important technology of our time," European Council ‌President Antonio Costa said in a post on X regarding the summit. "Europe must make the most of its benefits, from higher productivity to better public services. We must also manage the risks and changes it will bring — and help set global standards for responsible governance and safe, human-centric AI."
The summit took place at a time of mounting worries about the emerging technology, which promises to transform ‌industries, labor markets and societies.
It also came in the wake of a series of incidents involving rogue AI agents in recent months and the wider discussion about how the technology could harm humanity.

Tech leaders behind the technology have also fallen under scrutiny. As recently as this week, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was forced to resign after it was revealed that he had been in a relationship with a Chinese spy and a direct report in his company.
Finding Europe's role in the AI revolution
During the summit, a discussion occurred about where Europe fits in within the AI movement.
European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said she frustrated with the notion that Europe had "somehow lost the AI race."
She noted that the EU has "world-class talent, technological expertise and industrial experience to lead in AI."
"What we need now is to ensure that our ideas have the financing they need to grow and succeed in Europe," she added.
Will AI laws protect us? EU AI Act explained
EU foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said there is a "dark side" to AI.

"We can all already see this in the battlefield in Ukraine, where you have drones equipped by artificial intelligence to really train to find anybody to kill," Kallas, the former prime minister of Estonia, said at the event.

Leaders face questions on how to unlock AI's potential, how to catch up with China and the United States in the race for the technology, but also how to protect against the risks it poses to individuals and businesses.

The governments of Estonia and Finland wrote in a letter ahead of the summit that Europe must "establish EU-level arrangements for responding to serious AI incidents," calling for "developing advanced AI and governing it responsibly."

articles.title: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine
articles.summary: The fact the question of European security now features in discussions is viewed in Moscow as a victory, BBC Russia Editor Steve Rosenberg says.

blocks.text: Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine.
That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of Russia's neighbour nearly five years ago and who continues to reject the idea of a comprehensive ceasefire.
And what, in Moscow's view, is a prerequisite for peace?
The Kremlin spelt it out after talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner: "A new, long-term architecture of indivisible security and peace."
Translated from Kremlin-speak, it means Moscow wants to change the security set-up of Europe in a way that benefits Russia.
What Russia is pushing for is, potentially, the biggest change to European security arrangements since the end of the Cold War.

The Kremlin has put back on the table its controversial proposal from December 2021 – the "draft treaties" with the US and Nato which would not only have put the brakes on the alliance's eastward enlargement by giving Moscow cast-iron guarantees that, for instance, Ukraine and Georgia would never be allowed to join, but also rolled back Nato military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe which became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union.
Western leaders dismissed such demands as an unacceptable Russian ultimatum. Two months later Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The "draft treaties" were put away. Now they are out of the geopolitical filing cabinet, and being quoted again by the Kremlin.

What is more, Yuri Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy aide, has suggested that Moscow is about to "add certain new considerations" to its list of demands in light of Western efforts "to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia".
That does not mean, of course, that Western governments will accept them.
But the fact that the question of European security is featuring now in discussions on Ukraine is viewed here as a victory for Moscow.
"In December 2021 Russia actively proposed that Nato rethink the security system in Europe," wrote newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda earlier this week.
"Our proposals were almost laughed at.
"Having secured one victory by forcing the West to think about security, our diplomats need a second by making the West heed Russia's concerns about Nato enlargement."
The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, has called Russia's demands for a new European security architecture a "trap" designed to "shift attention away from a ceasefire".

"The sequencing of Ukraine-Russia talks is important," Kallas wrote on social media. "The priority should be securing a ceasefire, followed by a peace agreement. Only then can there be discussions on Europe's wider security architecture."
Europe's problem is that, right now, it is not at the table.
Moscow has had no desire to give it a chair. It has slammed European leaders for their military support for Kyiv and tough stance on Russia.
This week's peace talks in Abu Dhabi involved Ukraine, Russia and the US.
After his discussions in Moscow, Witkoff indicated that Putin had agreed to the idea of European representatives joining the next round of Ukraine peace talks.
But on Friday the Kremlin indicated a final decision on European participation had not been taken.

"Once we understand their true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to take a decision about dialogue on Ukraine in a wider format," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.
And what of Putin?
At the talks with Witkoff and Kushner he was sounding uncompromising and confident.
You can see why.
The Americans are knocking at his door and seeking a deal and the Europeans are contemplating contacts with him. Last month the leaders of Norway and Finland reached out and called him.

And next week in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, Putin may have a separate meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. Russian media are already comparing them to the "Big Three" - Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill - who met in 1945 to reorganise post-World War Two Europe.
And yet, after nearly five years of war, Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.
The Russian economy is under increasing pressure.
Ukrainian drone strikes continue to target Russian oil refineries, sparking fears of new fuel shortages.
But, so far, none of this has convinced the Kremlin leader to end the fighting.

articles.title: What's going on with the polar vortex?
articles.summary: Observations show the ring of fierce winds that rotate at the Earth's North Pole has changed direction. Scientists say it's a historic disruption and the earliest reversal on record. What could it…

image.caption: Cold snaps during winter can sometimes be linked to disruptions to the polar vortexImage: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: High up in the atmosphere, there's a ring of cold air swirling over the Arctic that can intensify, weaken, and shapeshift through the seasons. This is the polar vortex.
If it gets disrupted, this twisting pool of chilly air can influence the weather we experience, increasing the risk of a cold snap in the Northern Hemisphere.
Current observations show the vortex has weakened unprecedentedly early this year, with its winds reversing directions.
Earliest vortex disruption on record
It's not yet clear how the current disruption to the polar vortex will affect the Northern Hemisphere winter, but scientists agree it is a record-breaking event.

"As far as we know, this is the earliest stratospheric vortex disruption that has been observed," European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecast (ECMWF) principal scientists Tim Stockdale and Frederic Vitart told the AFP news agency.
The French meteorological agency Meteo-France, meanwhile, called it "an unprecedented event."

The early breakdown of the vortex "really increases the chance of cold air outbreaks across the latitudes where most of the densely populated population centers are across the Northern Hemisphere, US, Europe and East Asia," Judah Cohen, a climatologist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology told AFP.

blocks.caption: When the polar vortex is detabilized, it can send a blast of freezing temperatures further southImage: Adam Glanzman/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: What exactly is the polar vortex and how does it work?
The polar vortex is an enormous band of cold, low-pressure air that spins counterclockwise around the North Pole, about 10 to 50 kilometers (around 6 to 30 miles) above the surface.

It's closely connected to the jet stream, another band of powerful winds just below the vortex. The jet stream forms a boundary where the cold Arctic air meets warmer air from the tropics and subtropics.

The vortex can sometimes be a tight circle, keeping the coldest air locked around the North Pole over winter. It can also form uneven waves that dip southwards. And as it changes in strength and shape, that can influence the atmosphere below and alter the position of the jet stream, which drives the weather on the ground.
So, if the jet stream is more "wavy," and plunges south, it may also allow freezing Arctic air to spill southward.

One of the biggest influences that can provoke this kind of disruption is known as "sudden stratospheric warming." This is when temperatures in the polar stratosphere rise dramatically within a few days, causing the vortex's strong westerly winds to weaken.
This can push the vortex off its spot at the North Pole, make it split apart into multiple rings, or — as is happening now — cause the westerly winds to change direction.
It can take several weeks for the vortex to recover.
What does this mean for winter weather?

A previous polar vortex disruption contributed to the deadly Great Texas Freeze in February 2021, which caused more than a week of freezing temperatures that sparked power outages and killed hundreds of people.

But bone-chilling cold isn't a foregone conclusion. The Met Office, which is the UK's national weather and climate service, stresses that what's happening with the polar vortex can nudge odds in that direction, but it's not a switch that turns cold weather on and off.
Other weather patterns can also influence the outcome.
For example, there's a possibility El Nino, which is associated with milder winters, could "moderate or modify" the impacts, Cohen told AFP. But he added this was not certain.

The El Nino weather phenomenon, caused by the warming of surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, is currently intensifying and is expected to peak at the end of the year. The ongoing event has been classified as exceptionally strong and is disrupting weather around the globe.

Some research has also linked the rapid warming of the Arctic driven by climate change to increasing disruptions to the polar vortex. That means that, even as the planet warms, some areas may still experience more severe cold spells. But this connection is not conclusive and is still debated by scientists.
What happens when El Nino meets climate change?

articles.title: Ice hockey: Russia threatens against Canada and Germany over exclusion from tournaments
articles.summary: A fortnight after the CAS ordered ice hockey's governing body to reintegrate Russia into international play, a solution remains elusive. Now Russia has threatened to take legal action against two…

image.caption: While the Russia-based KHL remains one of the world's top leagues, Russia has been excluded from international play for yearsImage: Peter Kovalev/ITAR-TASS/IMAGO

blocks.text: "Should Canada and Germany refuse to allow the Russian team to participate, we will demand compensation, enforce the postponement of the competitions, and impose sanctions on the organizers," Russian Ice Hockey Federation President Vladislav Tretiak told the TASS news agency.
"There are rules: if a team does not take the ice, it receives a forfeit loss and sanctions are imposed," Tretiak added after a presidential sports council meeting in Moscow on Thursday.
"The IIHF as a way out — either allow us to participate or, if we cannot enter Canada, move the championship, don't hold it at all, or impose sanctions on Canada."

blocks.caption: Russian Ice Hockey Federation President Vladislav Tretiak was the Soviet Union's top netminder in the 1970s and early 1980sImage: Yuri Kochetkov/SNA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Canada refuses to bend on junior tournament
The threat comes after the Canadian government confirmed on Wednesday that it would not allow Russian players to play in the IIHF World Junior Championship starting on December 26 in Alberta.

"Canada's position is unequivocal: as long as Russia continues ⁠its war of aggression ​against Ukraine, there can be no return to business as usual," Canadian Secretary of State for Sport Adam van Koeverden said in a statement. "Canada will continue to stand with Ukraine."

Following last month's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling, in which it said that the security concerns the IIHF cited for barring Russian teams from taking part in international tournaments was not sufficient – the world governing body pledged to work to comply with the decision.

Norway then said it had been bumped from the World Juniors and had been informed by the IIHF that Russia would take its place. Several other national hockey associations said they had received a revised schedule for the tournament and stated that they would not play against Russia. The IIHF has not confirmed the change.
Men's tournament with Russia 'effectively impossible'

Germany has been watching developments related to the World Juniors and host nation Canada closely, as it is set to host the IIHF World Championship in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf starting on May 14. With several nations saying they will not play Russia and major sponsors threatening to pull out, a German government spokesman described the prospect of hosting the tournament under these conditions as "effectively impossible."
However, Germany has ruled out taking the Canadian approach.

Ronald Rauhe, Germany's minister of state for sport said on Wednesday that refusing to grant visas was "not a solution for the (German) ice hockey federation (DEB), nor is it a solution for successfully hosting a World Championship anywhere."
At the same time, though, he expressed support for the DEB in its wish to host the tournament as planned.

"We believe that we should channel all our energy and efforts into helping sport—and ice hockey in particular—find a solution, which would, of course, entail excluding Russia from the World Championship."
Munich's Olympic bid and the IOC's new stance on Russia

What makes things even more complicated for German officials are concerns that taking a hardline on Russia could jeopardize Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees bidding to host an Olympic Games to follow its lead. The IOC is set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process.

For now, though, the ball appears to be in the IIHF's court, after Ottawa confirmed its refusal to grant Russians visas to play in the World Juniors. How the dispute regarding that tournament gets resolved could go a long way to pointing the way forward for the men's tournament in Germany next May.

blocks.text: November 14, 2026 | 12:00am

“Every senior high school graduate should have the opportunity to become work-ready,” Angara posted on Facebook yesterday, adding that one of the main features of the new SHS curriculum is the job immersion.
STAR / Ernie Penaredondo

MANILA, Philippines — More than 61,000 work immersion slots were pledged by the private sector to boost the employability of senior high school (SHS) graduates, according to Education Secretary Sonny Angara.

“In addition to simplifying it, we have fewer subjects, more focus and more choices for our students. This job immersion will really prepare them so that they are more job ready and our Grade 12 graduates have a greater chance of getting a job,” he added.
Angara said they learned from experience that the chances of employment for SHS graduates are increased with longer immersion periods.

“Apart from that, our learners’ certification for the last two years is also free. We’re working very closely with TESDA (Technical Education and Skills Development Authority) and CHED (Commission on Higher Education) to make it seamless, smooth,” Angara added.
At the same time, he discussed strengthening the integration of Early Childhood Care and Development in basic education at the 86th executive committee meeting of the Department of Education.

articles.title: Swift passage of national cyber law urged
articles.summary: Amid rising cybersecurity attacks, the Cybersecurity Council of the Philippines (CSCP) yesterday pushed for the swift passage of a national cybersecurity law and urged both the government and private…

blocks.text: November 14, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Amid rising cybersecurity attacks, the Cybersecurity Council of the Philippines (CSCP) yesterday pushed for the swift passage of a national cybersecurity law and urged both the government and private sector to review their security systems to prevent digital breaches.

In a statement issued yesterday, the CSCP, which is dedicated to advancing cybersecurity awareness and policy development, called on the government and private sector to take immediate action as cyberattacks rise faster than organizations’ ability to respond.

Citing Viettel Cyber Security’s Cyber Threat Landscape Report, the CSCP said the country recorded 16,619 phishing attacks, 255 data breach incidents and 21 ransomware attacks in the first half of the year.
These breaches exposed about 335 million records and compromised over 19.2 million Filipino account credentials.

As such, the CSCP is pushing for the immediate approval of a national cybersecurity law to strengthen the country’s defenses against cyberattacks and protect critical systems and the delivery of essential services.

“The Council urges the Senate to act swiftly on its counterpart measure so that the country has a dedicated agency, clear standards and mandatory protections for critical information infrastructure,” the CSCP said.
It also called on both the government and private sector to conduct a cybersecurity health check immediately.

“Every Filipino organization should assume it is already a target – because it is. Hackers do not wait for budgets, for legislation or for the next board meeting,” CSCP chairman Donald Patrick Lim said.

“We are asking every agency head, CEO, school president and mayor to treat this as urgent: check your systems now, close the gaps you find and train your people,” he added, noting that most attacks begin with a single click by an untrained employee.

The CSCP urged organizations to take the following steps within the next 30 days: apply pending security patches, enable multi-factor authentication on all email and administrator accounts, remove inactive or unnecessary user accounts, check employee credentials against data leaks and ensure backups are kept offline and can be restored.
To help strengthen digital defenses, the CSCP is releasing a free cybersecurity health-check guide for organizations and conducting training sessions in partnership with industry and the academe.

“Cybersecurity is no longer just an IT (information technology) issue. It is a national security, economic and public trust issue. Our country needs to move forward safely – and that requires every sector to act today, not after the next breach,” Lim said.

articles.title: President Marcos to new Navy chief: Boost territorial defense
articles.summary: President Marcos ordered yesterday newly appointed Navy chief Vice Admiral Alan Javier to boost territorial defense and deepen ties with allies.

blocks.text: November 14, 2026 | 12:00am
President Marcos leads the Philippine Navy change of command ceremony as outgoing chief Rear Admiral Jose Ma. Ambrosio Ezpeleta (left) shakes hands with his successor Vice Admiral Alan Javier.
Noel Pabalate
MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos ordered yesterday newly appointed Navy chief Vice Admiral Alan Javier to boost territorial defense and deepen ties with allies.
Marcos gave the directive as he led the change of command and retirement ceremony at the Philippine Navy headquarters in Manila.
Javier has been named flag-officer-in-command of the Philippine Navy, succeeding Jose Maria Ambrosio Ezpeleta.

“Build on these gains. Strengthen our ability to defend our territory and protect our sovereign rights. Deepen our partnerships with our allies and friends and sustain our commitment to the welfare of every sailor and every marine,” Marcos said.
Javier’s extensive experience in logistics, an area fundamental to the operational readiness of the Navy, will be important in fulfilling the President’s directive.

“This administration has made significant investments in acquiring new naval assets. I am confident that your experience will serve you well in ensuring that this growing fleet remains capable,” Marcos said.
The President also hailed Ezpeleta, whom he said has led the transformation of the Navy by modernizing its capabilities and advancing its role in the country’s external defense.
“Under his leadership, the Navy expanded its external defense operations, strengthened its presence in the West Philippine Sea (WPS) and intensified maritime security efforts,” he said.
Marcos said under Ezpeleta's watch, the Navy facilitated 19 bilateral and 14 multilateral maritime cooperative activities with other like-minded nations to strengthen maritime security.
The Navy also participated in 16 bilateral and 22 multilateral exercises, including Exercise Balikatan and the Multinational Exercise Cobra Gold.
“Our sailors and Marines gained valuable opportunities to work alongside their counterparts and strengthen the partnerships,” Marcos said.
Transformation

In his speech, Javier vowed to continue transforming the country’s primary maritime military unit into a “stronger, more capable and mission-ready” force amid current and evolving challenges to the country’s territorial integrity and sovereign rights.

He acknowledged “the complexities of our maritime security environment and the strategic challenges confronting our country,” considering that his previous post was commander of the Western Command based in Palawan, which has jurisdiction over most parts of the WPS.

“I understand that the demands of the Philippine Navy go beyond maintaining operational readiness. We are called upon to serve as a critical component of the armed forces to protect our people and state, to secure sovereignty and to preserve the integrity of our national territory,” he stressed.

“These responsibilities are realities that our sailors and Marines confront every day, particularly those serving on the frontlines of our maritime domain. The mandate demands not only capable forces and credible capabilities, but most importantly, the wisdom for sound judgment, sustained commitment and unity of effort that are aligned with the strategic objectives for a comprehensive, active, archipelagic defense and deterrence,” he said. — Michael Punongbayan

articles.title: Trump’s late arrival won’t delay Asean closing ceremony
articles.summary: The closing ceremony of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit on Nov. 17 will proceed as scheduled despite the late arrival of United States President Donald Trump, the…
articles.byline: Rudy Santos, Rhodina Villanueva, Mark Ernest Villeza, Pia Lee-Brago

blocks.text: November 14, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The closing ceremony of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit on Nov. 17 will proceed as scheduled despite the late arrival of United States President Donald Trump, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said yesterday.

“Nothing will be pushed back. We’ll proceed as planned with regard to the preparations, especially on the closing ceremony,” the DFA’s ASEAN spokesman Dominic Xavier Imperial said at a media briefing at the International Media Center.
“However, the day will culminate with the ASEAN-US Special Summit. That summit will still take place despite the late arrival of the (US) president,” he added.
The ASEAN-US Special Summit will be held after the closing ceremony and handover of ASEAN chairship to Singapore.
Trump, the last world leader to arrive for the summit, is scheduled to land in Manila on Nov. 17 at 5:30 p.m., half an hour after the closing ceremony.

The ASEAN-US Special Summit is a high-level diplomatic meeting that brings together leaders from the ASEAN and the US to address shared regional and global challenges, deepen strategic ties and review cooperative frameworks.
The “only leaders” participation in the US-ASEAN Summit enable them to candidly discuss the agenda set for that summit and for identification of the measures that need to be addressed.
Imperial said President Marcos and Trump are scheduled to meet on the sidelines of the ASEAN Summit and that the latter will have bilateral engagements on Nov. 18.
Trump is likely to miss the East Asia Summit, the only leader-led forum wherein all key Indo-Pacific partners meet to discuss political, security and economic challenges facing the region.
Police operations
Even as over 19,000 police officers will be deployed for the ASEAN Summit, the Philippine National Police assured the public that regular PNP operations and community patrols will continue.
PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. directed regional and local commanders to maintain enough personnel in their areas to sustain crime prevention, patrols and emergency response services.
The National Capital Region Police Office, Police Regional Office 3 and 4A, as well as all Camp Crame-based units have been place under full alert from Nov. 13 to 19.
CAAP ready
The Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines (CAAP) said they are prepared to ensure the smooth arrival and departure of leaders and delegates for the ASEAN Summit.
CAAP director general Raul del Rosario said over 300 flights are expected to be affected by changes in schedule beginning today.
Airline companies have reached out to their passengers and promised appropriate assistance for everyone affected.
The Department of Health (DOH), for its part, has deployed nearly 300 medical personnel to respond to possible health-related incidents during the summit.
As of yesterday, the DOH has dispatched 42 medical teams consisting of 274 health care workers in venues where meetings and activities would be held.

Medical health desks were set up at the Philippine International Convention Center, the main venue of the summit, in the hotels where delegates were billeted and at the International Media Center inside the World Trade Center.

articles.title: SWS: Marcos administration's net satisfaction rating drops to -4 in September 2026
articles.summary: Filipino adults gave the national government a net satisfaction rating of -4 in September 2026, down from the previous survey, according to results released by the Social Weather Stations (SWS) on…

blocks.text: Filipino adults gave the national government a net satisfaction rating of -4 in September 2026, down from the previous survey, according to results released by the Social Weather Stations (SWS) on Friday.

Although SWS classified the -4 rating as “neutral,” it represented a five-point decline from the +1 recorded in June 2026, making it the second-lowest net satisfaction rating of President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr.’s administration. The latest survey was conducted from September 21 to 27, 2026.
In March 2026, the Marcos administration recorded its lowest net satisfaction rating at "poor" -13.

“Thirty-eight percent of adult Filipinos were satisfied, 18% were neither satisfied nor dissatisfied, and 42% were dissatisfied with the general performance of the current National Administration, for a net satisfaction rating of -4,” SWS said.
Performance subjects
In its Governance Report Card, SWS assessed the national administration's performance across various areas, with ratings ranging from “very good” to “bad.”

“The National Administration’s net satisfaction rating was very good on providing the youth with basic education in public elementary and high schools (+61) and improving the quality of children’s education (+50),” the survey said.

“It was good on helping the poor (+42, correctly rounded), implementing housing programs for the poor (+40), creating policies that will generate job opportunities (+40), helping victims of disasters (+36, correctly rounded), and developing science and technology (+30, correctly rounded),” it added.
The national government received “moderate” ratings for ensuring food safety, providing an efficient transportation system, and defending Philippine sovereignty in the West Philippine Sea.
Meanwhile, it received a “poor” rating for generating solutions to rising oil prices and a “bad” rating for eradicating graft and corruption in government and fighting inflation.
SWS said net satisfaction ratings declined across all 19 performance subjects compared with the previous survey.

“Compared to November 2025, when they were last surveyed, net satisfaction fell by 23 points for being prepared for strong typhoons, from moderate +28 to neutral +5, and by 14 points for helping victims of disasters, from very good +50 to good +36,” it added.
Regional ratings
The administration recorded its highest net satisfaction rating in Balance Luzon at neutral +7, followed by the Visayas at neutral -2, Mindanao at poor -17, and Metro Manila at poor -21.

"Compared to June 2026, net satisfaction with the National Administration fell by 10 points in Metro Manila, from poor -11 to poor -21. It fell by 7 points in the Visayas, from neutral +5 to neutral -2, and by 6 points in Balance Luzon, from moderate +13 to neutral +7. It stayed at poor -17 in Mindanao," SWS said.

The administration also recorded declines in net satisfaction ratings among 18- to 24-year-olds (+13 to -13), college graduates (-10 to -25), those with some senior high school through some college (+4 to -16), men (-3 to -6), and women (+6 to -1).

The net satisfaction rating improved but remained poor among those aged 35 to 44, rising by four points from -15 to -11. Meanwhile, it remained moderate among adults aged 55 and above, edging up by one point from +17 to +18.

The survey was conducted through face-to-face interviews with 1,500 adults aged 18 and above nationwide: 600 in Balance Luzon (or Luzon outside Metro Manila) and 300 each in Metro Manila, the Visayas, and Mindanao.
The sampling error margins were ±3 percentage points for national figures, ±4 points for Balance Luzon, and ±6 points each for Metro Manila, the Visayas, and Mindanao. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Democratic Senate leader Schumer set to face leadership challenge
articles.summary: Maryland Senator Van Hollen says "new leadership" is needed for Democrats following the party's recent midterm successes.

blocks.text: US Senator Chuck Schumer is facing a challenge to his position as US Senate majority leader from his fellow Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen, as the party prepares to take control of Congress after sweeping the midterm elections.
Van Hollen, 67, said in a post on X on Thursday that Americans voted for change earlier this month and "to deliver, we need new leadership".
Schumer, 75, has led Democrats in the chamber since 2017, serving as both majority and minority leader. He was first elected to the Senate in 1999.
Following the midterms earlier this month, his position has come under pressure by some left-wing Democrats who see him as too moderate and part of the party establishment.
Responding to the challenge, Schumer, who represents New York, said he welcomes "any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead".
He added that he is "proud of what we've accomplished together" in the midterms, and he has "the votes to continue as Democratic leader".

The vote on Senate leader will be held behind closed doors in early December and the winner will assume the role on 4 January, when Democrats take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives after their midterms successes.
The move by Van Hollen, who represents Maryland, marks the most significant step by a high-profile Democrat to challenge the party's existing leadership following last week's midterms victory.
Announcing his plans to run on X, he wrote that Americans had called on the party to "unrig an economy rigged against working people".
In recent years, Van Hollen has taken positions popular with those on the left of his party.
In 2024, he supported restricting weapons shipments to Israel and criticised the Biden administration over its role in the war in Gaza.
In an interview with MS NOW, Van Hollen - who has served in the Senate for nearly a decade - acknowledged that he is an "underdog" but added that he believes the race is "very much in flux".
Independent Senator Bernie Sanders and Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed have both publicly come out in support of Van Hollen - while others have also called for new leadership.
In a post on X, Sanders said he believes Van Hollen "will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families".
El-Sayed said the challenger would bring "bold leadership" and lead with both "courage and experience".
Others Democrats have publicly backed Schumer.
Senator Jacky Rosen of Nevada said: "He has the experience and the fight to continue leading our diverse caucus at this crucial moment".
Senator Kirsten Gillibrand said: "You will see, despite all the grumblings, enormous gratitude for the hard work he has done to get us to this position."

articles.title: German spies handed new powers to tackle 'hybrid threats' from abroad
articles.summary: German reforms mean foreign and domestic intelligence services will have greater powers to combat espionage, terrorism and sabotage.

blocks.text: Germany's foreign and domestic intelligence services are to be given greater powers to combat espionage, terrorism and sabotage after the country's parliament, the Bundestag, approved a major overhaul of its legislation.
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, who championed the bill, has called it a "reform of the century", necessary because of the increasing threats from foreign powers.
But the Left Party's security spokeswoman, Clara Bünger, said Dobrindt was creating a new German secret police.
The legislation gives numerous new powers to Germany's BND federal intelligence service, and its BfV domestic service, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution.
In the Bundestag, 309 MPs voted in favour of the new law on intelligence services, while 190 voted against and 71 abstained.
For historical reasons, German intelligence has mainly focused on gathering information rather than acting on it.
In future, German spies working for the BND, which is responsible for foreign intelligence, will be able to conduct covert operations abroad, including sabotage.
This could include paralysing the servers of state-sponsored hacker groups, disrupting disinformation networks, or even disrupting supply chains for weapons.

Agents for the domestic intelligence service, the BfV, will no longer to be limited to gathering information. For the first time they will be able to take protective action against property and IT systems, if specific threats are identified.

That means they will be allowed to dismantle or break explosives or weapons, divert or block data flows during cyber-attacks, delete or falsify data stored for malicious purposes, and plant false information on those involved.
Under certain conditions, BfV agents will also be permitted to enter homes covertly. However, the measure must always be authorised in advance.

They will also be given wider powers of digital surveillance, including monitoring encrypted telecommunications and carrying out online searches. They will also be allowed to use AI-supported data analysis and biometric image matching on the internet.
The government says the reform is needed because of an increase in foreign espionage, particularly from Russia, China and Iran.
"We are the target of hybrid threats," said Dobrindt. "Germany is a theatre of operations for terrorism, extremism and foreign powers."
In August, a drone carrying an explosive device was discovered at Leipzig Airport, close to Ukrainian cargo planes. However, it failed to explode as the bomb's detonator was apparently faulty.
German authorities say Russia was behind the attack.
The new law has been bitterly criticised by some opposition politicians, even though Dobrindt has said it is "madness" to think it means that Germany is creating a new secret police.
And Clara Bünger from the Left Party told public broadcaster ARD that the new law was "a monster… summoning ghosts that we will probably never be able to get rid of".
The separation between the police and the secret service, she warned, was "being eroded" - and Bünger said that had been a lesson learned from the Nazi era.
"This means the secret service is being granted executive powers and will not only be allowed to act pre-emptively, but will also be granted police powers."

However, Sonja Eichwede of the centre-left SPD, which is part of Germany's governing coalition, said the reforms would make a significant contribution to ensuring the country's democracy was "robust and resilient".

articles.title: Nvidia scandal fallout widens as Trump's treasury secretary blames cabinet colleague
articles.summary: Scott Bessent suggests Howard Lutnick’s commerce department failed to ban exports of Nvidia's chips to a firm thought to have links with China.

blocks.text: How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security?
ByRachel Clun
Business ReporterReporting fromNew York

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed the Commerce Department, run by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec Nvidia chips, as the fallout from the scandal widens.
Jensen Huang left Nvidia after revelations he had an affair with a former Megaspeed executive who was also allegedly a Chinese spy. The firm had been buying advanced chips from Nvidia.

Megaspeed had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it had been smuggling chips into China, reports said, but it is not on a list of firms that US companies are prevented from working with.
Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months".
"But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added.
There is growing pressure on Lutnick from both sides of politics to explain his department's actions.
He has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to keep all records relating to Nvidia and Huang.
Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images
Bessent said he was "frustrated" by delays in putting the company on the export control list and reports of leakage of AI chips into China.

"President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.

Last year, the Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it had been smuggling some of Nvidia's advanced AI chips into China, according to the New York Times. Megaspeed has been contacted for comment.

There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but separate reporting in the Financial Times said the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included.
However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia.
"The story has been thus far of Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he told CNBC's Squawk Box programme, external.

"The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?
"It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that."
Huang has been summoned to testify before the Senate Banking Committee about his affair with the former Megaspeed executive, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.
The Commerce Secretary has been summoned to appear before the committee in December.
"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," committee chairman, Republican Senator Tim Scott posted on X.

Democrats on key congressional committees have also asked the Commerce Department and Lutnick to keep all records relating to decisions to allow Nvidia to sell its advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, including all their communications with or about Nvidia and Jensen Huang.
Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E. Neal and Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden are starting investigations over the way Nvidia was allowed to sell these chips.
According to Neal and Wyden, Nvidia's advanced H200 chips could be sold to Chinese firms if they were first imported from their manufacturing facility in Taiwan into America for inspection.

A 25% tariff - a levy that is paid to the federal government - was imposed on those chips, under a section of the Trade Act that Neal and Wyden say is meant to allow the US president to take action against imports that risk national security.
"Trump's use of the statute appears to have done the opposite, undermining US national security and putting Americans at risk," they said.

articles.title: EXPLAINER: What caused the Microsoft outage?
articles.summary: Thousands of users worldwide were affected by a widespread Microsoft outage, with several institutions in the Philippines also reporting disruptions. Around 74 countries were affected by the outage,…

blocks.text: Published November 13, 2026 11:37pm
Thousands of users worldwide were affected by a widespread Microsoft outage, with several institutions in the Philippines also reporting disruptions.
Around 74 countries were affected by the outage, according to Down Detector.

In a report from GMA News Feed, Microsoft first announced the outage on X at 11:40 p.m. on November 12, Philippine time. The report said that they were investigating reported issues in Microsoft Teams in parts of North America.
Later, Microsoft said that it received reports of difficulty in accessing cloud-based messaging Exchange Online.
Down Detector said it has received 97,000 reports of difficulty accessing Microsoft Outlook in the US, as of 3:00 a.m. in the Philippines, November 13.
Meanwhile, there were 38,000 reports of issues with Microsoft 365, while 4,500 users reported problems with Microsoft Teams.
Down Detector said it received reports from the United Kingdom, India and New Zealand. Australia also said that its Federal Police at the Security Intelligence Organization was affected.
OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, was also affected. They said that they were probing issues with Microsoft connectors, which led to some of their tools malfunctioning.
In the Philippines, the Supreme Court issued an advisory on November 13 that its judiciary platform was affected. Because of this, some transactions may be delayed.

“The Supreme Court informs the public that the ongoing worldwide Microsoft 365 service outage has affected the Philippine Judiciary 365 (PJ365), including Microsoft Outlook. During this period, responses to emails and other transactions may be delayed,” the high court said.
Microsoft said that it was not increased traffic that caused this mass outage. The firm attributed the outage to some servers being unavailable, which affected its remaining infrastructure.

As of 4:14 a.m. in the Philippines, Microsoft said that based on their investigation, another possible reason for the unavailable servers was due to one “specific component” that focuses on the health of the servers.

“Our investigation indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component that's responsible for processing server health. We've taken steps to prevent additional servers from being impacted while we work to return the affected servers to service,” the tech giant said.
As of 2:12 p.m. in the Philippines, Microsoft said that it was continuously working to fix its frontend servers and restore its service infrastructure to a healthy state.—Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Cyber attacks and hybrid warfare: Germany gives sweeping powers to its police and intelligence services
articles.summary: Drone sightings and cyberattacks have heightened security concerns. How are the police preparing to meet these challenges? And how do intelligence services plan to counter threats from both domestic…

image.caption: A bomb disposal robot was deployed by police at Germany's Leipzig airport, after a drone was spotted nearbyImage: News5/AFP

blocks.text: Germany's intelligence agencies have been given wide-ranging new powers. The lawmakers in the Bundestag agreed to a reform package on Friday.

Under the new rules, the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) will be allowed to respond to cyberattacks by foreign powers with counterattacks of its own. The range of possible measures is broad, from deleting and manipulating data to disabling entire systems and, if necessary, even destroying physical weapons such as drones that could be deployed against Germany.

Under certain conditions, the agencies will also be permitted to enter homes and business premises covertly, for example, to prepare surveillance operations. They will, however, not be allowed to use force against people. An independent oversight board is to be established to monitor the agencies.
Opposition lawmakers specializing in domestic policy warned against granting powers that are too broad.
Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig
Separation of powers hampers procedures

The president of Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), Holger Münch this week again pointed out that today's hybrid attacks pose a new challenge to the organizations safeguarding the country's security. At his organization's annual meeting in Berlin this week, he said the "hybrid attacks" are challenging the "separation principle," which means that the police conduct investigations while intelligence services gather information. The exchange of data between the two is permitted only under strict conditions.

Münch has long objected to this strict division of responsibilities. He has been calling for expanded powers for the police and closer cooperation with the domestic intelligence agency, the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, which is responsible for countering espionage and sabotage.

The separation principle results from lessons learned from the Nazi dictatorship, when the Secret State Police (Gestapo) operated largely outside judicial constraints and served as the regime's central instrument of terror, used to oppress and murder Jews, Sinti and Roma, homosexuals, communists, social democrats, and many others. The Allied powers that defeated Nazi Germany in World War II then decided that the police and intelligence services should remain institutionally separate and be granted different powers.
Germany's spy agency: fact and fiction

Historian Sönke Neitzel of the University of Potsdam considers the separation principle understandable in its historical context. At the BKA's autumn conference, however, he described it as "nonsense" in light of today's threat landscape and said it was no longer necessary in a country that has been a constitutional democracy for decades.

While Neitzel considers the separation principle outdated, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the center-right Christian Social Union (CSU) wants to preserve it in its essential form. In his view, even a more extensive exchange of data does not violate the principle. At the same time, however, he has made clear that he wants to transform the domestically focused Office for the Protection of the Constitution and the foreign intelligence agency, the Federal Intelligence Service(BND), into "real intelligence services."

This legislative reform brings Dobrindt a significant step closer to that goal. Parliament pproved the interior minister's plans with the votes of the governing coalition of the conservative Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) and the Social Democratic Party (SPD).
As cyberattacks threaten Germany, can Berlin keep data safe?
Espionage, sabotage, and disinformation

Dobrindt insisted that Germany intends to take an active approach to defending itself against cyberattacks: "Anyone who attacks us in this way must know that we are prepared to strike back. They must know that their digital infrastructure, their server infrastructure, and their software will also be targeted by us."

BKA President Holger Münch welcomes Dobrindt's determination and points to the growing threat posed by cyberattacks. The line between criminal and state-sponsored actors is becoming increasingly blurred, he argues. As a result, both intelligence services and law enforcement agencies face the same challenge.

To underscore the scale of the threat as he sees it, Münch cited two statistics: in the first six months of 2026, crime originating from abroad rose by 24% compared with the same period the previous year. What concerns him most is that fewer than 5% of these cases are solved. The BKA chief considers this trend more dangerous than ever: "The state's promise of security can become fragile. Confidence in the ability of its institutions to act effectively and remain steadfast is declining."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Aide to fugitive Ukrainian ex-PM wounded in latest Moscow car bombing
articles.summary: Sergei Zavorotny, now a journalist and commentator, was previously an adviser to Ukrainian ex-prime minister Mykola Azarov.

blocks.text: A car bomb attack in Moscow has wounded a former adviser to Ukrainian ex-prime minister Mykola Azarov, Russia's Investigative Committee says.
Sergei Zavorotny, now a journalist and commentator, was behind the wheel of his black Toyota when the explosion happened and Azarov told Russian TV his condition in hospital was "rather critical".

The car bomb went off a day after a Russian colonel was killed in another explosion in St Petersburg, and both blasts are seen as part of a series of attacks on military and prominent figures linked to Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Zavorotny, 72, worked as a press aide to Mykola Azarov in Kyiv until 2014.
But when pro-Kremlin Ukrainian president Viktor Yanukovych was toppled from power, Azarov fled Kyiv for Russia and tried unsuccessfully to set up a government in exile.

In a 2020 US Senate report on interference in the 2016 American presidential election, Zavorotny is described at the time as an SVR [Russian foreign intelligence] officer involved in influence operations.

Russia's Investigative Committee said on Telegram on Friday: "Serhiy Zavorotny, a former adviser to the former Ukrainian Prime Minister Mykola Azarov, was injured while driving a car. He was taken to one of the city hospitals, where he is receiving medical care."
It added: "A set of necessary investigative actions is being carried out. A number of examinations will be appointed, including medical and explosives."
According to several unconfirmed reports, Zavorotny suffered a number of serious injuries after an explosive device was detonated remotely.
Russia said the car bombs are the latest in a series of attacks targeting pro-Kremlin figures.
On Thursday a car bomb in the Pushkinsky District of St Petersburg killed a member of the Russian military, again after it was attached to the base of the car and detonated remotely.
The man targeted in the attack is yet to be named officially, but reputable sources suggest he was a high-ranking figure in the 6th Guards Air and Air Defence Forces Army.
Overnight into Friday, Ukraine and Russia exchanged attacks on each other's territories.
Ukrainian authorities said a hospital had been targeted by Russian bombardment.
They added that three people, including a 17-year-old boy, were also killed in attacks across southern Odesa and Zaporizhzhia.
Russia said a Ukrainian strike on an industrial facility in the central Samara region killed four people.
And in the southern Volgograd region another four died after an industrial zone was hit by drones. A further person died in the Bryansk border region, an area that is often fired upon.
Ukraine said these were retaliatory attacks in response to Russia's persistent targeting of its cities.

articles.title: Global Microsoft outage stretches into 2nd day

image.caption: People walk outside at St. Michael's Hospital in Toronto on May 9, 2025. (Nathan Denette/The Canadian Press)

items: November 13Canadian hospitals, universities and government services impactedPeople walk outside at St. Michael's Hospital in Toronto on May 9, 2025. (Nathan Denette/The Canadian Press)In Canada, the outage has affected hospitals, universities, government departments and transportation services.Unity Health Toronto, which operates several hospitals including St. Michael's Hospital, declared a "code grey" on Thursday, indicating an infrastructure failure. The hospital network said staff were having difficulty sending and receiving emails, but patient care was not affected.Toronto's Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre and University Health Network also reported email disruptions.In Montreal, the CHUM hospital said the outage affected appointment requests and some internal activities. The Jewish General Hospital also said it was affected.Via Rail said some customers were not receiving emails about their trips and advised passengers to check its train tracker or sign up for text notifications.Several post-secondary institutions, including the University of Toronto, Seneca Polytechnic and George Brown Polytechnic, also reported email problems, although classes were expected to proceed as scheduled Friday.Some federal government departments and Toronto city hall also experienced email disruptions.-With files from CBC's Linda Ward

Microsoft outage affecting users in at least 74 countriesVerity StevensonA Microsoft Outlook logo seen on a laptop in Warsaw, Poland, amid an Outlook outage that has left users around the world without its crucial services. (Mladen Antonov/AFP/Getty Images)The outage has disrupted online services in at least 74 countries, according to online outage monitors.The disruption began around 1 p.m. ET on Thursday. Microsoft 365 has more than 430 million paid users worldwide.The impacts appear to vary among users. Some report no issues, while others have been unable to send or receive emails or access virtual meetings.The Japanese government reported having issues, and Australia's intelligence agency also reported disruptions.In the United Kingdom, some health-care providers have been unable to share patient records between services. Airlines have also reported difficulties communicating with customers, while some businesses in Asia have struggled to receive orders.-WIth files from CBC's Julia Chapman

Microsoft outage disrupts services worldwide for second dayVerity StevensonA malfunctioning Microsoft Outlook website on a screen in Lausanne, Switzerland, on Friday. (Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty Images)A massive Microsoft outage is continuing to disrupt businesses, hospitals and government services around the world this morning, more than 12 hours after problems first emerged.The outage has affected services, including Outlook email, Teams and its AI assistant, Copilot, leaving users unable to send emails, access calendars or hold virtual meetings.The disruptions have been felt across Canada and in dozens of other countries, affecting everything from hospital communications to airline customer services and financial transactions.Microsoft says the outage was caused by server issues, with no indication of a cyberattack. The company says it is seeing signs of recovery, but services have yet to be fully restored.-With files from Reuters

articles.title: LIVE UPDATES: 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila
articles.summary: Leaders and representatives of the 11 members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, and their allies, are gathering in Manila for the bloc's biggest event of the year

blocks.text: The global energy crisis, food security, and transnational crime are among the top issues on the table as Southeast Asian leaders and their allies converge in Manila.
The Philippines, chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations for 2026, is hosting the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits from Sunday, November 15, to Tuesday, November 17.

Aside from leaders and representatives of ASEAN’s 11 members, other world leaders will be in attendance, including United States President Donald Trump, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, and newly reelected Brazil President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is embarking on a state visit to the Philippines before the summit.
During the summit’s closing ceremony, the Philippines will also turn over the ASEAN chairmanship to Singapore, which will lead the bloc in 2027.

Check out this page for the latest ASEAN Summit news, photos, videos, and insights. For more updates and to share your own views, you can also join the Security and Global Affairs chat room in Rappler’s Muni app.

articles.title: Is the AI bubble bursting just as Anthropic goes public?
articles.summary: The sharp sell-off in tech stocks after the US midterms has cast doubt on Anthropic's looming IPO. Yet, with hundreds of billions still being invested, some think the AI party is still in full swing.

image.caption: Anthropic is aiming for a valuation of more than $1 trillion when it goes public next weekImage: Carlos Barria/REUTERS

blocks.text: 2026 was meant to be the year Wall Street’s trillion-dollar artificial intelligence (AI) bet started paying off. Instead, it’s turning into a test of nerves.
In the first half of the year, many AI stocks hit record highs as US hyperscalers like Google's Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft recorded bumper earnings.
Two of the largest AI players — Anthropic and OpenAI — announced plans for public listings, following SpaceX's much-hyped IPO in June, which briefly made Elon Musk the world's first trillionaire.
AI models, meanwhile, got noticeably better at difficult tasks in the race to beat human intelligence.
Post-midterm AI sell-off rattles global markets amid Big Tech jitters
AI doubts trigger market turbulence

The second half of 2026, however, has brought a lot more uncertainty. While the stock of Nvidia, a chipmaker, pushed even higher last month, many hyperscalers and chip or memory firms have seen their stock prices gyrate wildly.

Then last week, after the Democrats secured control of the United States Congress in the midterm elections, technology stocks sold off dramatically, with the Magnificent Seven — including Meta, Apple, Amazon and Tesla — losing more than $1 trillion in value in a single trading day.

In a further twist, the AI sector took another hit this week as Nvidia shares plunged nearly 10% over two days. The sell-off followed news that Nvidia's board — alongside the FBI — is investigating CEO Jensen Huang’s ties to a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy.
On Thursday, Huang resigned from the chipmaker when a second alleged marital affair was revealed, sending Nvidia's shares lower still.

blocks.caption: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is under scrutiny over an affair with an alleged Chinese spyImage: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Amid huge spending, big returns remain elusive

Wall Street is growing increasingly cautious about the sheer size of the AI outlay, amid warnings that future earnings may not justify the huge spending. Growing pressure on US lawmakers to curb the expansion of AI data centers has added to those doubts.
In September, investment bank Goldman Sachs estimated that hyperscalers need around $300 billion in annual AI revenue to break even on their spending, leaving a gap of roughly $230 billion.

"We're not in Kansas anymore," Dennis Dick, chief market strategist at the Canada-based Stock Trader Network, told DW, meaning that times have changed. Now, he said, investors are telling companies: "show me the money."
Fears that Democrats could regulate AI lead to global market bloodbath
AI stocks needed a 'healthy correction'

Other analysts think it's too soon to expect the AI bubble to burst, including Kit Rees, investment strategist at London-based wealth manager Quilter, who thinks last week's rout was a "healthy correction."
"We’re still in the very early innings of the AI build-out," Rees told DW. "There’s still a lot of excitement around this technology and investors will want to have a slice of the pie."

In addition to the roughly $800 billion invested in capital expenditures this year, AI hyperscalers plan to spend a further $1.2 trillion in 2027 and $1.4 trillion in 2028, according to Goldman Sachs estimates.
Questions over timing of Anthropic IPO

While OpenAI has delayed its public listing until next year, Claude-maker Anthropic still plans its IPO later this month. On Tuesday, the company said it would offer 825 million shares at between $70 and $78 per share.
Dick said Anthropic’s decision to go ahead amid the market sell-off left him scratching his head. “Is this the best timing?” he asked.
While Anthropic had originally targeted a valuation of over $2 trillion, it now thinks the firm could be worth around $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion.
Dick said the valuation depends on whether Anthropic can deliver on a forecast by Goldman Sachs of over $600 billion in revenue by 2030.

"If you get to a company with $600 billion in revenue, [a] $1.3 trillion [valuation] doesn’t sound that bad," he told DW. "But when you’re talking about a company with currently $52 billion in revenue, it sounds like it’s overvalued."
Other analysts, like Vivek Seth, chief executive officer of Shaires Holdings, are more bullish about the Claude-maker's prospects.

“Anthropic is a once-in-a-generation company,” Seth told Bloomberg this week, noting how it has grown rapidly and has strong institutional backing. “Its IPO will establish a market-clearing valuation as conditions stabilize.”
Signs to watch, not reasons to flee

With many investors already running for the hills, Rees isn’t convinced the AI bubble will burst in the way skeptics expect. She thinks they should watch for stronger signs that the AI trade is maturing.

This could be "a slowdown in AI-related revenues for companies, or signs of less demand or less appetite for financing companies’ AI plans, be it through debt or through equity offerings," Rees told DW.

There are early signs that investors have less appetite for AI-related debt. Borrowing costs for AI infrastructure firms like CoreWeave and Oracle have soared recently. Even the cost of insuring Nvidia’s debt against default has risen 76% in a month, CNBC reported last week.
"They [Oracle] have been spending, some people say, like drunken sailors," Dick told DW. "They’ve compromised their balance sheet to a point where the stock’s fallen 65% from the highs."
That has not stopped Oracle, along with Meta, Microsoft and Alphabet, from continuing to issue new AI bonds. Since the end of last month, the four AI giants have announced deals worth $67 billion.
Rees said another sign could be any new regulations that make it harder to build out US data centers.

This summer, New York and Texas temporarily paused new data center approvals. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat who takes office in January, wants new laws to stop data centers’ heavy power and water use from pushing up household bills.
Why US voters are fighting Trump's AI data center boom
Not 'different this time'

In his upcoming book "AI Mania: Blather, Bluster, and the Bubble of All Bubbles," economist Gary Smith compares the AI boom with earlier frenzies around railroads, automobiles, television and the internet. He warns of a "frightful crash" when the AI bubble eventually pops.

When the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, the tech-heavy Nasdaq stock market index lost nearly 80% of its value. Yet, previous bubbles have often lasted far longer than expected, making the timing of any crash hard to predict.
Joachim Klement, head of market strategy at UK-based investment bank Panmure Liberum, believes a reckoning could happen as early as next year.
"My core conviction is that the AI bubble will either burst in 2027 or in 2028, so sometime in the next two years,” Klement told Bloomberg last month.

articles.title: Iran says it destroyed US military radar in Bahrain in retaliatory strike
articles.summary:
First direct attack on US military installations for months was in response to US airstrike on communications tower

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it has targeted and…

blocks.text: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it has targeted and destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain – its first direct attack on US military installations for months – in response to a US airstrike on a communications tower in Sirik overlooking the strait of Hormuz.

“This is a serious warning to the aggressor enemy to end its aerial mischief and oil smuggling in the strait of Hormuz,” the IRGC said. “In the event of repeated violations and aggression, the IRGC aerospace force is on full alert to confront the enemy without constraint.”

Donald Trump has said in a series of media interviews over the past 24 hours that he will attack Iran only if necessary, claiming that Gulf countries such as Saudi Arabia have urged him to hold back from planned large-scale military strikes.
Trump announced that he had asked his vice-president, JD Vance, to end his interest in negotiating a new deal with Iran and instead focus on corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states.

Vance had been seen by the Iranians as the most trustworthy figure close to Trump, but they had rejected his request for a personal meeting with their negotiators to discuss the terms of a peace deal.

Vance has been in the forefront of Republicans saying the war led to the massive Republican losses in the midterms. Trump said he had been disappointed in the American public, since higher diesel prices was a small price to pay for preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.

An opinion poll in the UK shows 65% of the British public would oppose the US resuming the war in Iran, and only 14% would back it. The poll was conducted by YouGov for the Council for Arab-British Understanding (Caabu).
It also found 54% oppose UK bases being used by the US to mount attacks on Iran, with 29% in favour. Support for additional UK sanctions against Iran was found to be 45%, with 22% opposed.

The poll was conducted on Tuesday and Wednesday this week, before two Iranians were found guilty on Thursday of spying and planning attacks on journalists in the UK. The Iranian embassy has rejected the court judgment as an attempt to advance a political agenda.

Chris Doyle, the director of Caabu, said: “The British public are sceptical about any war on Iran and what it might achieve. What might make the Burnham government take note is the very high level of opposition to any further war amongst 2024 Labour voters, at 79%.”

Iran’s Assembly of Experts, a body of elected Islamic jurists responsible for choosing the supreme leader, has become the first governing institution in Iran to call for a review of the country’s defence doctrine, potentially leading to religious permission for Iran to try to acquire a nuclear weapon.

In a statement released on Thursday, the assembly called for reviewing Iran’s membership of the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, describing the move as an “unavoidable necessity” and a “public and national demand”.

The intervention carries a religious as much as political significance because the 88-strong assembly comprises senior clerics, most of whom are supposed to be qualified to exercise independent Islamic legal reasoning.

Iran has had a longstanding prohibition on nuclear weapons, based on a fatwa issued by the late supreme leader Ali Khamenei, but the relevance of the fatwa in the wake of the US attacks on Iran has been questioned widely inside political and security circles.
Whether Iran has the stockpiles of uranium or technology to build a nuclear weapon is contested.

The UN nuclear inspectorate has expressed alarm about a continued lack of information from Iran about its nuclear sites. It said: “Our concerns are growing over Iran’s refusal to allow access to design information or inspections of the Isfahan facility. We do not know the exact location of the Isfahan uranium enrichment facility or whether it contains nuclear materials. It is imperative that we carry out our verification activities in Iran without further delay.”

articles.title: Rosalía scoops historic third best album award at Latin Grammys
articles.summary: The Spanish singer is recognised for her fourth album Lux which was released last year to rave reviews.

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
Rosalía released her fourth album Lux last year to rave reviews
ByRiyah Collins
BBC Newsbeat
Spanish star Rosalía has made history as the first woman to win the best album award at the Latin Grammys three times, after being recognised for her project Lux.
The singer took home five trophies in total, including two for her track La Perla which was named song of the year and best pop song.
La Perla was also nominated for record of the year but missed out to Argentine singer Milo J's song Niño.

Rosalía released Lux last year to rave reviews and collecting her award at the ceremony in Las Vegas on Thursday, she said: "To all the people who told me I wasn't good enough, or that my music was too weird, I'm thankful I didn't listen."
The Barcelona-born artist then added: "Now I'm winning these prizes."
Rosalía, who opened the ceremony with a performance of some of her biggest songs, was honoured with the prize for best alternative music album.
She also picked up best shortform music video for her track Sauvignon Blanc.
The singer had previously won best album for El Mal Querer in 2019 and Motomami in 2022 - and her third Lux is also tipped to be a favourite when nominations are announced for the Grammys next week.

blocks.caption: Image caption, After a career spanning three decades, Daddy Yankee was recognised with a lifetime achievement award

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
After a career spanning three decades, Daddy Yankee was recognised with a lifetime achievement award
It was also a big night for Puerto Rican reggaeton legend Daddy Yankee, who won the person of the year award.
He performed some of his best-loved tracks including Gasolina and Con Calma, and was joined on stage by rappers including LL Cool J and French Montana.
Punjabi singer Diljit Dosanjh, who collabed with Daddy Yankee on Pokito, even took a break from his Aura India tour for the set, making him the first Indian artist to perform at the Latin Grammys.
Dosanjh superfan Devanshi Arora described the singer's appearance as "a cultural revolution".
"It's really invigorating and motivating to see someone from my country has made it all around the world," she tells Newsbeat.
She sees a lot of similarities between South American and Punjabi communities and hopes this leads to more collaborations - with a link-up between Dosanjh and Bad Bunny top of her wishlist.
Daddy Yankee was presented with the lifetime achievement award by Janet Jackson, who told him in Spanish that his music "has inspired an entire generation".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Diljit Dosanjh became the first Indian artist to perform at the Latin Grammys

blocks.text: Diljit Dosanjh became the first Indian artist to perform at the Latin Grammys
Accepting the prize for record of the year, Milo J seemed surprised to have won ahead of strong competition from Karol G, Jorge Drexler, Carin León as well as Rosalía.
The 20-year-old took home four trophies in the end and gave a shout out to Argentine folk music.
He described Niño as the song "I'm most proud of out of everything I've created so far".
"Long live Argentine folk music," he added.
Elsewhere, ARIA VEGA was named best new artist and songwriter of the year went to Sara Schell.
Additional reporting by Abu Bakar Yasin
